0.title: 2 Corinthians: Strength in Weakness
0.overview:
Second Corinthians is the most autobiographical of Paul's letters and, by many measures, the most emotionally raw document in the New Testament. Where Romans is a theological treatise and Galatians a polemical defence of the gospel, 2 Corinthians is a window into the interior life of an apostle under siege — attacked by opponents, misunderstood by the very church he founded, exhausted by suffering, and yet mysteriously sustained by a grace he cannot fully explain. It is the letter in which Paul most fully exposes the paradox at the heart of the Christian life: strength made perfect in weakness, treasure carried in jars of clay, life produced through death.

The letter was written from Macedonia, probably in AD 55–56, after a painful sequence of events: a “painful visit” to Corinth that went badly (2:1), a severe letter that followed (2:3–4; 7:8), anxiety about how the Corinthians would respond, and then the relief of Titus's report that most had repented (7:6–7). Paul writes in the aftermath of that partial reconciliation, addressing a church that has largely come back to him — but not entirely, since a group of opponents (often called the “super-apostles” or “false apostles”) still commands a following and challenges his authority.

The letter falls into four broad movements. Chapters 1–7 address the ministry of suffering and reconciliation: Paul defends the authenticity of his apostleship by pointing to suffering as its credential, not its disqualification, and unfolds a breathtaking theology of the new covenant ministry. Chapters 8–9 address the collection for the Jerusalem church — a sustained theology of generosity rooted in the self-giving of Christ. Chapters 10–13 are the “fool's speech,” Paul's sharp and ironic defence of his apostleship against the super-apostles, climaxing in the account of his thorn in the flesh and the word that defines the entire letter: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”

The letter's central theological contribution is its theology of weakness and glory. Paul's opponents measured apostleship by rhetorical skill, impressive presence, and spiritual fireworks. Paul measures it by the cross: authentic ministry looks like dying and rising, like carrying in the body the dying of Jesus so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested. This is not merely Paul's personal psychological coping; it is a fundamental claim about how the kingdom of God advances — through the cruciform shape of those who carry it.

1.title: The God of All Comfort and the Yes of Christ
1.overview:
The letter opens with one of Paul’s most sustained reflections on suffering — not suffering as a problem to be solved but as the very medium through which God works comfort and the apostle’s ministry becomes credible. The word “comfort” (paraklēsis) appears ten times in the first seven verses, announcing the chapter’s theme: God is the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort, who comforts in every affliction so that we may comfort others in their afflictions. Suffering and comfort are not opposites; they are the two sides of the same apostolic coin.

Paul then defends his apparently erratic travel plans — he had promised to visit Corinth twice, had not done so, and his opponents were using this as evidence that he was unreliable and untrustworthy. Paul’s response moves from the particular (his travel plans) to the universal (the character of God’s promises in Christ): all the promises of God find their Yes in Christ. The God who does not contradict himself in Christ does not contradict himself in Paul’s plans either. The apparent change of plans was not fickleness but pastoral mercy — Paul decided not to come in order to spare them another painful visit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The God of All Comfort
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The greeting situates Paul and Timothy as “apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God” (vv. 1–2) — a phrase that will become crucial in the letter’s defence of Paul’s ministry against those who question its legitimacy. The blessing that follows (vv. 3–7) is the densest concentration of the word paraklēsis (comfort/encouragement/consolation) in the entire New Testament: God is the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.

The logic is precise and important: Paul is not simply saying that suffering produces empathy. He is saying that the comfort God gives in suffering is not merely personal — it is transferable. It becomes the equipment for ministry to others. The suffering apostle is not a damaged vessel attempting ministry despite his wounds; he is a vessel prepared for ministry through them. This reframes the opponents’ attack entirely: they point to Paul’s suffering as evidence that God has not blessed his ministry; Paul says his suffering is the very mechanism by which God is equipping his ministry.

The Asiatic affliction of vv. 8–11 is one of the most dramatic personal disclosures in Paul’s letters: “we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.” He does not identify the specific danger (imprisonment? illness? a near-riot?), but he is explicit about the spiritual effect: he received the sentence of death in himself, so that he would not rely on himself but on God who raises the dead. The extremity of the suffering produced the depth of the trust.

The section then closes on two notes that are easy to hurry past. In v. 10 Paul says the same verb three times in three tenses — God delivered, will deliver, and will deliver again — so that memory of past rescue becomes the ground of confidence about the next one. And in v. 11 he tells a church four hundred miles away that their prayers were part of the machinery of his survival, and gives a startling reason for wanting them: not chiefly that he should be delivered, but that many should give thanks. The rescue is aimed at the volume of worship it will produce.
verseByVerse.theology:
The phrase “Father of mercies and God of all comfort” (ho patēr tōn oiktirmōn kai theos pasēs paraklēseōs, v. 3) is a carefully constructed title. Oiktirmōn (mercies) is the plural of the Hebrew rahamim — the compassions, the deep gut-level feeling of compassionate care (from the same root as rehem, womb). Paraklēsis (comfort) shares the root with paraklētos (Comforter/Helper — the title of the Holy Spirit in John 14–16). God himself, through the Spirit he sends, is the source and supply of all genuine comfort. No human comfort is ultimate; all genuine comfort is God’s own comfort mediated through creaturely means.

The suffering-comfort dynamic in vv. 4–7 is the pastoral theology of the cross applied to ministry. The wound is the credential. Those who have been comforted in their own affliction have something to give that those who have only known ease cannot supply. This is not a glorification of suffering for its own sake but a recognition that God wastes nothing — not even the darkest experiences of his servants.
verseByVerse.examples:
A pastor who has gone through a severe depressive episode returns to ministry and finds that his counselling of those suffering from depression has taken on a different quality. He is not simply applying techniques; he is giving what he has received. His people sense it. This is the dynamic Paul describes — not therapeutic expertise but the transferable comfort of one who has been there and been comforted by the God who is there.

And v. 11 puts the same dynamic in reverse. A member of the congregation who has never taught, never led and never travelled prays through the week for a missionary she has met once. Paul’s sentence says that her praying is not a gesture of support alongside the real work; it is a shoulder genuinely under the load. Churches that publish requests and never report the outcomes rob such people of the best half of it — the thanksgiving that Paul says was the point of the rescue in the first place.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every letter Paul wrote begins by naming himself, and the words he chooses are never decoration. Here they are the thesis of the whole letter compressed into six words: an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God.

Picture the room. The letter is being read aloud in a rented hall in Corinth, and the people listening are not united about the man who wrote it. Some love him. Some have been told, persuasively, by teachers with better credentials and a better manner, that Paul is unimpressive in person, weak, inconsistent, possibly a fraud. And the first thing they hear is a claim about where his commission came from. Not from a committee. Not from the church at Jerusalem. Not from the Corinthians themselves, who might therefore withdraw it. From the will of God.

That is not vanity. It is the only ground on which a servant of God can stand when the people he serves are weighing him. If his standing came from their approval, their disapproval would end it. Paul is about to spend thirteen chapters being misunderstood, and he begins by putting his authority somewhere his critics cannot reach it (cf. Gal. 1:1).

There is a practical edge to this that reaches well beyond apostles. Anyone who has served in a church for long has felt the ground move: the elder who is quietly criticised, the Sunday school teacher who overhears what a parent thinks, the pastor who discovers that a group has been meeting to discuss him. The temptation in that moment is to build a case — to gather evidence, to win the argument, to reclaim the room. Paul will do some of that later and hate every minute of it. But he starts somewhere else, and it is the right place to start: by the will of God. If God put you where you are, the room does not have the authority to remove you from it, and the room’s good opinion was never what was holding you up.

And Timothy our brother. Not my assistant. Timothy had been with Paul since the second journey, had been sent into the hardest situations, and is here given a name that levels rather than ranks. The man defending his own apostolic authority does not use that authority to elevate himself above the young man standing beside him.

To the church of God that is at Corinth. Read that again slowly, because the possessive is startling. This is the congregation that had split into factions, tolerated incest, sued one another in pagan courts, got drunk at the Lord’s Supper and quarrelled over spiritual gifts. It is the church of God. It belongs to him. It is at Corinth the way a ship is at anchor — located there, not owned there. Whatever a congregation is like on a bad Sunday, its deed of ownership is not in the hands of the people who spoil it.

With all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia. Achaia was the Roman province covering southern Greece — Athens, Cenchreae, and the scattered believers in between. The letter was meant to travel. That is worth knowing when the tone gets sharp in chapter 11: Paul knew that his most personal, most wounded words would be read out in villages he had never visited.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. A greeting so familiar that it slides past the ear. Slow it down. Grace is God giving what was not earned; peace is what grace produces when it lands — the war over, the account settled, the relationship restored. And they come from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, from both, out of one source, as naturally as water comes from a spring. Paul is about to write a letter soaked in tears. He opens it by wishing on his critics the two things he most needs himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has just been through the worst year of his life. He will describe it in a few verses as a burden beyond his strength that left him despairing of life itself. And the first thing out of his mouth is not a complaint. It is a blessing.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Jewish habit of prayer began this way — barukh attah Adonai, blessed are you, Lord — and Paul takes the ancient opening and fills it with the name of Jesus. The God he blesses is identified by his relationship to the Son. There is no access to the Father that goes round Christ, and no comfort in this chapter that is not finally the Father’s comfort reaching us through him.

Then two titles, and they are worth taking apart because they are the ground the entire chapter stands on.

The Father of mercies. The Greek is oiktirmoi — plural, mercies, compassions — standing behind the Hebrew rahamim, which comes from the word for a womb. It is not a legal term. It is the word for what a mother feels when her child is hurt: the involuntary lurch in the stomach, the movement toward the pain before any decision has been made. To call God the Father of mercies is to say that compassion is not something God occasionally does. It is something God fathers — every genuine mercy in the universe traces its paternity back to him.

And God of all comfort. The word is paraklēsis, and it will appear ten times in five verses. English has weakened it. We hear comfort and think of a warm drink and a soft chair — something that takes the edge off. The Greek is built from para (alongside) and kaleō (to call): it means to be summoned to someone’s side. It is the word for what a defence counsel does in a courtroom, what a friend does when he sits down on the edge of your bed at two in the morning. Its cousin is paraklētos, the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit in the upper room (Jn. 14:16). Comfort in this sense does not remove the trouble. It puts someone beside you in it, and the someone is God.

Notice the reach of the word all. Not the God of some comfort, or of religious comfort, or of the comfort that arrives once the crisis is over. Every real consolation you have ever received — the friend who said the right thing, the sleep that finally came, the verse that surfaced from nowhere at four in the morning, the hand on your shoulder in the corridor outside the ward — every one of them came out of his treasury. There is no other supplier. Those were not distractions from God while you waited for him to act. They were God acting.

And this is why the verse is a blessing rather than a complaint. Paul is not thanking God for suffering. He is blessing God for who God turned out to be inside it. A man can only write this sentence on the far side of something. The titles are not from a systematic theology; they are from the field. He found out.

Blessed be he, then. Not because the affliction was light — it was not, and he will say so. But because when the strength ran out there was Someone already alongside, whose compassion is not a decision he makes but a nature he has, and whose supply of consolation had no visible floor. The Father of mercies. The God of all comfort. He has never once been found to be less than his names.

verseByVerse.quote: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the sentence that governs the letter, and its most important word is the little phrase in the middle: so that.

Who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.

Read it as a chain and count the links. God comforts us. That comfort makes us able. What we then give away is not our own invention but the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God — the same substance, handed on. Comfort in this verse behaves less like a private consolation and more like water in a bucket line: it is given to you in order to be passed along, and the God at the head of the line has more.

Two words are worth pinning down. Affliction is thlipsis, from a verb meaning to press or crush — the pressure of a weight, not the sting of a scratch. And notice the two adjectives Paul pairs with it. God comforts us in all our affliction so that we can comfort those in any affliction. The comfort received in one kind of trouble is transferable to another kind. The woman who was carried through a bereavement is not disqualified from sitting with the man losing his business. What she has to give is not a technique specific to grief. It is God.

Which answers the objection almost every Christian raises at this verse, usually silently. I have nothing to offer. I do not know what to say. I have never been through what she is going through, and the people who have will do it better. Paul’s logic dismantles that. The qualification is not that you have suffered the same thing. The qualification is that you have been comforted by God, and the currency you hand over is his, not yours. You are not being asked to be wise. You are being asked to be there, with what you were given.

Here is a test you can run tonight. Think of the hardest stretch you have lived through — the diagnosis, the redundancy, the marriage that nearly went, the year you could not pray. Now ask: who got the benefit of it? If the honest answer is nobody, this verse says something has been left in the bucket. God did not comfort you merely so that you would feel better. He comforted you so that you would be able — and the ability he built in you is currently sitting unused while somebody two rows behind you on Sunday is going through it now.

There is a hard implication in the other direction too, and it is worth naming honestly rather than letting the reader work it out and feel cheated. If comfort is given to be passed on, then some of what God allows into your life is allowed for someone else’s sake. That is a costly thought and Paul does not soften it; he will say it outright in verse 6. It does not mean your suffering is only instrumental, as though you were a training exercise for somebody else’s benefit. It means that nothing in it will be wasted — not the sleepless nights, not the questions you could not answer, not even the months you handled it badly. God is not merely repairing you. He is equipping you.

And this is precisely what Paul’s opponents could not see. They looked at a beaten, imprisoned, shipwrecked man and concluded that God was plainly not blessing his ministry. Paul looks at the same evidence and says: this is not the damage to my ministry, this is the making of it. The wound is the credential (cf. 2 Cor. 12:9).

verseByVerse.quote: For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.

Paul now tells us where the comfort of verse 4 comes from, and the answer raises a question that every careful reader ought to ask. In what possible sense does a Christian share in the sufferings of Christ? Did the cross leave something outstanding?

Take the hard question head on, because a vague answer here does real damage. The New Testament is emphatic that the atoning work of Christ is finished and unrepeatable. He offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins (Heb. 10:12); at the end he said It is finished (Jn. 19:30). Nothing you suffer adds a gram to the payment for your sin, and any teaching that suggests otherwise has cut the ground from under the gospel. When Paul speaks elsewhere of filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions (Col. 1:24), he is not topping up the atonement. He is saying that the sufferings of the Messiah continue to spill over into the age of the church through the people who carry his message.

So what is being shared? Look at how the risen Christ addressed Saul on the Damascus road: not why do you persecute my followers but why do you persecute me? (Acts 9:4). The Head feels what happens to the body. When Paul is flogged for preaching Jesus, the blows fall on a member of Christ, and Christ counts them as his own. That is the sharing. It is not that our pain completes his; it is that his life has been so joined to ours that our pain is drawn inside his.

Two things follow, and both are the kind of thing a suffering believer needs at three in the morning.

First, the arithmetic is exact. The word rendered share abundantly is used on both sides of the sentence — the sufferings overflow, and so does the comfort. Whatever the measure of the one, the other is poured at the same rate. That is not a promise that the pain will be small. It is a promise that it will never outrun the supply. If the flood rises, so does the boat.

Second, the channel is named: through Christ. The comfort does not arrive from a distance, dispatched by a God who has heard about suffering. It comes through the one who was in it — whose friends fell asleep while he prayed, who was misrepresented at his trial, who was abandoned by the people he had healed, and who cried out that God had forsaken him. There is no experience of yours that he learned about second-hand.

Not every hardship qualifies as sharing in Christ’s sufferings; a broken leg is a broken leg, and Paul is speaking specifically of what comes upon a person for the sake of Christ. But do not draw that line too tightly. Paul is not building a hierarchy of holy pain. He is telling a church that despises weakness that the sufferings of their apostle are not evidence against him — they are the family likeness.

And look what that does to the cross. It was not simply an event that happened once and was banked. It is a shape, and the Lord who bore it has bent the whole life of his people into conformity with it, so that dying and rising is not an interruption of the Christian life but its rhythm. He goes first into every dark place his people are asked to enter, and he comes out. That is why there is comfort in the world at all.

verseByVerse.quote: If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.

This is one of the strangest sentences in the letter, and if it does not stop the reader it has not been read properly. Paul says that his afflictions are for the Corinthians. Not merely useful to them afterwards. For them. Aimed at their benefit.

Stand it up next to what was actually happening. The Corinthians were sitting in relative comfort, comparing their apostle unfavourably with more impressive teachers, and complaining about his travel arrangements. Paul was somewhere in Asia being crushed to the point of despair. And his reading of the situation is that the crushing was on their account.

How can that be? In two ways, and the verse gives both.

The first is the one we have already met: what he receives in affliction he hands on. He is being taken through it so that he will have something real to give them, which is why the sentence works just as well the other way round — if we are comforted, it is for your comfort. Both halves of his experience are theirs. His bad years are their supply.

The second is nearer the surface than we notice. A watching church learns what the gospel can carry by seeing what it carries a man through. Doctrine held under no pressure teaches nothing. When the Corinthians heard that Paul had been beyond his strength and had not let go of Christ, they were being handed evidence about the strength of the one he was holding. That is why he adds and salvation — not that his suffering saves them, but that it is part of the means by which God keeps them in the faith they were saved into.

Then the last clause, which does not flatter them: which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer. There is a condition here. The comfort is not received by studying Paul’s hardships from a safe distance. It is received in the place where the same pressure is bearing on you. A spectator gets nothing from this verse. A sufferer gets everything.

The word for patiently endure is hypomonē — literally a remaining under. Not gritted teeth and not resignation, but staying put under a weight instead of crawling out from under it. The comfort of God is not found by the man who has arranged his life to avoid all pressure. It is found by the one who stayed.

There is a quiet dignity being handed to ordinary Christians here, and it deserves saying plainly. Most believers will never be flogged for the gospel. They will be passed over at work for being honest, or lose a friendship over what they believe, or carry a chronic illness for thirty years without much notice being taken. Paul’s phrase is the same sufferings. He does not put his own martyrdom-grade trials in one category and their smaller griefs in another. Whatever is borne under the pressure of belonging to Christ belongs to the same stock, and draws on the same comfort.

So the arrangement is this. God afflicts his servant; the servant receives comfort; the church receives the comfort through him; and in receiving it under their own pressure, they are held. Nobody in that chain is a bystander, and nothing in it is wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.

Paul has been describing what suffering does. Now he says what he expects it to produce in them, and the word he reaches for is startling: unshaken. The Greek is bebaia — firm, secured, the word used of a legally binding contract or an anchor that holds. His hope for this church is not a wish. It is a settled expectation.

Consider who he is talking about. This is the congregation of 1 Corinthians. He has had to write to them about lawsuits, incest, drunkenness at the Lord’s table and factions formed around preachers. Since then there has been a visit so painful he cannot bring himself to repeat it and a letter written out of much affliction and anguish of heart. If any pastor ever had grounds for saying I have lost hope for that church, it is this one about this church.

And his hope for them is unshaken. Not because he has revised his opinion of their behaviour, and not because he is being polite. Read the reason he gives: for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort. His confidence is not in their track record. It is in the settled pattern of how God deals with his people — that he never takes anyone into the affliction without taking them through to the consolation. Paul is sure of them because he is sure of God.

That is a lesson worth learning for anyone who has given up on someone. Hope that rests on a person’s performance is shaken every time they fail, which is why so much Christian hope for other people is exhausted by about the third disappointment. Hope that rests on God’s character survives the failures, because it was never resting on the record in the first place. Who have you written off? The question is not whether they deserve better. It is whether the God who has not finished with you has finished with them.

Notice too the direction of the sharing. Twice now Paul has said that his sufferings are theirs, and here he adds that their sufferings are his. This is not a leader keeping a professional distance and managing a congregation. There is one experience running through both, and no clean line between the man in the pulpit and the people in the seats.

There is also a searching implication in the order of the clauses, and it should not be smoothed over. The sharing in comfort is promised to those who share in the sufferings. It is the same condition as the verse before. If a person has arranged a Christianity that costs nothing, he should not be surprised that it consoles nothing. The deepest comforts of God are not stored where the weather is fine.

But for those who are in it — who are in the middle of something now and cannot see the end of it — here is the promise, and it is stated as a certainty rather than a possibility. You will also share in our comfort. Not may. Will. The one who has never yet brought a child of his into affliction and left him there is not going to begin with you (cf. Ps. 30:5; Rom. 8:18).

verseByVerse.quote: For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.

Of all the sentences Paul wrote, this is among the ones the church has most needed and least expected. The apostle who wrote that we are more than conquerors, who told the Philippians to rejoice always, who sang hymns at midnight with his back opened by rods, here says in plain words that he came to the point of despairing of life itself.

Take the words as they stand. Utterly burdened renders a double intensifier — kath’ hyperbolēn, beyond all proportion, the phrase our word hyperbole comes from. Beyond our strength is hyper dynamin: past the limit of what he could carry. And despaired is exaporeomai — literally to be without a way out, at the end of every road, no exit visible in any direction. He is not saying that things were difficult. He is saying he could see no way he was coming out of it alive, and he stopped expecting to.

He does not tell us what it was. The riot in Ephesus recorded in Acts 19 is the usual guess; some think a near-fatal illness, others an imprisonment we have no record of. The silence is frustrating and it may be a mercy, because a named crisis would let the reader file it under somebody else’s category. As it stands, whatever is crushing you fits the gap.

Now hold this verse where it will do the most good, because there are readers for whom it is oxygen. There are Christians who have come to a place where they no longer wanted to be alive, and who have carried, on top of that darkness, the private conviction that a real believer could never get there. They have heard that despair is unbelief. They have concluded that whatever it is they have, it disqualifies them.

This verse takes that conclusion away from them. The man who despaired of life itself is the man who wrote Romans 8. He was not backslidden when it happened; he was in the middle of the most fruitful ministry in Christian history. He was not weak in faith; he was an apostle. And he was not ashamed of it afterwards — he wrote it down, in a letter, to a church that already thought he was too weak, knowing they would read it aloud.

Scripture has more of this than we usually admit. Elijah sat under a tree and asked to die (1 Kgs. 19:4). Jeremiah cursed the day he was born (Jer. 20:14). Job did the same. The psalmist wrote that darkness was his closest friend (Ps. 88:18) and God put it in the hymnbook. And in Gethsemane the Lord himself said that his soul was very sorrowful, even to death (Mk. 14:34). The Bible does not hand us a faith that floats above the water. It hands us a faith that has been to the bottom.

So if that is where you are: you are not outside the faith, and you are not the first one here. The blackness is real and this verse does not pretend otherwise — note that Paul never says he was mistaken about how bad it was. What it says is that this place, too, has been walked by the saints, and that the next verse is about to explain what God was doing in it. There is a next verse. That is rather the point.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.

The first sentence darkens the picture before the second lifts it. The sentence of death is to apokrima tou thanatou, and apokrima is a legal word: the official answer of a court, the verdict handed down. This is not a mood. It is a man who has heard the judgment read out and knows the appeal has failed. Inside himself, the case was closed.

Then comes the word that turns the whole letter, and it is one of the smallest in the sentence: but that was to. There was a purpose. The thing had a design.

This is the point at which honest readers need care taken with them, so let it be said carefully. Paul is not saying his suffering was pleasant, or light, or that he understood it at the time. He is not saying that every affliction comes with an explanation attached, and he is certainly not handing us a sentence to say breezily at a funeral. He is saying, looking back, that the crushing was not random. It was aimed. And the target was his self-reliance.

Consider what it takes to reach that target in a man like this. Paul was formidable. He had the training, the languages, the stamina, the courage, the intellect, the personal history with the risen Christ. If anyone had resources to fall back on, he did. And that is exactly the problem, because a man with resources will use them, and will keep on using them, and will never in his life discover what God can do at the point where the resources are gone. There was no way to teach Paul this except to take him past the end of himself.

So here is the test, and it is uncomfortable. Where does your confidence actually rest? Not the answer you would give in a Bible study — the answer your body gives at three in the morning. When the letter arrives, what do you reach for first? The savings, the contacts, the plan, the argument you have rehearsed? There is nothing wrong with any of those, and God gave them. But if you have never once been past the end of them, then you do not yet know from experience whether the God you profess actually holds. Paul knows. It cost him everything he had to find out.

And notice the name he gives God at the moment of extremity: not the God who prevents death, not the God who explains death, but God who raises the dead. That is a very deliberate choice of title. If the verdict of death has been passed and cannot be appealed, then what you need is not a rescuer who gets you off the charge. You need a God whose power operates on the far side of the sentence being carried out. And that is the God Christians have. Paul is not comforting himself with the thought that he will probably survive. He is resting on the fact that whether he survives or not, the God he serves has already emptied one tomb and has publicly committed himself to emptying the rest (cf. Rom. 4:17; 1 Cor. 15:20).

That is the ground floor beneath every Christian who has run out of options. When there is nothing left to rely on, there is still the God who raises the dead — and he does his best work precisely there. He did not begin the world’s salvation from a position of strength but from a sealed grave in a garden, with the case closed and the verdict carried out. Death is not the place where his power stops. It is the place where it was displayed.

verseByVerse.quote: He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.

Three tenses of the same verb in one short verse: he delivered, he will deliver, he will deliver again. Past, future, and future once more, as if Paul cannot say it enough times.

The word is rhyomai — to snatch out, to drag someone clear of danger. It is what a man does when he pulls a child out from under a falling wall. And notice that Paul’s memory and Paul’s expectation are wired together. Because God did it, God will do it. The past tense is not nostalgia; it is evidence, and the evidence is what his hope is built on.

This is one of the most practical habits in the Christian life and one of the most neglected. We are creatures with astonishingly short memories for mercy. We can be delivered in March and be certain by August that God has abandoned us, because we never wrote March down. The Israelites did this on a national scale for four hundred years. Paul does the opposite: at the moment he most needs confidence about the future, he goes back and looks at what has already happened. What has God already carried you through that you would have sworn at the time you could not survive? That is not sentiment. That is data, and it is admissible.

But now the harder question, and it must not be dodged, because a reader will hit it within seconds. What about the times he does not deliver? Paul himself, writing this, has perhaps seven or eight years left before a Roman sword ends his life. The deliverance he is so sure of did not, in the end, keep him out of Nero’s hands.

The answer is in the title he used one verse earlier. The God he is trusting is God who raises the dead, and a God like that has a wider definition of rescue than we do. Paul says as much to Timothy at the end: The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom (2 Tim. 4:18) — written from prison, weeks before his execution. He did not mean he expected to be released. He meant that the sword would be the last thing that ever happened to him, and that on the far side of it he would be safe. Deliverance is not always deliverance from; sometimes it is deliverance through. Not one child of God has ever failed to arrive.

So do not read this verse as a guarantee that the scan will be clear or the job will be saved. Read it as the promise it actually is: that nothing will take you out of his hand, and that whatever it costs to get you home, he will pay it (cf. Jn. 10:28).

On him we have set our hope. The verb is in the perfect — a decision made that is still standing. Not a hope he feels when circumstances allow, but a stake driven into the ground, still there in the morning. Paul had put his weight on God before the crisis and he has not shifted it since.

And it is worth seeing what has happened to a man over the course of eight verses. He began crushed beyond his strength and expecting to die. He ends certain that he will be delivered again. Nothing in his circumstances has changed between verse 8 and verse 10. What has changed is what he is looking at.

verseByVerse.quote: You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.

Paul has just described a deliverance so far beyond his own resources that he had already written himself off. And then he tells a church four hundred miles away that they have work to do in it.

The verb translated help is a vivid one — synypourgeō, to work underneath alongside, the picture of several people getting their shoulders under the same load. It is not a request for good wishes. Paul is treating the prayers of ordinary Corinthian believers as genuine labour applied to his actual survival.

Which raises the question every thinking Christian asks about prayer and usually never gets answered from a pulpit. If God had already decided to deliver Paul, what did the praying change? And if the praying changed it, is God being steered by us?

The answer Scripture gives is not that God is persuadable, but that he is generous. He ordains the end and he ordains the means to it, and he has chosen to make the prayers of his people one of the means. A father who could carry the box himself asks the four-year-old to take the other end, and the child really is carrying it. Nothing is being pretended. The father has arranged a world in which the child’s effort genuinely bears weight, because he wants the child in the work and not merely watching it. So it is here: the deliverance was God’s from first to last, and it came through the prayers of many, and both halves of that sentence are true.

What follows is worth pausing over, because Paul’s reason for wanting their prayers is not the one we would give. He does not say so that I will be delivered. He says so that many will give thanks. The point of the rescue, in his mind, is the volume of worship it will generate. Every person who prayed for him becomes a person who will hear that it was answered, and every one of those becomes a voice raised in thanksgiving. He wants the prayer list long because he wants the choir large.

That reorders something in most of us. We tend to ask for prayer so that our situation will improve; the thanksgiving afterwards, if it happens at all, is a private postscript. Paul is thinking the other way round. God’s answer to a request is not the end of the transaction — it is the raw material of praise, and the more people involved in the asking, the more glory comes back to God in the getting.

Two things follow for ordinary church life, and neither is small. The first: tell people what to pray for, and then tell them what happened. A congregation that hears the requests and never hears the outcomes is being robbed of the best half. The second: if you have prayed for someone and never learned the result, you have a thanksgiving still owed and unpaid.

And notice, finally, what this does to the smallest member of that church. Somewhere in Corinth there was a believer with no gift anyone could name, no money, no standing, who had never travelled further than the harbour. Paul’s sentence puts that person’s shoulder under an apostle’s survival in Asia. There are no bystanders in the kingdom. The work of the church is done by people whose names are not recorded, and the God who keeps the record has never once mislaid one of them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–24 — The Yes of God in Christ and Paul’s Changed Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul defends his integrity against the charge of fickleness (v. 12). His conscience, he says, testifies that he has conducted himself with simplicity and godly sincerity — not by worldly wisdom but by the grace of God. His letters say what they mean; there is nothing hidden between the lines (vv. 13–14), and where understanding is only partial now, he sets the final vindication on the day of our Lord Jesus, when he and they will boast of one another.

The specific grievance surfaces in vv. 15–17: he had planned to visit Corinth twice, on the way to Macedonia and again on the way back, and the plan changed. His opponents used the broken itinerary as a brick in a larger case about his character — he vacillates, therefore he cannot be trusted, therefore neither can his gospel. Then comes the great theological pivot (vv. 18–19): the question of Paul’s reliability points to the question of God’s reliability. Paul did not waver the way a person waffles between yes and no, “because the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes.”

All the promises of God find their Yes in Christ — and through Christ they find their Amen, to the glory of God (v. 20). This is one of the most compressed and important statements about Christ and the Old Testament in the entire Pauline corpus: every promise has been fulfilled in Christ, every divine commitment ratified through him. The assurance that the Yes includes the believer is then grounded in four acts of God in vv. 21–22 — he establishes, anoints, seals, and gives his Spirit as a down payment.

Only at the end (vv. 23–24) does Paul give the real reason for the change of plans, and he gives it under oath: he stayed away to spare them. A second painful visit would have meant discipline exercised in person on a church only half repentant. The man accused of unreliability had in fact been protecting the people filing the complaint — and he immediately guards against sounding like a lord withholding punishment: “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy.”
verseByVerse.theology:
“All the promises of God find their Yes in him” (v. 20) — hosai gar epangeliai theou, en autō to nai. This is the hermeneutical key to the entire OT: every promise — to Abraham, to Moses, to David, through the prophets — is fulfilled in Christ. Not some promises, not the specifically messianic ones, but all of them. This does not mean every OT text is directly about Jesus; it means the entire trajectory of divine promise reaches its destination in him. The “Amen” that believers add in worship (dia autou to amēn) is their ratification of what God has already declared: yes, it is so, in Christ.

The Trinitarian shape of vv. 21–22 is worth noting: God establishes (the Father), anointed (chrisas — sharing the root with Christos), and sealed with the Spirit, giving the Spirit as a deposit (arrabōn — the down payment guaranteeing the full inheritance, as in Eph. 1:14). The three persons are active together in the believer’s assurance.
verseByVerse.examples: A church member accuses her pastor of inconsistency when he changes a ministry plan he had announced. He is tempted to defend himself by cataloguing the reasons. This passage suggests a different approach: the goal is not to vindicate the decision but to demonstrate that the change came from genuine care for those affected — the same reason Paul stayed away from Corinth. Integrity is not the absence of changed plans; it is the transparent, godly motivation behind all decisions, including the changes.

verseByVerse.quote: For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you. For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand— just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you.

The tone changes here. Paul turns from what God has done in his suffering to what his critics have been saying about his character, and the charge behind these verses is that he is a man who cannot be trusted — that his letters say one thing and his intentions are another, that there is a hidden Paul behind the written one.

His answer begins with a word that ought to make us uneasy: boast. It will run through the whole letter (it appears some twenty-nine times) and it will eventually turn into open sarcasm in chapters 10 to 12. Paul knows perfectly well that boasting is a sickness; he has already told this church that if anyone boasts he should boast in the Lord. But when a minister’s integrity is being publicly dismantled, silence is not humility. It leaves the people he serves with no ground to stand on. So he speaks, and he is careful about what he claims.

What he claims is the testimony of our conscience. Not the verdict of the Corinthians, which is currently divided, and not his own self-assessment, which he elsewhere says proves nothing (1 Cor. 4:3–4). Conscience is the internal witness that watches what we actually do when nobody is looking, and Paul’s is not accusing him.

Two words describe how he has lived. Simplicity is haplotēs — singleness, the state of being one thing rather than two. Its opposite is the double life: the man in the pulpit and the different man in the car afterwards. And godly sincerity is eilikrineia, a word the ancients loved to derive from sunlight and judging — something held up to the light to see whether it is flawed all the way through. Roman potteries were known to fill cracks in inferior pots with wax and polish over them; hold the pot to the sun and the wax showed. Paul is saying: hold my ministry to the light. There is no wax.

Then the crucial qualifier, which keeps this from being self-congratulation: not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God. He does not claim to have generated his own integrity. He is boasting about something he received.

For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand — just as you did partially understand us — that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.

Here is the specific accusation answered. There is nothing between his lines. What the letter says on the surface is what he means underneath, and there is no code, no manipulation, no second layer for the initiated. Anyone who has been on the receiving end of a message that had to be decoded — from a colleague, a relative, a leader — knows what a rare and restful thing this is. Plain speech is a form of love, because it refuses to make the other person guess.

And notice how far ahead he is looking. Partially they understand him now, and that partial understanding is painful; but he sets his hope on the day of our Lord Jesus, when the misunderstanding will be finished on both sides. On that day, he says, they will boast of him and he of them — mutual pride, all the accusations dissolved.

That is worth holding if you are living inside a relationship where you have been misjudged and cannot fix it. Some misunderstandings do not get resolved in this life; some people will go to their graves with the wrong idea of you, and no amount of explaining will shift it. Paul, an apostle, could not clear his name in Corinth by writing about it. What he does instead is put the date of the hearing in the future and leave it there. There is a day coming when everything hidden is brought to light (1 Cor. 4:5) — and on that day the vindication will not be yours to arrange, which is precisely what makes it worth waiting for.

verseByVerse.quote: Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace. I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea. Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace. I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea.

Now we get the actual grievance. It sounds almost too small to have generated three chapters of self-defence: Paul had announced a travel plan and had not kept to it.

The plan was generous. Corinth twice — on the way north to Macedonia and again on the way back — instead of the single visit they had expected. He calls it a second experience of grace, which tells us what he thought a visit from an apostle was for: not an inspection, a gift. Then the itinerary changed, and by the time this letter is written the double visit has not happened at all.

It seems trivial. It was not, and it is worth understanding why, because the same dynamic operates in churches now. Paul’s opponents were not really interested in his diary. They were building a case about his character, and a broken travel plan was the most available brick. The pattern is familiar: a small verifiable failure is seized on, not for its own sake, but because it can be made to stand for a large unverifiable one. He changed his plans, therefore he is unreliable; he is unreliable, therefore his gospel cannot be trusted either.

Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say Yes, yes and No, no at the same time?

Two questions, both expecting the answer no. Vacillating translates a word suggesting lightness — the flightiness of a man whose word weighs nothing. And according to the flesh does not mean sinful appetite here; it means deciding the way a person decides who has no reference point beyond his own convenience. The doubled Yes, yes and No, no is the picture of a man saying both at once to different audiences, agreeing with whoever is in the room.

Underneath the specific charge lies a question worth answering plainly, since every Christian faces it. Is it a failure of integrity to change your mind?

Clearly not, or Paul is condemned by his own defence. Scripture nowhere requires that a plan once announced must be executed regardless of what has happened since. What it requires is that the reason be honest. The sin is not the changed plan; it is the changed plan made for self-serving reasons and then dressed up as principle. Paul will tell them in verse 23 exactly why he stayed away, and the reason turns out to be mercy toward them — the very people now complaining.

So here is the test to run on yourself when a commitment has to be dropped. Not can I justify this?, since almost anything can be justified given a few minutes. Ask instead: if the person affected could see my actual reasoning, would it look like care for them or convenience for me? That is the line between Paul and the man he is accused of being. And where the change costs somebody else something, say so out loud rather than letting it be discovered — which is exactly what Paul is doing here, in writing, to a church that has every reason to read it uncharitably.

The remarkable thing is that he takes the accusation seriously at all. He could have dismissed it as beneath him; an apostle does not owe the Corinthians his itinerary. Instead he explains himself, at length, to people who have not earned the explanation. That is what pastoral love looks like when it is inconvenient.

verseByVerse.quote: As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes.

Watch what Paul does here, because it is one of the most audacious turns in his letters. He is defending a change of travel plans. Within two sentences he is describing the character of the eternal Son of God. That is not evasion; it is the recognition that the two questions are finally one question. A messenger’s reliability is not a private matter about his diary. The people who heard the gospel from his mouth cannot easily hold that the man was double-tongued and the message was not.

So he stakes the answer on something larger than himself: as surely as God is faithful. God does not say one thing and mean another. And the Son who was preached in Corinth — by three named men, so this is not one man’s word — was not a figure of Yes and No. In him it is always Yes.

Then verse 20, which is one of the great summits of the New Testament and is often quoted without anyone noticing what it actually claims.

For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.

All of them. Not most, not the obviously messianic ones, not the ones about a coming king while the rest are left in the file. Every commitment God has ever made to his people has arrived at its destination in Jesus Christ.

Set that against the Old Testament and see the scale of it. God promised Abraham a land, a seed and a blessing that would reach every nation on earth — and centuries later Abraham’s descendants were a small, conquered, disappointed people, and the nations were not blessed. He promised David a son whose throne would never end — and the line of David finished in a blinded king led away in chains to Babylon. He promised through the prophets a new covenant, a cleansed heart, a shepherd, a return, a servant who would be pierced for transgressions. Century after century the promises accumulated and none of them were fully paid. Anyone reading the Old Testament and stopping at Malachi is looking at four hundred years of silence and an enormous outstanding balance.

Paul says the account was settled in one Person. The land, the seed, the blessing to the nations, the throne, the covenant, the cleansing, the shepherd, the servant — every one of them says Yes in Jesus Christ. He is not the recipient of the promises; he is the fulfilment of them, and the God who made them has never once said No.

This is why the church says Amen, and why the word is more than a signal that the prayer has stopped. Amen is a Hebrew word meaning it is firm, it is so, and it belongs on the human side of the transaction. God says Yes; the church says Amen. He makes the commitment; we countersign it. And even the countersigning is through him — we do not have the standing to say it on our own.

Take that into an ordinary week. The promise that God works all things for good, that nothing separates you from his love, that he will never leave you, that he who began a good work will complete it — on a hard Tuesday every one of those feels like it might be provisional, pending your performance. This verse says that all of them have already been answered Yes in Christ, and that the answer was given before you were born and does not come up for review.

And consider what that reveals about him. Every hope God ever raised in a human heart — every altar, every sacrifice, every prophecy, every unfinished story in the Hebrew Scriptures — was reaching toward someone. It reached him. There is no promise of God anywhere in the Bible that terminates somewhere other than in Jesus Christ; he is where the whole thing was always going. To him, therefore, the Amen, and the glory, for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.

Paul has just said that God’s promises are all Yes in Christ. The obvious question follows: how does an ordinary believer know that the Yes includes him? These two verses are the answer, and they are among the clearest statements of Christian assurance in the New Testament.

Notice first who is doing the work. It is God who establishes — every verb in the sentence has God as its subject and believers as its object. Nobody here is establishing himself. And notice the little phrase with you: Paul puts himself and his critics inside the same sentence, held by the same hands. Whatever else is unresolved between them, this is not.

Four things are said, and they build.

Establishes. The verb is bebaioō — the same root as the unshaken hope of verse 7, a legal word for confirming a contract so that it will stand up in court. It is in the present tense: not a thing God did once, but something he is doing continually. Your standing is being actively maintained, today, by someone other than you.

Anointed. In the Old Testament, oil was poured on the head of a prophet, a priest or a king to mark him out as set apart for God’s work. The word here is chrisas, from the same root as Christos — the Anointed One. Paul is saying that believers share in the anointing of the one they are named after. The office is no longer for a select few; every Christian has been marked out for God’s service. There is no such thing as a lay member of the body of Christ.

Sealed. A seal in the ancient world did two jobs. It marked ownership — sacks of grain and amphorae of wine were stamped with the merchant’s sign — and it guaranteed that the contents had not been tampered with in transit. Both meanings apply. The Holy Spirit in a believer is God’s stamp saying this one is mine, and his guarantee that what he has sent will arrive intact (cf. Eph. 1:13–14).

A guarantee. The word is arrabōn, a commercial term from the ancient Near East, and it is startlingly concrete. It means the down payment — not a sample, not a gesture of goodwill, but the first instalment of an agreed price, which legally binds the payer to hand over the rest. In modern Greek the same word is used for an engagement ring.

Sit with that for a moment, because it changes what the Christian life feels like. Whatever you have known of God — the moments when Scripture came alive, the peace that arrived from nowhere, the love for people you used to have no time for, the strange homesickness for a country you have never seen — that is not the whole payment. It is the deposit. And a deposit is not merely a promise of more; it is the same currency as the rest, paid early. What awaits you is not different in kind from your best hour with God. It is that, without the interruptions, for ever.

So here is the question to put to yourself when assurance is thin, and it is not the question we usually ask. We ask do I feel saved? — which is asking the weakest witness in the room. Ask instead: has God established, anointed, sealed and paid a deposit on someone he intends to abandon? The security of a Christian does not rest on the strength of his grip on God. It rests on four completed actions of God on him, and every one of them was taken while he was still at his worst.

And see the whole Trinity at work in one short sentence. The Father establishes; the anointing and the standing are in Christ; the Spirit is given as the deposit and the seal. Three persons, one operation, one purpose: that the people God has claimed should certainly arrive. He has never lost one, and he has staked his own name on the delivery.

verseByVerse.quote: But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I call God to witness against me — it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth.

At last the real reason. Paul stayed away, and it was not weakness, and it was not indifference. It was mercy.

He introduces it with an oath, which is not something he does lightly — I call God to witness against me, inviting divine scrutiny on his own motives and accepting the consequences if he is lying. The Corinthians could not see inside him. God could. It is a solemn way of saying: the reason I am about to give is the true one.

And the reason is that a visit would have been a confrontation. There had already been one painful visit, and another would have meant discipline exercised in person on a church only half repentant. He did not want that for them. So the man accused of being unreliable turns out to have been protecting the very people who were filing the complaint, and could not say so at the time without making it worse.

There is a whole ministry philosophy buried in that. It is often easier to confront than to wait. Confrontation feels decisive, and it discharges the tension in the person doing it. Paul chose the slower, more humiliating road: absorb the criticism, let them think what they will, and give the situation time to ripen. Anyone who has held back a hard conversation for the sake of the other person, and been thought cowardly for it, is standing where Paul stood.

Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.

He seems to catch himself. Talk of sparing them could sound like a man describing the punishment he graciously withheld, so he corrects the impression immediately, and in doing so gives the New Testament one of its sharpest statements on spiritual authority.

Lord it over is kyrieuomen — to exercise dominion, to act as lord. The same verb Jesus used of the rulers of the Gentiles when he told his disciples that it would not be so among them (Mk. 10:42–43). Note carefully what Paul disclaims dominion over: your faith. He has apostolic authority; he does not pretend otherwise, and he will use it in chapter 13. But it does not extend to standing between a believer and God.

This needs saying plainly, because it has been ignored with great damage. There are churches where a leader’s approval functions as the measure of a member’s standing with God; where questions are treated as rebellion; where major life decisions require clearance; where people are told that to leave is to leave the Lord. Every one of those is the thing Paul is refusing here. A minister who makes himself the gatekeeper of another Christian’s relationship with God has taken a place that is not his, and the New Testament calls it lording it.

What is offered instead is startling: we work with you for your joy. Fellow workers, on the same side of the table, and the goal is not compliance but gladness. Any authority in the church that produces fear rather than joy has misunderstood its own job description.

And the reason he gives is the most generous line in the chapter: for you stand firm in your faith. This is the church of the factions and the lawsuits, the one that has been listening to men who despise him. And his verdict on them is that they are standing. Not because they are impressive, but because they are held (cf. Rom. 14:4).

That is where the chapter comes to rest. Paul does not need to control them, because their faith was never resting on him. He planted, he watered, he wrote and he wept — and the one who keeps them upright is Christ, who has never yet let a believer fall out of his hand. The apostle can afford to be gentle, because the outcome was never in his keeping.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia:<sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>3</sup>Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,<sup>4</sup>who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.<sup>5</sup>For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.<sup>6</sup>If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.<sup>7</sup>Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.<sup>8</sup>For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.<sup>9</sup>Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.<sup>10</sup>He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.<sup>11</sup>You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.<sup>12</sup>For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you.<sup>13</sup>For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand—<sup>14</sup>just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.<sup>15</sup>Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace.<sup>16</sup>I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea.<sup>17</sup>Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?<sup>18</sup>As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No.<sup>19</sup>For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes.<sup>20</sup>For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.<sup>21</sup>And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us,<sup>22</sup>and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.<sup>23</sup>But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth.<sup>24</sup>Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.

2.title: Forgiveness, the Aroma of Christ, and the Triumph of God
2.overview:
Chapter 2 completes Paul’s account of his changed travel plans, addresses the situation of a specific offender in Corinth, and then rises to one of the most exalted passages in the letter: the image of God leading his apostles in triumphal procession, spreading the aroma of Christ everywhere. The movement from the particulars of Corinthian church discipline to the cosmic triumph of the gospel is characteristic of Paul — the mundane and the magnificent are always in the same letter, often in the same paragraph.

The offender in vv. 5–11 is almost certainly not the man of 1 Corinthians 5 (the incestuous man) but the person who had directly challenged and insulted Paul during the painful visit. The Corinthians had punished this person; Paul now urges forgiveness and reaffirmation of love — not as a relaxation of discipline but as its completion. Discipline without restoration is not discipline; it is punishment. The goal was always restoration, and the goal has been reached: the punishment is sufficient, the person should be forgiven and comforted, and the failure to forgive would give Satan an advantage.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Severe Letter and Forgiveness of the Offender
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul explains why he chose to write a severe letter rather than make another painful visit (vv. 1–2): he did not want to cause grief to those who should be his joy, and he says the disarming thing that they are the only people who can make him glad. He writes of anguish and tears (vv. 3–4) — his own emotional cost in writing that letter. He was not writing to cause pain but out of the abundance of his love for them. The severe letter was an act of love, not punishment.

Now the situation has changed. The offence, he insists, was not chiefly against him but against the whole church (v. 5), and the offender has been punished sufficiently by the majority (v. 6). Paul’s instruction is precise: forgive him, comfort him lest he be swallowed by excessive sorrow (v. 7), and ratify your love for him publicly (v. 8). The purpose was never destruction but correction, and correction has been achieved.

Verse 9 gives the letter’s wider aim, and it is easy to hurry past: Paul wrote to prove them — to see whether a church that had received the gospel would act on it when acting was costly. The obedience being tested is not loyalty to Paul personally but obedience “in everything,” which is precisely where half-obedience always fails.

The failure to now extend forgiveness would give an advantage to Satan (vv. 10–11, pleonektēthōmen hypo tou Satana — be outwitted, swindled by Satan) — because unforgiveness in a church community is exactly the foothold the enemy exploits. Paul adds a phrase that is easy to overlook: “for we are not ignorant of his designs” (ta noēmata autou — his schemes, his thoughts, his strategies). The enemy’s primary weapon in a reconciling community is the refusal to forgive.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage teaches that church discipline has a defined goal: restoration, not condemnation. This is the consistent NT pattern: Matthew 18:15–20, Galatians 6:1, 1 Corinthians 5. Discipline protects the community and pursues the restoration of the erring member. When the discipline has achieved its purpose, continuing to withhold forgiveness becomes its own sin — a sin that Satan is actively happy to see, because it fractures the community and communicates to the world that the church’s gospel of forgiveness does not apply internally.
verseByVerse.examples: A church elder who was removed from office after a moral failure has spent two years in genuine repentance and restoration. The leadership has quietly re-engaged him in limited service; but a vocal minority insists that any restoration is a betrayal of those he hurt. This passage does not minimise the hurt — Paul explicitly says the offender has caused grief to some extent (v. 5). But it insists that the goal of discipline is always restoration, and that the refusal to forgive when repentance is genuine is not faithfulness; it is a gift to the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you.

The word another carries a whole episode in it. Somewhere between the writing of 1 Corinthians and this letter, Paul went to Corinth and it went badly — so badly that he cannot bring himself to describe it, and so badly that he will not risk repeating it. The Acts narrative says nothing about this visit. We know of it only because of the scar tissue it left in these chapters.

Piece the sequence together and the letter makes far more sense. Paul planted the church. He wrote 1 Corinthians. Then he made a short, unplanned crossing from Ephesus — the painful visit — during which someone in the congregation confronted and humiliated him publicly, and the church did not defend him. He went home. He then wrote a letter out of tears, which we no longer have, calling them to deal with the man. Titus carried it. Paul then waited, in agony, for news of how they had taken it. That waiting is what he is writing out of.

So the changed travel plans of chapter 1 turn out to have this behind them. He did not stay away because he was avoiding trouble. He stayed away because a second confrontation, arriving before they had had time to respond, would have destroyed something.

For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained?

This is one of the most disarming sentences in Paul, and it is worth reading twice, because what it exposes is that the apostle needs them.

His argument is simply this: you are my joy. There is no reserve supply. If I come and wound you, I have wounded the only people who can make me glad, and I will go home emptier than I came. A man who did not care could confront them and feel nothing. Paul cannot confront them without paying for it himself, because the people he would have to hurt are the people his happiness depends on.

Notice what that does to the picture of authority the Corinthians had been forming. They had been told he was a domineering figure who wrote fierce letters from a safe distance and was unimpressive in the room. Here he is telling them that they hold his gladness in their hands.

There is a searching question in this for anyone who has to speak hard truth to another person — a parent, an elder, a friend, a manager. Not am I right? Usually you are, and being right is the cheapest part of it. Ask instead: will this cost me anything? If a rebuke costs the person delivering it nothing, something has gone wrong upstream. It has become an exercise of position rather than an act of love, and the one receiving it can always tell the difference.

Real correction is expensive at both ends. That is why so little of it is done well, and why the little that is done well is remembered for a lifetime by the person who received it.

verseByVerse.quote: And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice, for I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice, for I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.

Here is the severe letter, and here is what it cost to write.

First, a word about what it was, because a reader who meets the phrase will want to know. Paul refers here and in 7:8 to a letter he wrote between 1 and 2 Corinthians, sent instead of a visit, dealing with the man who had wronged him. We do not have it. Some have suggested it survives as chapters 10 to 13 of this letter, or as the fragment at 6:14–7:1, but neither proposal fits well, and the straightforward reading is that it is simply lost. That is worth sitting with for a moment. The Spirit of God preserved every word the church would need and did not preserve every word Paul wrote. Scripture is not the complete archive of apostolic correspondence; it is what God intended his people to have.

Now look at the cost. Much affliction. Anguish of heart. Many tears. The word behind anguish is synochē — a pressing together, a constriction, the feeling of the walls closing in. He did not dash it off. He wrote it the way you write something at one in the morning after four attempts, with your hands shaking.

And he says plainly what the aim was: not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you. That sentence should be printed above every difficult conversation in the church. The letter caused pain — he does not deny it and will admit as much in chapter 7 — but pain was not the purpose. Love was the purpose, and the pain was the route it had to take.

Which gives an unusually clear test for anyone about to say a hard thing. Rebuke that comes out of anger wants the other person to feel what you feel. Rebuke that comes out of love wants the other person to be restored, and would gladly skip the whole episode if there were another way. The two can use identical words.
