Against that blindness Paul sets what he actually preaches (v. 5): “not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” The minister is not the subject of his own message; he is the doulos — the slave — of the congregation, and he is that for Christ’s sake, which is precisely what keeps his service from becoming flattery.

Then the counter-declaration (v. 6): God, who said “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. Creation and new creation are parallel: the same God who spoke light into primordial darkness speaks light into darkened human hearts.
verseByVerse.theology:
The identification of Christ as “the image of God” (eikōn tou theou, v. 4) is one of Paul’s most direct Christological statements, paralleled in Colossians 1:15. Christ is not merely like God or a representative of God; he is the very image — the precise visible representation — of the invisible God. To see Christ is to see God (John 14:9). The glory of God is concentrated in the face of Jesus Christ (v. 6) — not in theophanies or visions or mystical experiences, but in the specific person of Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen.

The parallel between Gen. 1:3 (“Let there be light”) and v. 6 (“God who said Let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts”) is one of the NT’s most striking statements about the nature of conversion: it is a creative act of God, analogous to the original creation. Regeneration is not human spiritual development; it is the same divine fiat that created light from nothing. This is the Reformers’ point: regeneration precedes and enables faith; it is not faith that produces the new birth but the new birth that produces faith.
verseByVerse.examples: A campus minister explains the gospel to a sharp philosophy student who has engaged with every argument and remains unconvinced. He is tempted to find a better argument. This passage suggests a different diagnosis: the issue may not be intellectual but spiritual — a blinding that no amount of superior argument can overcome. The appropriate response includes not abandoning the argument (Paul commends himself to the conscience) but adding sustained prayer for the God who speaks light into darkness to do so in this particular darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart. But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart. But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.

The therefore reaches back to the whole of chapter 3 — the covenant that does not fade, the veil removed, the glory that transforms. Everything in this chapter about weakness and wasting away is being said by a man who has just described what he has been given.

Two phrases before the main point. This ministry — the new covenant ministry, the staggering thing he has been describing. And by the mercy of God, which is how a man who had hunted Christians to their deaths accounts for holding such a commission. He never once speaks of it as an achievement.

Then: we do not lose heart. The verb is enkakeō — to grow weary and give up, to run out of nerve, to quit. He will say it again in verse 16, and the two occurrences bracket the whole passage. Everything between them is his answer to the question of why he has not stopped.

That is worth naming plainly, because losing heart is one of the commonest and least discussed conditions in the Christian life. It is not usually a crisis of doctrine. It is the slow arrival of a Tuesday on which you cannot see the point of continuing — the class you have taught for eleven years with nothing to show, the marriage you have prayed about since the children were small, the neighbour who is politely unmovable. Nobody announces that they have lost heart. They simply do slightly less, and then a little less than that.

Paul’s guard against it is not willpower. It is the sentence he has just written: this ministry is not his, and it came by mercy. A man carrying something he earned has to defend it, and will eventually be too tired to. A man carrying something he was given has a different relationship to his own exhaustion.

Then verse 2, and it is a striking list of things he has ruled out. Disgraceful, underhanded ways — literally the hidden things of shame, whatever a man would not want brought into the light. Cunning is panourgia, readiness to do anything, the word used of the serpent in Eden. And tamper with God’s word is doloō, a term from the trade in wine and precious metals: to adulterate, to dilute, to alloy. It is the sister of the peddler’s word in 2:17.

What does tampering actually look like? Rarely a denial. Usually a dilution: the doctrine kept but drained of force, the demand quoted but never pressed, the warning read out in a tone that says nobody here need worry. It also runs the other way — the verse hardened past what it says, used to control people. In both directions the operator has decided he knows better than the text what the text should do.

Against all of it Paul sets one method: the open statement of the truth. Say it plainly, in public, and let it do its own work on the conscience. No technique, no leverage, no management of what people are allowed to know. It is a slower way to build anything, and it is the only way anything gets built that will still be standing when the man who built it is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

Paul has just said he states the truth openly. The obvious objection follows at once: then why does it not work? Why do intelligent, decent people hear the clearest possible presentation of Christ and remain entirely unmoved?

His answer is not that the message needs improving. It is that there is a third party in the room.

The god of this world. The phrase is startling, and it needs care, because it must not be heard as though the universe had two gods in it. Paul has just written that there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things (1 Cor. 8:6). Satan is a creature; he was made, he is on a leash, and he has a date. What the title means is that he is the god people actually serve — the power this age treats as ultimate, worshipped in a thousand forms that never carry his name. Jesus called him the ruler of this world and said in the same breath that he would be cast out (Jn. 12:31).

And his method here is specific: he has blinded the minds. Not persuaded, not argued. Blinded. The verb is a single decisive act. He does not need to make people believe something false about Christ; it is enough that they cannot see him at all.

Now be careful with the pastoral use of this, because it can be turned into an excuse for laziness and it can be turned into cruelty. It does not mean an unbeliever is innocent — Paul calls them unbelievers, and blindness of this kind is never against a person’s will; it is the confirmation of a direction already chosen. Nor does it license writing anyone off; the man writing this was as blind as anyone has ever been, eight verses from a synagogue and armed with warrants.

What it does mean is that if you have explained the gospel to someone you love, patiently and well, and nothing has happened, you have not necessarily failed. You are not up against a shortage of argument. You are up against a blindfold, and blindfolds are not removed by better reasoning. That is why the same Paul who reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath also asked churches to pray for him, and why the campus argument that cannot be won should be followed home with intercession rather than a better book.

And notice what the blindfold is designed to prevent them seeing: the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. Four genitives stacked up, each opening into the next, and they arrive at a person.

The image of God — eikōn, the exact visible representation. Not a likeness, not a good approximation. Paul says the same to the Colossians: he is the image of the invisible God (Col. 1:15). And the Lord himself put it beyond argument to a disciple who wanted a vision of the Father: whoever has seen me has seen the Father (Jn. 14:9). The invisible God has made himself visible in one place only, and that place is a Galilean carpenter who was executed outside a city wall. That is the light the enemy is working so hard to keep from human eyes — and it is worth asking why he should trouble himself so greatly over one face, unless there really is nothing else to see.

verseByVerse.quote: For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.

One sentence, and it settles what a Christian minister is for.

Begin with the negative, because Paul evidently thought it needed saying. Not ourselves. That is a warning about the most natural drift there is. Nobody sets out to preach himself. It happens by increments — the illustration that makes the speaker look perceptive, the anecdote that establishes his credentials, the gradual discovery that a certain kind of story gets a certain kind of response. The message stays orthodox. The subject quietly changes.

It is worth being concrete about the modern shapes, since the ancient ones were different in dress only. The ministry organised around one personality. The teaching whose real content is the teacher’s experiences. The platform that requires a photograph. None of these declares itself; each one simply moves the light a few degrees until it is falling on the wrong face.

The test is not whether a preacher mentions himself — Paul mentions himself throughout this letter. It is what the hearer goes away thinking about. If people leave impressed with the man, something has gone wrong, however sound the doctrine was.

Then the positive: Jesus Christ as Lord. That was the earliest Christian confession, three words long, and it cost people their lives, because in the Roman world the sentence Caesar is Lord was the loyalty oath and only one of the two could be true. To say Jesus is Lord was to say that the emperor was not. It has never been a private religious preference. It is a claim about who is actually in charge.

And then the phrase that turns the whole thing: with ourselves as your servants. The word is doulos — not a hired helper but a slave, someone with no independent agenda. The apostle who has spent three chapters defending his authority now defines his relationship to the very people questioning him as slavery to them.

The order matters. He is not their slave because they are the customer and the customer is always right; he has just refused to trim the message for them. He is their slave for Jesus’ sake. His master sends him to serve them, so serving them is obedience to someone else, which is precisely what keeps his service from becoming flattery. A man who serves people for their sake alone will end up telling them what they want. A man who serves them for Christ’s sake will tell them the truth and stay.

And where did the shape of that come from? From a Lord who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mk. 10:45); who on the last night took a towel and washed the feet of the men who were about to abandon him. Authority in his kingdom runs downwards. He established it that way by doing it first, and no one has ever found a lower place than the one he took.

verseByVerse.quote: For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

Verse 4 said the mind is blinded. This verse says what God does about it, and Paul reaches all the way back to the first page of the Bible for the comparison.

Go back and stand there. The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. There is no dawn coming, because there is no sun. There is nothing to strike a light from and nobody to strike it. Whatever is going to happen must come from outside the situation entirely. And God said, Let there be light, and there was light (Gen. 1:3).

Paul says that is what conversion is.

Take the parallel seriously, because it decides how a person thinks about his own salvation and about everyone he is praying for. The darkness in Genesis did not cooperate. It did not reach toward the light, or make itself receptive, or take a first small step and get helped the rest of the way. It could not, and it was not asked to. Light arrived because God spoke, and the moment he spoke there was no darkness left to consult.

This is why the Reformed tradition insists that the new birth comes first and faith follows, rather than the other way round. It is not a piece of theological machinery imposed on the text; it is what this verse says. A blinded mind cannot decide to see. But when God says let light shine into a particular human heart, that heart will believe, as certainly as the deep filled with light on the first day.

Which takes the anxiety out of two things at once. First, your own standing: if the light in you was lit by God, then the flickering you are so worried about is not evidence against you, because you did not light it and you are not keeping it burning. Second, the person you have given up on. Nothing in their hardness is a problem for a God whose speciality is speaking into a void. He is not looking for a promising surface.

Then the destination of the light, and every word of the phrase is deliberate: the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

Not the knowledge of doctrine, though doctrine is how it comes. Not a light that shows you yourself, though it will. God’s glory has been given a location, and the location is a human face. Moses asked to see that glory and was told you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live (Ex. 33:20); he was put in a cleft of rock and shown the back of God going past. The thing Moses was refused is what has been given to ordinary believers.

And it is a face that was spat on, that had a crown of thorns pressed above it, that was turned toward Jerusalem and would not turn away. There is the glory of God — not in the fire on Sinai, not in the whirlwind, but in the face of a man dying for his enemies. Whoever has once seen it never quite recovers, and there is nothing else in the universe that repays looking at in the same way. Let light shine out of darkness. It did, and it does, and the darkness has never once been able to hold it out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Treasure in Jars of Clay
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (v. 7). The treasure is the gospel, the knowledge of the glory of God in Christ, the ministry of the new covenant. The jars of clay (en ostrakinois skeuasin) are the apostles themselves — fragile, disposable, cheap. In the ancient world, clay jars were used for storage and then discarded; they were the opposite of the precious vessels made of silver and gold. Paul deliberately applies the most dismissive vessel-image he can find to himself and his co-workers.

The purpose of the fragile vessel is explicit: to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us. If the vessel were impressive — if Paul were eloquent, physically imposing, healthy, successful, and unopposed — then the question of the power’s source would be at least ambiguous. The fragile vessel makes the power’s source unambiguous. This is the logic of the cross applied to ministry: the most obviously weak and foolish means is chosen so that no flesh can boast before God (1 Cor. 1:27–29).

Paul then lists the contrasts that fill out the jar-of-clay theology (vv. 8–9): afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not driven to despair, persecuted but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed. Each pair has the same structure: real difficulty + divine preservation. And then the deepest statement (v. 10): “always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies.” Verse 11 restates it with the emphasis moved to the body that ages and fails — the life of Jesus manifested “in our mortal flesh” — and v. 12 states the exchange at its starkest: “So death is at work in us, but life in you.” The death and resurrection of Jesus are not merely past events in Paul’s theology; they are the present pattern of apostolic ministry.

The section then names where the whole arrangement is heading. Because Paul believes, he speaks (v. 13), and because he knows the God who raised the Lord Jesus will raise him too (v. 14), suffering is investment rather than loss. And v. 15 gives the terminus: it is all for their sake, so that as grace reaches more and more people, thanksgiving increases — to the glory of God. The end of apostolic suffering is a rising volume of praise.
verseByVerse.theology:
The four contrasts in vv. 8–9 are not merely biographical observations; they are a theological programme. The pattern of affliction-but-not-destroyed is the pattern of the cross applied to the messengers of the cross. The phrase rendered “the death of Jesus” (tēn nekrōsin tou Iēsou, v. 10) uses a noun that means the process of dying, death-at-work, rather than the event. Paul is not saying that he dies as Jesus died, but that the same dying-of-Jesus that produced life for the world is at work in Paul’s ministry, producing life for the churches. The apostle’s weakness and suffering is the medium through which resurrection life is communicated. It is worth noting the honesty of v. 8: the verb behind “driven to despair” is the very word Paul used of himself in 1:8, where he says he despaired of life itself. He is describing the normal condition, not issuing an absolute guarantee.

Verse 13 — “I believed, and so I spoke” — quotes Psalm 116:10 in the Greek Old Testament, the psalm of a man who faced death and was delivered, who then declared that he believed and therefore spoke. Paul applies the psalm to the apostolic situation: even in the face of death, the minister speaks because he believes, and the faith of the psalmist and the faith of the Christian are shown to be one and the same pneuma. The resurrection of Jesus (v. 14) grounds this confidence — the same God who raised Jesus will raise us, and bring us with you into his presence.
verseByVerse.examples: A senior pastor of a large church steps down due to a serious health diagnosis and is replaced by a younger, more energetic successor. He struggles with the sense that his fragility is a disqualification. This chapter is addressed precisely to him: the jar of clay is not a disqualification from ministry; it is the precondition for God’s power being unambiguously visible. The question is not whether his vessel is strong enough but whether the treasure is still present — and treasure in a cracked jar leaks light rather than hiding it.

verseByVerse.quote: But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.

This is the sentence the whole letter turns on, and it is built out of the most ordinary object in the ancient world.

Jars of clay — ostrakina skeuē. Not the household’s good pottery. These were the cheap, unglazed, mass-produced containers used for oil, grain, water and refuse; they cracked, they chipped, they were thrown out and replaced without a thought. Archaeologists find them by the ton because nobody ever bothered to look after one. The word Paul uses is the root of ostracon, the broken shard people scribbled notes on because it was worthless.

Into that he puts this treasure — the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, straight from the previous verse. The most valuable thing in existence, stored in the container you would use once and discard.

It is not an accident and Paul says so: to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us. The mismatch is the point. Read it the other way and the logic is obvious. If the apostle had been physically imposing, magnetic, healthy, wealthy and universally admired, then when people came to Christ under his preaching the question of where the power came from would be permanently ambiguous. Some would credit God; many would credit Paul; and Paul himself, being human, would eventually have credited Paul. The cheap jar removes the ambiguity. Nobody looks at a cracked storage pot and concludes that the light is coming from the pottery.

This has enormous pastoral consequences, and they need saying plainly to the people who most need them.

If you have ever thought that your weakness disqualifies you — the health that limits what you can commit to, the temperament that makes you dread the door, the education you did not get, the failure everybody remembers, the age you have reached — this verse is aimed directly at you. Your fragility is not an obstacle God is working around. It is the design. He chose the container precisely because nobody would mistake it for the treasure.

And there is a warning folded into the comfort. A church, a ministry or a Christian can work very hard at not looking like a clay pot: the polished presentation, the projected confidence, the careful concealment of anything that might suggest struggle. The trouble is that the strategy succeeds. People are impressed, and being impressed is not the same as seeing God, and they go away thinking well of us. The gospel travels furthest through people who are visibly unequal to carrying it.

Consider how far this pattern goes. God had a Son to send and no shortage of options for how to send him. He chose a village nobody rated, a manger, a working man’s hands, and finally an instrument of execution reserved for slaves. The treasure has always come in the cheapest possible container, and the reason has always been the same: so that when the light gets out, there can be no argument about whose it is.

verseByVerse.quote: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;

Four pairs, hammered out in the same shape each time: a real blow, then a limit. Paul is describing what it is actually like to be a clay jar with a treasure in it.

Take them one at a time, because each pair says something different.

Afflicted, but not crushed. The first word is the pressing weight of thlipsis again; the second means squeezed into a corner with no room left. The pressure is real and total — in every way — but there is always still room to move. Not comfort. Room.

Perplexed, but not driven to despair. This is the most interesting pair in the list, and it is a small masterpiece of honesty. The two Greek words are the same verb, one of them intensified: aporoumenoi all’ ouk exaporoumenoi — at a loss, but not at an utter loss. And exaporeomai is precisely the word Paul used in 1:8 about the affliction in Asia, where he says he despaired of life itself. So he is not claiming that a believer never goes under. He has already told us that he did. What he is describing here is the normal condition, not an absolute guarantee: usually bewildered, not usually finished. Anyone who has been through the worse thing will notice that Paul does not pretend it cannot happen.

Persecuted, but not forsaken. The word is the ordinary one for being hunted or chased. Men pursue him; God does not abandon him. Behind it stands the promise repeated all through Scripture and quoted to nervous Christians ever since: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb. 13:5).

Struck down, but not destroyed. The picture is of a man knocked to the ground. He does go down. What does not happen is the finishing blow.

Now notice what this list does not promise, because misreading it has hurt people. It does not say a Christian will be spared affliction; all four blows land. It does not say he will feel calm; he is perplexed. It does not even say he will stay standing. It says something narrower and far more durable: that in every case there is a floor, and the floor holds.

Test it against your own history rather than against a theory. Think of the year you were sure you would not survive. You are reading this. That is not luck and it is not your resilience — you know how thin that was at the time. Something held, and it was not you.

There is one more thing to see, and it is the reason the list has this shape. Paul is describing his own life in the pattern of somebody else’s. His Lord was afflicted, perplexed in Gethsemane, persecuted from Bethlehem onwards, struck down at Calvary — and in his case the last blow fell. He was crushed. He was forsaken; he said so out loud in the dark. He was destroyed, and buried, and the stone was rolled across.

Which is why there is a floor under his people. The one place the sequence ran all the way to the end, it ran to the end for us — and came back out on the third day. Every but not in this list was bought at a cross where there was no but not at all.

verseByVerse.quote: always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.

Paul now names what the four blows amount to. This is not simply a hard life. It is the death of Jesus being carried about in a human body.

The word behind death here is nekrōsis, and it is worth knowing that it means the process rather than the event — the dying, the putting to death, death at work. Paul is not saying he re-enacts Calvary. He is saying that the dying which happened once to Jesus is somehow still operating, and that it is operating in him.

And notice always, twice. Not in seasons of persecution. Continuously, as the settled condition of the life.

Then the purpose, also twice: so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested. The verb means to be made visible, brought into the open. Here is the mechanism at the heart of this whole letter. The dying is not the price paid for the ministry; it is the medium of it. Resurrection life becomes visible in a human being at exactly the points where that human being is being emptied out.

Which is why it is nearly always the wrong question to ask why God has not removed the difficulty. Watch where people actually see the life of Jesus. Not in the Christian whose life has gone well; there is nothing to explain there, and the world explains it easily. They see it in the man who lost the job and did not become bitter. In the widow who still sings. In the couple who buried a child and are still in church, still kind, still able to sit with someone else who is grieving. Something is showing through, and it is not personality, because personality does not survive that.

Then the second half of the pair changes the wording in a way that repays attention: in our mortal flesh. Not in some spiritual compartment. In the body that gets tired, ill and old. The place where the dying is most obvious is the place where the life is to be displayed.

Notice too the phrase being given over to death. It is passive, and in Paul the passive normally has God behind it. He is not merely suffering the consequences of a dangerous job. He is being handed over — the same verb used of Christ himself, delivered up for our trespasses (Rom. 4:25). Someone is administering this.

That should be said carefully, because it is not a sentence to be tossed at a person in fresh pain. But it is the truth Paul is living on. He is not the victim of circumstance. He is in the hands of a God who is doing something deliberate with a life, and who is not being careless with what it costs.

And it is a good deal easier to bear when you see whose pattern it is. He carried his cross through the streets before any of his people carried anything. The dying that is at work in them is his dying, and it is going the same way his did — through a Friday nobody could explain, to a morning nobody expected.

verseByVerse.quote: So death is at work in us, but life in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So death is at work in us, but life in you.

Nine words. Paul has said something like it before in this letter and he will say it again, but never this starkly.

The two halves are held apart deliberately: death here, life there. The apostle absorbs one and the church receives the other. His losses are their gains, and the transaction is not metaphorical — the beatings that took the skin off his back were the price of the gospel arriving in Corinth at all.

The verb translated at work is energeitai, from which we get energy: something operating, exerting force. Death is not merely present in Paul. It is busy.

Stop and consider what it takes for a man to write this to that church. They had questioned his credentials, compared him unfavourably with better speakers, and complained about his travel arrangements. He tells them that death is doing its work in him so that life can do its work in them, and he says it without a trace of self-pity or invoice. There is no after all I have done for you. It is simply the arrangement, and he is content with it.

The principle is far wider than apostles, and once you see it you will see it everywhere. Nearly everything good in your life came to you because it cost somebody else something. The parents who went without so there would be school fees. The missionaries who are buried in the country they went to. The believers who were burned so that the Bible could be read in English in an ordinary house. Whoever it was who prayed for you for years and died before it worked. Life in you; death in them. You are, all of you, standing on ground that was bought.

Which turns the question round. Whose life is your death producing? It is a hard question because most of us have arranged our lives to keep the cost low. But if the pattern of the kingdom is that death here produces life there, then a life that costs nothing is producing correspondingly little, and no amount of activity disguises that. The people whose ministry outlives them are almost always the ones who were spent.

Say it, though, without turning it into a lever. Paul is not shaming them into gratitude; this is not a bill. He is telling them how the kingdom moves, and he is glad to be where he is.

And he is glad because he did not invent the arrangement. He is standing inside it at second hand. There was a death that was at work in one man on one afternoon, and the life it produced runs out to every believer who has ever lived and will not be exhausted when the last of them is raised. Death is at work in us, but life in you — Paul only ever says at a small scale what his Lord did at the largest scale there is, and it is the deepest logic of the universe: someone goes down so that someone else comes up.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak, knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak, knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.

Paul has just said that death is at work in him. The obvious question is why he keeps talking. Here is the answer, and it comes in two parts: because he believes, and because of what he knows about the end.

The quotation is from Psalm 116, and the whole psalm is worth having in view. It is the song of a man who had been at the edge — the snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me — who called on the Lord and was heard. In the Greek version Paul used, the line runs: I believed, and so I spoke. The psalmist was in mortal danger and he opened his mouth about God anyway.

Paul says he has the same spirit of faith. Not the same opinions — the same disposition, the same instinct, the same inability to keep quiet. It is one of the clearest statements anywhere that the faith of the Old Testament saint and the faith of the Christian are the same thing, in the same Spirit, separated by a thousand years and no difference in kind.

And note the logic: we also believe, and so we also speak. Speech is not an extra that follows faith for the more confident sort of believer. It is faith surfacing. What a man truly believes will eventually get out of him, and when it does not, that is worth thinking about rather than merely regretting.

Which is a kinder way into the subject than the usual one. Most Christians carry a low-grade guilt about not speaking of Christ more, and the usual remedy is a course on how to do it. This verse suggests looking further upstream. Silence is very often not a technique problem but a sight problem: we have stopped seeing him clearly enough to have anything pressing to say. Fix the gaze, and the tongue tends to follow. Nobody needs to be taught how to talk about something they cannot get over.

Then the second reason, and it is the ground under everything: knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also. Not hoping. Knowing. The resurrection is not a doctrine Paul holds; it is the fact that makes his arithmetic work. If death is genuinely at work in him and there is nothing on the other side, then he is simply being consumed. If there is a resurrection, he is being invested.

And then the phrase that shows what he is really looking forward to: and bring us with you into his presence. Not bring us home. Not even raise us in glory. With you. After everything — the humiliating visit, the letters, the men who despised him — what he pictures at the end is arriving in the presence of God with these very people beside him. He expects to see the ones who wounded him there, and the thought gives him pleasure.

That is what resurrection hope does to a quarrel. It puts everyone concerned in the same room, standing in front of the same face, and makes the present disagreement look exactly as large as it is going to look then.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.

Here Paul tells us where the whole thing is going, and the destination is not what most people would guess.

It is all for your sake. All of it — the afflictions, the perplexity, the daily handing over to death, the dying at work in his body. Every bit of it is aimed at them. He has said this three times now in four chapters (1:6, 4:12, and here), and the repetition is not accidental. He wants them in no doubt about who the suffering is for.

Then a chain with three links, and it is worth following them in order because each one produces the next.

First, grace extends to more and more people. The verb suggests something spreading outward, gaining ground. The suffering of one man is not a closed loop; it is how the gospel gets to the next town.

Second, it may increase thanksgiving. Every new person reached is a new voice added. Grace multiplies, and gratitude multiplies with it, because a person who has been given something he could not earn will say so.

Third, and this is the terminus: to the glory of God. That is what all of it is finally for. Not Paul’s vindication, not even the Corinthians’ comfort — those are real, and they are on the way to something else.

Sit with that for a moment, because it quietly rearranges the way most of us think about our own troubles. The usual Christian question in hardship is what is God teaching me? It is a good question and it has a real answer. But it is a smaller question than this verse is asking. Paul’s question is not what he is getting out of his affliction. It is how many mouths will end up thanking God because of it.

That is a genuinely different way to hold a hard season, and it is available to ordinary people, not only apostles. The illness that has made you dependent has given several people the chance to serve, and some of them are praying for the first time in years. The redundancy that humiliated you is being watched by your children, who are learning what a man does when the money stops. You may never see the accounting. Paul, writing this, could not see most of his either.

Notice also the shape of what he expects at the end. Not a report on results. A rising volume of thanks.

And that is the note the passage lands on, because it is the note the universe lands on. God is not accumulating servants or achievements. He is gathering worship — voice after voice, from places nobody planned, most of them belonging to people who were given something they never earned and could not repay. Every grace that goes out comes back as thanksgiving, and the whole long enterprise of the gospel exists so that the number of people who have reason to praise him should be as large as it can possibly be made.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–18 — The Outer and Inner; the Seen and Unseen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul draws out the practical consequence of the jar-of-clay theology (v. 16): “So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.” The outer self (ho exō hēmōn anthrōpos — the outer person) is the physical, mortal, visible body — the jar of clay itself, subject to ageing, illness, and death. The inner self (ho esō) is being renewed (anakainoutai — present passive, ongoing action) day by day. The outer and inner are moving in opposite directions simultaneously, and the phrase “we do not lose heart” deliberately picks up v. 1, bracketing the whole chapter.

The basis for this equanimity is a radical revaluation of time and weight (v. 17): “this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison.” The word translated “weight” (baros) answers to the Hebrew kabod (glory/weight — the glory of God as a weighty, substantial reality). The comparison is deliberately asymmetrical: the affliction is light and momentary; the glory is heavy and eternal. And the affliction is not merely contrasted with the glory; it is actively preparing it (katergazetai — working out, producing). Suffering is not the obstacle to glory; it is the mechanism by which glory is prepared. This is a thing a man may say about his own affliction; it must never be said to another’s.

Verse 18 supplies the condition on which both the renewal and the weighing depend: “as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen.” The verb (skopeō) means to take aim at, to fix attention — the sustained look, not the glance. The unseen is looked at by attending to what God has said about it, and supremely by beholding the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The seen/unseen contrast (v. 18) is not Platonic dualism — Paul is not saying that the material world is bad and the spiritual world is good, or that the body is a prison from which the soul escapes. He is making an eschatological point: what is currently visible (the suffering, the wasting body, the opposition) is temporary; what is currently invisible (the renewed inner person, the weight of glory being prepared) is permanent. The resurrection of the body (ch. 5; 1 Cor. 15) will make the invisible visible — the glory will become physical and permanent in the resurrection.
verseByVerse.examples: An elderly woman in a nursing home, her body failing, tells her pastor that she has never felt closer to God. She cannot explain it; the outer self is clearly wasting away. But there is something else. This verse names what she is experiencing: while the outer is being destroyed, the inner is being renewed day by day. The renewal is not despite the physical decline but somehow through it — the loosening grip of the outer on the inner’s attention, the daily reminder that this is not home, the intensified gaze at the unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.

The phrase from verse 1 comes back, and now we can see what it cost him to say it. He does not lose heart — and he is telling us in the same breath that he is falling apart.

Take the honesty of it first. Our outer self is wasting away. The verb means to be ruined, corrupted, destroyed by degrees; it is used of a house rotting and a garment eaten through. Paul is not talking merely about persecution. He is talking about the body: the eyes that are worse than they were, the strength that does not come back after a hard week, the accumulating record of what has been done to him. He is somewhere in his fifties and he is running out.

Christian faith does not require anyone to be brave about this or to pretend it is not happening. There is no verse here about ageing gracefully. There is a blunt admission that the jar is cracking, written by a man who could see it happening to himself.

But set against it, in the same sentence, is a second process: our inner self is being renewed day by day. The verb is passive and continuous — it is being done, and it is being done now. Not restored to what it was; the word means made new, made afresh. And day by day, in the ordinary increments in which the other process is also happening.

Two things are going on in the same person at the same time, in opposite directions. One is visible and everybody can see it. The other is invisible, and it is the one that is going to last.

This is the verse for a hospital chair, and it should be given away freely. Anyone who has sat with an elderly believer knows the strange phenomenon it describes: a body plainly failing and something else plainly not failing. The conversation goes somewhere unexpected, or a hymn surfaces from sixty years ago, or the person says with complete simplicity that they are not afraid — and you leave the room having received rather than given. The outer self was telling the truth about the outer self and nothing else.

It is worth asking what the renewal actually runs on, because it is not automatic. Nothing in this verse suggests that decline by itself produces spiritual growth; plenty of people grow old and merely become more themselves. The next two verses give the answer — a way of counting the affliction, and a direction of gaze. The renewal happens in people who are looking at something.

So here is the honest question for anyone still healthy enough to ask it. Both processes are already running in you; the first began some years ago whether or not you have noticed. The only real question is whether the second one is running too, because the day is coming when it will be the only thing you have left, and it is not built in an afternoon. Everything you are doing now to attend to the inner self is provision laid down for a season you cannot yet imagine — and every believer who has arrived there has found the supply was already waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,

Read that sentence beside the man who wrote it and it becomes almost outrageous.

By the time he reaches this letter Paul had been flogged five times with thirty-nine lashes, beaten with rods three times, stoned and left for dead, shipwrecked three times, and had spent a night and a day adrift at sea. He had been hungry, cold, sleepless and betrayed. He had recently despaired of life itself. And he calls it light. He calls it momentary.

Nobody may say that sentence to a sufferer on Paul’s behalf. It is a thing a man may say about his own troubles and nobody may say about another’s. Handled carelessly it becomes the cruellest verse in the New Testament: cheer up, it is only light and momentary, said to a woman who has buried a child. Paul is not minimising anything. He has spent four chapters refusing to minimise it.

What he is doing is weighing. Both key words are comparative. Light means light in comparison; momentary means brief in comparison. Put a real weight on a scale with nothing on the other side and it is heavy. Put the glory on the other side and the same weight rises. The affliction has not changed. Something has been added to the other pan.

The word weight is the point of the whole verse. Behind it lies the Hebrew kabod, which is the ordinary Old Testament word for glory and literally means heaviness. Glory in the Bible is not brightness or reputation; it is substance, mass, the sheer solidity of God. So Paul sets a weight against a weight, and this is not a promise of something ethereal to compensate for something painfully solid. What is coming is heavier than what is happening.

Then he says the affliction is preparing it. The verb means to work out, to produce as a result. The suffering is not merely followed by glory; it is doing something. There is a line running from the hardest thing in your life to the weight of glory, and it is a line of cause. Nothing is being wasted and nothing is merely being endured.

Beyond all comparison renders a phrase Paul builds by piling one intensifier on another — literally according to excess unto excess. He has run out of Greek. It is the same word that gave him the utterly in chapter 1 when he was describing how far past his strength he had been pushed, and here he uses it twice in a row, straining language at the other end of the scale.

Which is worth holding on to when comfort feels thin. He is not saying the glory will be worth it, as though it were a fair exchange narrowly won. He is saying the two things cannot be put on the same scale at all — that the heaviest grief a human being can carry will one day be found to have been the lighter object in the comparison, and that we do not currently have the vocabulary to say why. Everyone who has arrived has agreed. Nobody has ever come to the end and said it was too much.

verseByVerse.quote: as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

The verse begins with as, and it is doing real work. This is the condition. The affliction prepares a weight of glory as we look — the renewal of verse 16 and the weighing of verse 17 both happen in people whose eyes are pointed somewhere particular.

The verb is not the ordinary word for seeing. Skopeō means to fix attention on, to take aim at; it is the root of our word scope. It describes the deliberate, sustained look — a man sighting down a line, not a man glancing.

Then the obvious objection, which any honest reader raises immediately: how do you look at something you cannot see?

The answer is not mysticism, and it is not pretending. Paul has already told us where the unseen is made visible. The glory of God is in the face of Jesus Christ (v. 6), and it is beheld in the gospel (3:18). You look at the unseen by looking at what God has said about it, until it becomes as real to you as the things in the room. That is what faith actually is in practice: not a feeling, but attention paid to the invisible on the authority of God’s word about it.

Which makes this an intensely practical verse rather than an ethereal one. The looking is done in ordinary places — a Bible open at a kitchen table before anyone else is awake, a hymn sung on the way to work, a truth deliberately turned over during a hospital wait instead of the phone. The word behind look implies aim, and aim implies effort. Nobody drifts into this. The seen presses itself on you free of charge; the unseen has to be attended to.

Then the reason, and it is where the argument lands: the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal. Transient means for a season — temporary, on a timer.

Notice how completely this reverses the ordinary way of counting. We call the visible real and the invisible abstract. Paul says the opposite. The mortgage, the diagnosis, the argument at work, the state of the nation — these are the things with an expiry date on them. The unseen things, which feel thin because we cannot get our hands on them, are the ones with no end.

Guard it from one misreading, though. This is not the old idea that matter is bad and spirit is good. Paul believes in the resurrection of the body and is about to spend a chapter on it. He is not saying the physical is unreal. He is saying the present arrangement is temporary, and that what is now invisible will one day be the most solid thing there is.

So the whole chapter comes to rest on where a person is looking. The jar is cracking; the treasure is not. The outer is going; the inner is being made new. What can be seen is on its way out, and behind it, entirely steady, is a glory with a face — the one thing in the universe that will still be there when everything currently visible has finished happening.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart.<sup>2</sup>But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.<sup>3</sup>And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing.<sup>4</sup>In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.<sup>5</sup>For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.<sup>6</sup>For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.<sup>7</sup>But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.<sup>8</sup>We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair;<sup>9</sup>persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;<sup>10</sup>always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies.<sup>11</sup>For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.<sup>12</sup>So death is at work in us, but life in you.<sup>13</sup>Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak,<sup>14</sup>knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.<sup>15</sup>For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.<sup>16</sup>So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.<sup>17</sup>For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,<sup>18</sup>as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

5.title: The Heavenly Dwelling, the Judgment Seat, and the Ministry of Reconciliation
5.overview:
Chapter 5 continues the eschatological meditation of chapter 4 and arrives at two of the most important theological statements in all of Paul: the ministry of reconciliation (v. 18–20) and the great exchange (v. 21). The chapter opens with the tension between the groaning present existence and the confidence of future glory — the “earthly tent” of the body will be dissolved, but a building from God awaits, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. In the meantime, believers groan, longing to be clothed with the heavenly dwelling, not because they want to escape embodiment but because they long for glorified, resurrection embodiment.

The motivation for Paul’s ministry (vv. 11–21) is then unpacked: the fear of the Lord, the love of Christ, the conviction that one died for all. These three motivators — accountability, love, and the atonement — together explain why Paul does what he does at enormous personal cost. The new creation declaration (v. 17) is the hinge: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has gone, the new has come. And then the ministry of reconciliation: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them. Paul’s ministry is an embassy of this reconciliation — we implore on Christ’s behalf, be reconciled to God. The chapter ends with v. 21, one of the most precise statements of the doctrine of substitutionary atonement in Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Heavenly Dwelling and the Judgment Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “earthly tent” (v. 1, hē epigeios hēmōn oikia tou skēnous) is the mortal body — a temporary, portable structure. If it is destroyed by death, Paul says, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. The contrast is between tent (temporary, human-made) and building (permanent, God-made). This is not merely a contrast between death and life; it is a contrast between two kinds of embodiment: the present mortal body and the future resurrection body.

The groaning in vv. 2–4 is important: Paul does not say the believer longs to escape the body but to be “further clothed” — to have the resurrection body put on over the present one, so that what is mortal is swallowed up by life. This guards against a Platonic reading: the hope is not disembodied existence in a spiritual realm but full, glorified, resurrection embodiment. The Spirit is the deposit guaranteeing this (v. 5) — the same down-payment theology as 1:22, and the reason the longing itself is evidence rather than wishful thinking.

Verses 6–8 then describe the believer’s settled courage and his present address. To be at home in the body is to be away from the Lord; the Christian therefore walks by faith and not by sight (v. 7) — a contrast not between faith and thinking but between believing a Lord one has not seen and seeing him face to face. That sight is what v. 8 anticipates: to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, immediately and consciously (cf. Lk. 23:43; Phil. 1:23). Verse 9 draws the practical conclusion — at home or away, the ambition is unchanged: to please him.

The goal of the section is the judgment seat of Christ (v. 10): we must all appear before it, that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. This is not the judgment that determines salvation — that is settled in Christ. It is the assessment of what believers have done with their lives as believers — the accounting of stewardship (cf. 1 Cor. 3:10–15 where works are tested by fire). The fear of the Lord (v. 11) that follows from this awareness of the judgment seat is a primary motivator of Paul’s ministry.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment seat of Christ (to bēma tou Christou, v. 10) is a significant and sometimes neglected doctrine. Reformed theology insists on two distinct judgments: the justification that settles the believer’s eternal standing (entirely by grace, through faith, in Christ — Rom. 8:1: “no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”) and the assessment of the believer’s life and works (1 Cor. 3:10–15; 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 22:12). At the bēma, salvation is not at stake; stewardship is. This distinction protects the gospel of grace while maintaining genuine accountability for the quality of the Christian life.
verseByVerse.examples: A Christian professional justifies a series of ethical compromises in his career with the thought that “grace covers everything.” He is not wrong about grace — but he is using it as a licence rather than a motivation. The judgment seat of Christ does not threaten his justification; it does call him to account for the quality of his stewardship. Paul says the knowledge of the judgment seat motivates him to “persuade others” (v. 11) — it is a motivating, not a threatening, reality for the justified believer.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.

Paul has just said his outer self is wasting away. Now he says what happens when the wasting finishes its work, and he does it with two buildings.

The tent. He is a tentmaker; this is the trade he worked at in Corinth beside Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18:3). He knows exactly what a tent is worth. It goes up in a morning and comes down in an afternoon. It keeps out most of the weather. The stitching fails, the goat-hair stretches, and one season it will not be worth mending. Nobody grows attached to a tent, and nobody expects one to last.

That is the body — and notice he does not despise it. A tent is a real shelter and a good one for the journey. It is simply not a house.

A building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. Three things about it, and each answers something about the tent. It is from God rather than run up by human hands. It is a building, permanent, with foundations. And it is eternal, so the question of how many more seasons it will take never arises.

What is this house? Not, in Paul’s mind, a heavenly location instead of a body. He is about to spend three verses insisting that he does not want to be unclothed. The building is the resurrection body — the same reality he described at length to this church already, sown in dishonour, raised in glory; sown in weakness, raised in power (1 Cor. 15:43). What is promised is not escape from embodiment but the exchange of a temporary body for a permanent one.

And notice how the sentence opens: we know. Not we hope, not we like to think. It is the settled knowledge of a man who has staked his life on it, and the ground of the knowledge is that it has already happened once, in a garden, to a body that had been in a tomb for three days.

The word destroyed should not be softened either. It means taken down, dismantled — what you do to a tent when the camp moves. Paul is not pretending death is gentle. He is saying it is a dismantling, and that a dismantling is not the end of the story when there is a house already standing.

Which is a good deal more comfort than it may first appear, particularly for anyone watching a body fail. What is happening in that hospital bed is real and it is being described accurately here: a shelter coming apart. Nobody is being asked to call it something else. But the same sentence says that the person inside is not homeless. The building is not being built when the tent falls; the verb is present tense — we have a building. It is standing now, in the heavens, waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling, if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling, if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.

Paul groans. It is worth pausing there before anything else, because a great deal of Christian talk about death is bright in a way this verse is not.

The word stenazō is a deep, inarticulate sound — the noise a person makes under a weight, not a complaint formed into words. He uses it of the whole creation in Romans 8, which has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now, and of believers who groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption (Rom. 8:22–23). It is the sound of something that knows it was made for more than this.

So Christian hope does not require pretending to be comfortable. Anyone who has been ill for a long time, or has watched someone they love become someone they have to care for, knows the groan. This verse says it is not unbelief. It is the correct response to a tent in a storm.

But look what the groaning is for. Not for release, not for the end of consciousness, not even simply for heaven. Longing to put on our heavenly dwelling — a clothing word. The house has become a garment, and the desire is to have it on.

Then the difficult half-line: if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked. This has puzzled readers for centuries and it deserves a straight answer rather than a shrug.

The image is consistent with everything around it. To be naked is to be without a body — a self with no dwelling, exposed, uncovered. In the Greek world that was the goal: the soul at last free of the flesh, the immortal escaping the mortal. Plato would have called it salvation. Paul calls it nakedness, and shrinks from it.

That is a deeply important correction, because Christians have absorbed far more of the Greek idea than they realise. Ask most believers what happens at death and the answer will be about the soul going to heaven, and there it stops. That is real and it is precious — Paul will say in six verses that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord. But it is not the hope of this chapter, and it is not the end. It is the interval. The Christian hope is a body: a real one, on a real new earth, standing up out of a grave.

And the reason Paul recoils from nakedness is that God made us to be embodied and called it very good. Human beings are not souls temporarily inconvenienced by flesh. The body is not the problem; death is the problem, and the answer to death is not escape from the body but the resurrection of it.

So the longing in this verse is a strong one to have, and it is worth checking what your own longing is actually aimed at. If it is chiefly to be finished with pain, that is honest and God is not offended by it. But there is a larger thing to want, and it will bear more weight: not to be rid of the tent, but to be at last properly clothed — and everything necessary for that has already been done in the body of a man who came out of a grave in one piece.

verseByVerse.quote: For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened — not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

He says the groan again, and this time he says why. Being burdened — the word means weighed down, pressed by a load. It is the same root Paul used in chapter 1 of the affliction in Asia that was beyond our strength.

Then he corrects a misunderstanding before it can form, and the correction is the heart of the verse: not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed.

Two different desires, and the difference matters enormously. To want to be unclothed is to want to be finished — to have the thing taken off and nothing put in its place. To want to be further clothed is to want something put on over the present one. The Greek carries that quite literally: a garment drawn on top of what is already being worn.

So Paul is not longing for the end of his existence, nor even chiefly for relief. He is longing for the moment when the mortal thing he is wearing is covered by something so much more alive that the mortality disappears inside it.

Which brings the last phrase, and it is one of the great images in Scripture: so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. The verb is katapinō — to gulp down, to swallow whole. It is the word used in chapter 2 of a man being swallowed by sorrow, and it is the word Isaiah used of God’s promise that he will swallow up death forever (Isa. 25:8), which Paul quotes in triumph at the end of 1 Corinthians 15.

Notice which way round it runs. We speak of death swallowing people; every funeral has that shape, the person going down and the ground closing over. Paul reverses it. Life is the mouth. Mortality is what gets swallowed.

Picture the difference. A candle blown out is unclothed: the light removed, dark where it was. A candle carried outside at sunrise is swallowed up by life: nothing has been taken away, and there is so much more light that the flame is no longer needed. That is the Christian hope, and it is worth getting straight, because most of us instinctively imagine death as the first picture and hope for the best.

There is a plain pastoral use for this. If you have ever caught yourself wanting simply to stop — the tiredness that is deeper than sleep, the private wish to be finished — this verse does not condemn you. Paul was carrying that weight when he wrote it. What he does is take the desire and correct its aim. What you actually want is not to be switched off. It is to be so thoroughly alive that everything currently wearing you out is swallowed and gone. And there is only one place in the universe that has ever been offered, by a Lord who went into the ground himself and came out with mortality swallowed whole.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.

Everything in the previous four verses has been about longing. Now Paul says where the longing came from.

He who has prepared us for this very thing is God. The verb means to work something up, to fashion it for a purpose. The homesickness is not a temperament and not wishful thinking; it was manufactured. God made you for the building, and then he made you want it.

That is worth turning over, because it explains something most people notice and few can account for. There is a restlessness in human beings that no arrangement of circumstances satisfies. Get the house, the health, the family, the settled work — and there remains a thin persistent ache that something is not yet right. We usually treat it as a fault to be corrected by acquiring one more thing. Paul says it is a fitting, deliberately made, and it corresponds to something real.

Then the evidence: who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee. The word is arrabōn again, met already at 1:22 — the down payment that legally commits the payer to hand over the rest. Not a token of goodwill. The first instalment, in the same currency as the balance.

So the argument runs like this. You were built for the resurrection body. You can tell, because you groan. And to prove that the groaning is not a cruel joke, God has put a deposit in your hands, and the deposit is not a thing but a Person.

Take that seriously and it changes how a believer reads his own spiritual experience. The moments when Scripture has come alive; the peace that arrived when there was no reason for it; the affection for people you would once have avoided; the fact that you want God at all — those are not the whole payment and they were never meant to satisfy you. They are the first instalment, deliberately given so that you would know what is coming and be unable to settle for less.

Which is why a Christian who is spiritually alive is often more homesick rather than less. The deposit does not quiet the longing. It confirms it.

And here is a test worth running when assurance is thin. You will be tempted to look for proof in the strength of your feelings, which rise and fall with sleep and circumstance. Look instead for the deposit. Is there anything in you that was not there before — any hunger for God, any grief over sin that is more than embarrassment, any love for his people that has no natural explanation? That is not your achievement. It is money already paid into the account by someone who does not default, and every penny of it is a promise about the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.

Paul has been groaning for four verses. Now, without contradiction, he says he is always of good courage. Both are true at once, and any account of the Christian life that has to choose between them has gone wrong somewhere.

The word is tharreō — to be confident, to take heart. And always: not on good days. The courage does not depend on the groaning having stopped.

Then a startling admission: while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord. It is a strong word — living abroad, resident in a foreign country. Paul is saying that the present life, even at its best, is an absence. He has had the Damascus road, the third heaven, revelations he is not permitted to describe, and he still calls this away from the Lord.

Nobody should be told to feel guilty about the distance, then. Every Christian knows the frustration of it — the prayers that feel like speaking into a next room, the sense that the best moments were glimpses rather than sight. That is not a defect in your discipleship. It is the address you are currently living at.

And here is the reason, in one of the most quoted and most misused sentences in the New Testament: for we walk by faith, not by sight.

Take the misuse first. It is regularly used to mean that Christians should act on impressions without evidence, or that asking sensible questions is a lack of faith, or that the less you know the more spiritual your decision. That is not what the words mean. Sight here translates eidos — appearance, form, the visible thing itself. Paul is not contrasting faith with thinking. He is contrasting faith with seeing Christ face to face, which is what verse 8 goes on to describe. The believer walks now on the testimony of a Lord he has not yet seen; one day he will see him and the walking by faith will be over.

Which makes the sentence a description before it is a command. This is simply the condition of every Christian who has ever lived. Nobody in the church has seen him. Not the apostles now — even Paul, after the road to Damascus, is walking the same way you are.

Note the verb too. Not we stand by faith or we feel by faith. We walk. It is the ordinary word for daily conduct, one foot in front of the other, going somewhere on a road you cannot see the end of. Faith is not primarily a state of certainty; it is a way of moving in the dark on the word of someone who can see.

And that is why the courage is possible while the groaning continues. A man walking a mountain path at night with a guide he trusts is not comfortable and is not lost. He may say both things in the same breath, and Paul does.

verseByVerse.quote: Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

The two words are swapped round. In verse 6 he was at home in the body and away from the Lord; now he says he would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. And this verse is where a Christian goes when someone he loves has died.

So take the question directly, because it is the one people actually ask at a graveside: what happens to a believer at the moment of death?

Paul’s answer here is as plain as it could be. Away from the body — and immediately at home with the Lord. There is no gap, no waiting room, no period of unconsciousness. He says the same thing to the Philippians from prison: my desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Phil. 1:23). And the Lord himself said it to a dying criminal who had nothing to offer and no time left: today you will be with me in paradise (Lk. 23:43). Today.

This rules out the idea, held sincerely by some, that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. It is difficult to see how being asleep for centuries could be called far better, or how it could be described as being at home with the Lord at all. The New Testament’s language is of presence, and of presence now.

It also rules out something at the other extreme, and it should be said clearly because grieving people are sometimes told otherwise. There is no purgatory here — no interval of purging for believers who died imperfect. Paul, who knew what he still was, expects to be at home the moment he is away. The reason is not that he had reached a standard. It is verse 21, thirteen verses further on: the exchange has already been made.

Hold together, though, what this chapter holds together. Being with Christ without a body is far better — and it is still not the end. Verse 4 called that state nakedness and Paul did not want it for its own sake. The full hope is further clothing: the resurrection body, the new creation, the dead raised. So a Christian funeral is properly two things at once. The person is with the Lord today, and there is a morning coming when they will be given back their body and it will never fail again.

And notice the one word Paul uses for it: home. Not a reward, not a destination, not even a place. Home is where a person stops being a stranger. The whole of this life he has described as living abroad. Death, for a believer, is the end of the foreign posting.

Which means the last enemy has been made into a door. That was not true before a certain Friday. It cost the Lord of glory his own descent into the ground to change what death is for everyone who belongs to him — and now the worst thing that can happen to a Christian is that he goes home.

verseByVerse.quote: So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.

Having settled where he is going, Paul says what he intends to do in the meantime. Whether we are at home or away — living or dead, in the body or out of it — the aim does not change: to please him. The word for aim is a term of ambition; it means to count something an honour, to make it your driving purpose. This is what he wants.

Then the reason, and it is one many Christians are surprised to find in their Bibles: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.

The word is bēma. Anyone in Corinth knew what one looked like; there was a stone platform in their own marketplace where Paul had once stood before Gallio (Acts 18:12). A bēma was the raised seat from which a magistrate gave verdicts — and also the platform at the games from which the judge awarded the crowns.

Two questions arise at once, and both need answering plainly.

First: does a Christian face judgment? Paul says we must all appear, and the we is believers. Yet the same apostle wrote that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:1). Both are true because two different things are in view. The verdict on whether you belong to Christ is not reopened; it was settled at the cross and cannot be revisited. What is assessed at the bēma is what you did with the life you were given after that verdict was passed. He wrote about this to this same church a letter earlier: the foundation is Christ and cannot be relaid, but what a man builds on it is tested by fire, and some of it burns, though he himself will be saved (1 Cor. 3:15).

Second: should that frighten a believer? Paul does not seem frightened; he moves straight from it to ambition, not to dread. But he plainly does not treat it as nothing either. The honest position is that a Christian may lose a great deal there — the years spent on things that turned out to be nothing, the gifts unused, the reputation protected instead of spent — and will lose nothing of Christ.

Notice what he has done in the body. Not what he intended, not what he believed about doing. The body is where the Christian life is actually conducted: the hands, the diary, the money, the tongue. This is the same body Paul has just called a tent that is coming down, and here he says it is the very place where a life is either laid up or wasted.

Which turns the thought from a threat into something more searching and more useful. Take this week as it actually was — the hours, the conversations, the things you gave attention to. That is what will be looked at, by someone who loves you and who died for the failures in it. A Christian who lives with that in view does not become anxious. He becomes deliberate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Ministry of Reconciliation and the Great Exchange
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul identifies three motivators for his ministry.
