First, the fear of the Lord (v. 11) — the awareness of accountability at the judgment seat just described, which drives him out to persuade people rather than inward into anxiety. He guards this at once from being heard as self-promotion (v. 12): he is not commending himself again but arming the Corinthians with an answer to those who boast about outward appearance rather than what is in the heart. Verse 13 answers the charge that he is unbalanced: whatever in him goes past what people find reasonable is for God, and his sober, measured teaching is for them.

Second, the love of Christ (v. 14) — not Paul’s love for Christ but Christ’s love for Paul, the love that “controls” or “compels” him (synechei hēmas — presses in on us, constrains us, leaves no room for any other direction). The logic: one died for all, therefore all died; and he died for all so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and was raised for them (v. 15). Because of that, Paul no longer assesses anyone by outward standards, not even Christ, whom he had once judged that way and got catastrophically wrong (v. 16).

Third, the new creation (v. 17): the old order is gone; everything is new; and all this is from God. The newness is a matter of being in Christ, not of how a believer feels on a given Thursday.

The ministry of reconciliation (vv. 18–20) is Paul’s description of the gospel as embassy work: in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them. The word katallassō (reconcile) is a commercial and relational term for the restoration of a broken relationship, often through the settlement of a debt or grievance. God has taken the initiative — not waiting for the world to come to him but going out to reconcile. The ministry of reconciliation is the extension of this divine initiative: “we implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.”

The chapter ends with v. 21 — arguably the most theologically compressed statement of the atonement in Scripture: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” This is the great exchange: Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness. It is the double imputation at the heart of Reformed soteriology — our sin imputed to Christ, his righteousness imputed to us — stated in its clearest and most unambiguous form.
verseByVerse.theology:
The judgment seat of Christ (to bēma tou Christou, 5:10) is a significant and sometimes neglected doctrine. Reformed theology insists on two distinct judgments: the justification that settles the believer’s eternal standing (entirely by grace, through faith, in Christ — Rom. 8:1: “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”) and the assessment of the believer’s life and works (1 Cor. 3:10–15; 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 22:12). At the bēma, salvation is not at stake; stewardship is. This distinction protects the gospel of grace while maintaining genuine accountability for the quality of the Christian life.

“In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself” (v. 19) — the agency is God’s. Reconciliation is initiated, accomplished, and offered by God, not by humanity. The word order matters and is often misquoted: it is not that God was waiting to be reconciled to humanity, as if he needed to be persuaded or appeased by a more merciful Son. Rather, God himself was the reconciler — the one who, in Christ, removed the obstacle that prevented humanity from being reconciled to him. The obstacle is sin; the removal is the cross, and v. 21 states its cost.

Verse 21 — “he made him to be sin who knew no sin” — requires precise handling. “Made him to be sin” (hamartian epoiēsen) does not mean Christ became a sinner or had sinful desires. It means God treated Christ as the sin-bearer — the one who stood in the place of sinners, receiving the judgment that sin deserves. The Old Testament background is the sin offering: in Leviticus the offering itself is called by the same word as the sin it carried, the animal becoming the sin-bearer, and Isaiah says it without a picture at all — “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isa. 53:6). The result: we “become the righteousness of God” — not merely receive a righteous verdict but are constituted righteous in him, which is why the standing cannot be damaged by a bad week.
verseByVerse.examples: An evangelism trainer teaches his church that the goal of evangelism is to persuade people to make a decision for Christ. This passage suggests a deeper framework: the goal is to implore people, on Christ’s behalf, to be reconciled to God — as ambassadors of a reconciliation that God himself has already accomplished and is already offering. The difference is not merely semantic: the ambassador does not create the peace; he announces and conveys the peace that the King has already made.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.

The judgment seat has an immediate effect on Paul, and it is not the one we might expect. It does not send him into anxious self-examination. It sends him out to talk to people.

Knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. First, that phrase, because it is badly worn and often emptied out. The fear of the Lord is not terror of a God who might turn on you; that is precisely what the gospel removes. Nor is it merely respect, which is how it is usually softened. It is the awe of a creature who has grasped what God actually is — that this is the one before whom nations are a drop from a bucket, and that one day you will stand in front of him. A man who has felt that does not treat other people’s eternity as a conversational risk.

So he persuades. The word is the ordinary one for winning someone over by argument. Paul is not manipulating and not merely announcing; he is reasoning with people, working to change their minds, because he believes what he has just said about the bēma.

There is a quiet challenge in the connection. Most Christian silence about Christ is not really shyness. It is that we have stopped believing anything much is at stake. Recover the seriousness and the awkwardness stops being decisive.

Then Paul turns back to his critics, and verse 12 is delicately done. He knows how the previous chapters have sounded — he raised the objection himself at 3:1 — so he says it again: we are not commending ourselves to you again. His purpose is not to be admired. It is to put something in their hands: giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer the others.

That is a generous piece of pastoral strategy. The Corinthians were caught between two sets of teachers and had nothing to say when Paul was disparaged in front of them. He is arming them, not defending himself.

And notice the fault line he draws: those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart. Literally, boasting in the face rather than the heart. The rival teachers had presence, polish, credentials and delivery. Paul had a wasting body and a speaking manner his critics thought contemptible.

The church has never stopped needing that line drawn. We assess by the face still — the platform manner, the confidence, the numbers, the production. And God has said from the beginning how he assesses, in the words spoken to Samuel while he was busy admiring the wrong brother: the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7). The awkward implication is that the most impressive Christian you know may not be the one God is most pleased with, and neither of you can currently tell.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.

A short verse, and it lets us hear one of the accusations being made about Paul.

Beside ourselves translates existēmi — literally to stand outside oneself, the word for being out of one’s mind. Somebody had said Paul was unhinged. It was not a new charge against him; Festus would later shout it across a courtroom, Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind (Acts 26:24). His own Lord had the same thing said about him by his family, who went out to seize him, for they were saying, He is out of his mind (Mk. 3:21).

What lay behind it in Corinth we cannot be certain of. Perhaps his ecstatic experiences — he will mention being caught up to the third heaven in chapter 12, and clearly did not talk about it often. Perhaps simply the shape of his life: a man of formidable training who could have had a comfortable career, who instead crossed provinces on foot, took beatings, and refused payment. To a sensible observer that looks like a man who has lost his balance.

And Paul does not deny it. He allocates it. If we are beside ourselves, it is for God. Whatever in him goes past what people find reasonable is between him and God, and God is the one it is for.

Then the other half, which is just as important: if we are in our right mind, it is for you. The word is sōphroneō — sober, self-controlled, sane. He is not choosing between the two. He is saying that when he is measured and careful, that too is a service; it is for their sake, so that they can be taught.

There is a real pastoral wisdom in that division, and it has a use. Christians frequently feel pulled between two accusations: from one side, that they are excessive, fanatical, disproportionate about religion; from the other, that they are too restrained, too ordinary, not zealous enough. Paul’s answer is that both intensity and sobriety have their place, and that what determines the place is who each is for. There is a passion that belongs between you and God and does not need an audience — the hours in prayer nobody knows about, the tears over Scripture, the extravagance in giving that would embarrass you if it were discussed. And there is a sober, patient, unremarkable steadiness that belongs to the people you serve, because they need teaching more than they need to watch you burn.

The failure comes when the two are swapped: the intensity performed in public where it can be seen, and the sobriety kept for private life, where zeal quietly cools. The Lord warned about exactly that — the giving and praying and fasting done to be seen, which has already had its reward (Matt. 6:1–6).

Keep them the right way round, and a Christian can be entirely unembarrassed about being thought excessive, because the excess is not aimed at the people doing the assessing.

verseByVerse.quote: For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.

Here is the engine of Paul’s life, and he names it in four words.

First, whose love? The love of Christ can grammatically mean Paul’s love for Christ or Christ’s love for Paul, and the sentence itself decides it. Look at what follows the word because: not a description of Paul’s devotion but of Christ’s death. It is Christ’s love for him that is doing the driving. That distinction is not academic. A ministry powered by how much you love Christ will run exactly as far as your affections do, which on a bad week is not far. A ministry powered by how much he loved you has a fixed and finished event underneath it.

Controls us is synechei — to hold together, to press in from both sides, to hem in. It is used of a crowd pressing round a man, and of a river channelled between banks. The picture is not a whip driving him forward but walls preventing him going anywhere else. A river between banks is not restricted; it is given force. Take the banks away and you have a swamp.

Then the conclusion he has reached: one has died for all, therefore all have died. This is representation, the great Pauline idea. What happens to the one counts as having happened to those he stands for — as Adam’s act counted for the race that came from him (Rom. 5:18–19). So when Christ died, those who are in him died; the old self, the old account, the old standing, went into the grave with him.

Two words in that sentence have been argued over for centuries, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise: for all. Reformed theology has always held that Christ’s death actually accomplished redemption rather than merely making it possible — that he did not die to create an opportunity but to save a people, and that everyone he died for in that sense will certainly be brought home. Others, reading these words, hold that the death was for every person without exception and is applied on believing. Both sides are trying to protect something real: one the sufficiency and freeness of the offer, the other the effectiveness of the cross. What is beyond argument in this verse is its logic — that his death was for people, in their place, and that it did something to them and not merely for them.

And then the purpose, which is where the passage lands: that those who live might no longer live for themselves. That is the whole Christian ethic in one line, and it is not first a rule but a consequence. A man who has died is finished with running his own affairs. The only question left is whose he now is.

So here is the test, and it is the plainest one in the chapter. Whose life are you living for? Not what you would say — what the diary and the bank statement say. Almost every human being alive is living for himself and has never noticed, because there is nothing unusual about it. The strange thing, the thing that needs explaining, is a person who is not. And there is only one event in history with the power to produce it.

verseByVerse.quote: From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.

If one died for all and all died, then everything has to be looked at again. Paul begins with how he looks at people.

According to the flesh means by the world’s standards of assessment — the face rather than the heart, exactly the fault line drawn in verse 12. It is the reflex by which we file a person within seconds of meeting them: the accent, the clothes, the job, the health, the usefulness. Paul says that reflex has been retired.

He then gives the decisive example, and it is himself. We once regarded Christ according to the flesh. Saul of Tarsus had assessed Jesus of Nazareth by exactly those criteria — an executed provincial with no standing, a blasphemer, obviously nothing. He had been completely confident and completely wrong. A man who has made that mistake about that person never trusts his own first assessment of anyone again.

Then verse 17, which is one of the best-known sentences in the New Testament and one of the most misheard.

If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The Greek is even more abrupt than the English: if anyone in Christ — new creation! There is no verb. And the phrase new creation was not, in Paul’s world, a term for personal improvement. It was the great promise of the prophets about the world itself: behold, I create new heavens and a new earth (Isa. 65:17). Paul takes that cosmic vocabulary and says it has already begun, and where it has begun is inside people.

Now the misheard part, because this verse has quietly wounded a great many honest Christians. Read as a description of how you feel, it is crushing: the old has passed away — and yet the temper is still there, the same fears, the same failure on a Thursday afternoon that has been there for thirty years. Many conclude the verse cannot be true of them.

But look at what the sentence actually says. It does not say if anyone feels new. It says if anyone is in Christ. The newness is a matter of location, not of sensation. It describes what is true of a person who has been transferred into Christ, on the authority of God who transferred him — and it was as true on the day it happened as it will be on the last day.

Which is why the honest Christian’s experience is not evidence against it. What has passed away is the old order you belonged to: the guilt, the condemnation, the ownership, the dominion of sin over you. What remains is the mopping up, and the mopping up is real work that takes a lifetime. But a man does not stop being a citizen because he still has an accent from the old country.

And notice the little word at the centre of it: behold. It is a word for pointing at something. Paul is not describing an inward process; he is drawing attention to an event that has already happened — the new creation begun, in Christ, in the middle of an old world that does not yet know it has been superseded.

verseByVerse.quote: All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.

Paul now names what has happened, and the word is one of the warmest in the New Testament.

Reconcile — katallassō — is not a religious term at all. It belongs to ordinary life: the ending of a quarrel, the restoration of a relationship that had broken down. It is what happens when two people who could not be in the same room are in the same room again.

Which tells you what the human problem is, underneath everything else. Not chiefly ignorance, or unhappiness, or unrealised potential. Estrangement. There is a relationship that is broken, and it is the one every other relationship was hanging from.

Now watch the direction, because it is everything. All this is from God. He is the one who reconciles. He is not the party being talked round. In every human quarrel, the offended person is the one who has to be approached, and the offender does the approaching. Here the offended party crossed the room.

Note carefully what that does and does not mean. It does not mean there was nothing to settle. Paul will say in three verses exactly what it cost, and the cost is the measure of how real the estrangement was. Human sin is not a misunderstanding that God waved away; it met the full weight of his opposition to it, and the meeting happened at the cross. What the verse rules out is the picture of a reluctant God being softened by a merciful Son. God himself is the reconciler. He was in Christ doing it.

Then the phrase that carries the whole gospel in six words: not counting their trespasses against them. It is an accounting term — not entering the item in the ledger. The debts are real and they are not being recorded. Paul says the same thing in Romans by quoting David: blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin (Rom. 4:8).

Stop there for a moment, because most people carry a version of that ledger inside them. There is a page in you with things on it you would not want read out — words to a parent now dead, a year you would give anything to have back, something nobody knows. You have been keeping the account even if God is not. This says the entry was not made. Not excused, not minimised, not forgotten in the sense of being overlooked. Charged to somebody else.

And then, astonishingly, the last clause of each verse: gave us the ministry of reconciliation, entrusting to us the message of reconciliation. God did the work and then handed the announcement to human beings — to the very people who had been on the wrong side of the quarrel. He could have written it in the sky. He chose to say it through the mouths of the reconciled, which means that the ordinary Christian talking awkwardly to a colleague is carrying something that was placed in his hands on purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.

Paul now names the office. An ambassador — presbeuō, the verb used of an imperial legate — is the personal representative of a sovereign in foreign territory. He does not compose the message; he carries it. His authority is entirely borrowed, and it is absolute while he is carrying it, because to hear him is to hear the one who sent him.

Three things follow from that, and they matter for anyone who has ever felt unqualified to speak about Christ.

The message is not yours to adjust. An ambassador who improved on his instructions would be recalled. This is the safeguard against every attempt to make the gospel more agreeable — and also the relief, because you are not responsible for whether it is well received.

The authority is not yours either, and that is the encouragement. The dignity of an ambassador has nothing to do with his personal impressiveness. A shy man with a letter from a king has more standing in that room than a magnificent man without one.

And the posting is foreign. Christians live in a country that is not theirs, representing a King the locals do not acknowledge. That accounts for a good deal of the strangeness of the Christian life. You were not meant to feel entirely at home here.

Then comes the sentence, and the tone of it is remarkable: God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.

Both verbs are words of entreaty. God does not summon; he appeals. Paul does not command; he implores. This is the Almighty, the offended party, the one who was in the right throughout — pleading with the people who wronged him to accept the peace he has already made at his own expense.

There is nothing else like it in the history of religion, and it ought to stop us. We think of God as the one who must be approached carefully. Here he is the one doing the approaching, and not with terms but with entreaty.

And notice who is being addressed. This is written to a church. Paul is imploring people who are already in the pews to be reconciled to God, and the reason is worth sitting with. It is entirely possible to be inside the congregation, holding the doctrine, doing the duties, and never to have made peace — to be at church and not at home. If the whole thing has been an arrangement you inherited rather than a quarrel that was ended, then this verse is not about the neighbours. It is addressed to you, and it is not a threat; it is a plea.

The word be reconciled is passive. Nobody reconciles himself. It has all been done; the only thing left is to stop refusing it. That is what the King is pleading for, through the mouths of his own ambassadors, in the third decade after his Son came to make it possible.

verseByVerse.quote: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

Twenty-two words in Greek, and there is nothing in Scripture more densely packed. Luther called this kind of sentence the great exchange. Take it apart slowly.

He made him to be sin. The subject is God the Father; the object is his Son. And the verb is deliberate and terrible: not he allowed, not it happened to him. God did this.

What can it mean? Not that Christ became sinful — the next clause forbids it, and so does the whole New Testament. It means that God treated him as though the sin were his. Everything that the sin of his people deserved was laid on him and dealt with there. The Old Testament had been teaching the shape of it for fifteen centuries: a hand laid on the head of an animal, guilt transferred, the innocent dying in the place of the guilty; and Isaiah had said it without a picture at all — the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isa. 53:6).

Who knew no sin. The one word in the sentence that could be said about no other human being who has ever lived. Not merely that he did not commit sins, but that he had no acquaintance with it from the inside: no divided motive, no appetite that had to be resisted, no private version of himself. His enemies watched him for three years looking for something and went away having to hire witnesses who could not agree.

And it is this one — the only person in history with nothing whatever owing — who is made sin. That is why the cry from the cross is what it is. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? is not a moment of confusion. It is what being made sin sounds like from the inside, in the one relationship that had never had a shadow across it since before the world was made.

So that in him we might become the righteousness of God. Now the exchange completes, and notice how far it goes. It does not say we might be forgiven, though we are. It does not say we might be treated as though we had not sinned, though we are. It says we become the righteousness of God — that his own standing before the Father is credited to us, and we are looked at in it.

Feel the two halves against each other. He got what was ours: the guilt, the charge, the abandonment. We get what was his: the standing, the welcome, the Father’s pleasure. Nothing was averaged; each side received the other’s whole account.

And everything turns on the last two words, in him. This is not a transfer of a substance into the believer, as though righteousness were now a quality you possess and might mislay on a bad week. It is true of you because of where you are. Which is why a Christian at his worst is no less righteous before God than at his best — the standing was never generated by the performance, and cannot be damaged by it.

There is nothing to add here and nothing to apply. He was made what he was not, so that we might be made what we could never be. The sinless one hanging in the place of the guilty, and the guilty walking away wearing his righteousness — this is what the Father planned, what the Son bore, and what the Spirit was sent to seal, and it will be the subject of the singing when this world is over.

Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer.<sup>17</sup>Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.<sup>18</sup>All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation;<sup>19</sup>that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.<sup>20</sup>Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.<sup>21</sup>For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

6.title: The Open Heart, the Catalogue of Hardships, and the Unequal Yoke
6.overview:
Chapter 6 continues the appeal of chapter 5, applying the ministry of reconciliation to the Corinthians themselves: do not receive the grace of God in vain. Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8 — “In a favourable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you” — and announces: “Behold, now is the favourable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” The urgency is eschatological: the time of grace is now; the window is open; do not treat it as ordinary.

Paul then delivers a remarkable self-commendation (vv. 4–10) — not of his achievements but of his sufferings and paradoxes. In afflictions, hardships, calamities; in beatings, imprisonments, riots; in labours, sleepless nights, hunger. And through it all: purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love, truthful speech, the power of God. The paradoxes of vv. 8–10 are among the most beautiful in the NT: treated as impostors but true; unknown yet well known; dying yet alive; punished yet not killed; sorrowful yet always rejoicing; poor yet making many rich; having nothing yet possessing everything.

The chapter then shifts to one of the most practically contested passages in Paul: the unequal yoke (vv. 14–18). Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers — what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? What fellowship has light with darkness? What accord has Christ with Belial? This passage has been applied to marriage, business partnerships, interfaith worship, and church membership. Its primary application in context is likely to idolatrous worship practices — but its principle extends to any relationship of spiritual partnership that requires compromise of the gospel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Open Heart and the Catalogue of Hardships
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul pleads with the Corinthians not to receive the grace of God in vain (v. 1) — not to treat the gospel as something received and then set aside. The Isaiah citation in v. 2 (Isa. 49:8) is drawn from the second Servant Song, where God addresses the Servant: “in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Paul applies it to the present moment: now is that day. Every moment of the church age is a day of salvation — but the doubled “behold, now” creates urgency. The grace that has been offered must not be allowed to lie dormant.

Verse 3 states the discipline that governs everything after it: he puts no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with the ministry. The concern is not his reputation but the removal of every avoidable barrier between a person and the gospel — while the one obstacle that must never be removed is the cross itself.

Paul then commends himself as a minister of God — not by citing credentials or impressive deeds but by cataloguing what he has endured and the character it has produced. The list in vv. 4–5 is grouped in threes: afflictions, hardships, calamities; beatings, imprisonments, riots; labours, sleepless nights, hunger. This is the resume of genuine apostolic ministry, and what is missing from it is any mention of results. Then comes the fruit (vv. 6–7): purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love, truthful speech, the power of God. The weapons of ministry are not rhetorical brilliance or social influence but the armour of righteousness, carried for the right hand and for the left.

The seven paradoxes of vv. 8–10 then set the world’s assessment against the reality: through honour and dishonour, slander and praise; treated as impostors and yet true; unknown yet well known; dying and behold alive; punished and not killed; sorrowful yet always rejoicing; poor yet making many rich; having nothing yet possessing everything. Each pair reads the visible half of the sentence and then supplies the half only God can see. The pairing of genuine sorrow with unbroken joy (v. 10) is one of the most useful things in the letter for ordinary Christians: the joy is not a denial of the grief but runs at a level the grief cannot reach.

The heart appeal at the close (vv. 11–13) is one of Paul’s most personal moments: “We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open.” The word “wide open” (peplatyntai — widened, enlarged) is the word for a heart expanded in generosity and love. Paul’s heart is not constricted toward the Corinthians; their hearts are constricted toward him — splanchna, the inward parts, cramped into a narrow space. He asks them, as to children, to widen their hearts also, and he asks without leverage: not for an apology, not for agreement about the past, only for room.
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue of hardships (vv. 4–5) is one of several in 2 Corinthians (cf. 4:8–9; 11:23–29; 12:10). Together they constitute Paul’s theology of the cross applied to ministry: the authentic apostle is identified not by spectacular results or impressive presence but by the pattern of cruciform suffering. This does not glorify suffering for its own sake; it identifies the shape that kingdom advance takes in a world that crucified its King. Those who carry the message of the cross will bear in their bodies the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: A young minister enters a hard urban church plant with ambitions of rapid growth and visible impact. After three years, he has a small congregation, many failures, and a life that looks more like Paul’s catalogue than his vision board. He questions his calling. This passage is the specific word for him: the catalogue of hardships is not evidence of failed ministry but of authentic ministry. The question is not whether ministry is fruitful by visible metrics but whether the minister is conducting himself with the character described in vv. 6–7.

verseByVerse.quote: Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

He has just implored them, on Christ’s behalf, to be reconciled to God. Now the second half of the appeal: having received grace, do not let it lie there.

Working together with him. The word is one Paul made his own — a fellow-worker, a colleague on the same job. It is a staggering way to describe the relationship between an apostle and God, and it should not be softened into metaphor. God does the work; he does it through people; and the people are genuinely working.

Then the appeal: not to receive the grace of God in vain. The phrase means to no purpose, emptily — a gift that arrives and produces nothing.

This raises a question honest readers ask and deserve a straight answer to. Can a Christian receive grace and have it come to nothing? Does this passage threaten someone’s salvation?

Take it carefully. Paul has just told this church that they are a new creation, sealed and guaranteed by the Spirit; he does not now suggest that God’s work in them might quietly fail. What he is warning against is a life in which the grace received makes no difference — grace treated as a transaction completed rather than a relationship begun. That can describe two different people. It can describe a believer who is wasting years he will not get back. It can also describe someone who has all the appearance of faith and has never actually come. Paul does not sort them here, and neither should we; the warning is addressed to everyone in the room and is meant to be taken personally rather than assigned to somebody else.

Then he quotes Isaiah 49:8, and it repays knowing where the words come from. In Isaiah, God is speaking to his Servant — the one who will be a light for the nations and whose work will reach to the end of the earth. God tells the Servant that his cry has been heard and his day of help has come.

Paul takes that promise, made to Christ, and says it is being handed on. And then he does something with it that should stop the reader: Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Twice behold, twice now. The prophecy is not approaching. It is here, and it is here today.

Which is worth saying plainly, because almost everyone reading has a version of later. Later, when work settles. Later, when the children are older. Later, when I have got a few things straightened out. Scripture never speaks about God’s dealings in the future tense of convenience. It says today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb. 3:15), and it says it because a heart that intends to respond eventually is already hardening while it waits.

Nobody has been promised the favourable time twice. And notice, before that thought is allowed to become merely frightening, what the word actually is. Not now is the day of warning. Now is the day of salvation — the door standing open at this moment, on the authority of a promise made to the Servant and kept.

verseByVerse.quote: We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry,

A short verse, and a discipline that costs more than it looks.

The word for obstacle is proskopē — something you strike your foot against, a stumbling block. Paul’s concern is not that he might be criticised. It is that something about him might become the reason a person does not come to Christ.

Note the range: in anyone’s way. Not just the sympathetic, not just the congregation. Anyone.

He was fiercely practical about this. It is why he refused financial support from Corinth, working nights at a trade so that nobody could say he was in it for money (1 Cor. 9:12–15; 2 Cor. 11:7–9). It is why he arranged for the collection to be carried by men the churches themselves had chosen, so no accusation could be made about the handling of it (8:20–21). It is why he became all things to all people — not to be liked, but to remove every avoidable barrier between a person and the gospel.

Distinguish two things here, because confusing them has done harm in both directions.

Some obstacles must not be removed. The cross is a stumbling block by nature; Paul says so (1 Cor. 1:23). A gospel adjusted until nobody trips over it has been tampered with — the very thing he renounced in 4:2. If people are offended by sin being called sin, or by Christ being the only way, that offence is the gospel doing its work and it is not to be smoothed away.

But every other obstacle is ours to deal with, and there are more of them than we like to count. The manner that makes people feel small. The money question that was never explained. The political opinion nailed to the pulpit as though it were doctrine. The way we speak about people who are not in the room. The reputation for being unreachable, or unforgiving, or slightly dishonest about small things. None of these is the gospel. All of them can be, and regularly are, the reason somebody stops listening.

So here is a test that can be run this week, and it is uncomfortable because the answer is usually available immediately. Think of someone you know who is not a Christian and who knows you are. Is there anything in how you have behaved toward them that gives them a legitimate reason not to take you seriously? Not an excuse — a reason. Something you would have to explain away.

If there is, that is a stone in the road, and it is yours to move rather than theirs to climb over. The apostle worked half the night with his hands for years to avoid leaving one.

And notice how the sentence ends: so that no fault may be found with our ministry. Not with him — with the ministry. He is not protecting his name. He is protecting the message from being discredited by its messenger, which is the only reason a Christian’s reputation is worth anything at all.

verseByVerse.quote: but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger;
verseByVerse.commentary:
but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger;

His rivals came with letters. Paul offers a different sort of credential, and this is the first of the great hardship catalogues in the letter.

Notice the heading he puts over the whole list: by great endurance. The word is hypomonē, met already at 1:6 — a remaining under, staying put beneath a weight. It is not the ability to avoid trouble but the refusal to walk out from under it. Everything that follows is offered as evidence of that one thing.

The list comes in three groups of three, and they move from the general to the sharply particular.

First, three broad words for pressure: afflictions, hardships, calamities. The middle one means, literally, a narrow place — being wedged where there is no room. The third means a strait or tight corner. This is the shape of the life: pressed, hemmed in, cornered.

Second, three things done to him by other people: beatings, imprisonments, riots. Each of these has a face attached to it. Someone swung the rod. Someone turned the key. A crowd gathered and decided. In chapter 11 he will give the numbers, and they are appalling: five times thirty-nine lashes, three beatings with rods, one stoning.

Third, three things he did to himself for the sake of the work: labors, sleepless nights, hunger. The word for labours means toil to the point of exhaustion. The sleepless nights are not insomnia but nights deliberately spent — travelling, working at his trade, praying, sitting up with people. The hunger is not fasting; it is going without because there was nothing.

What is striking is what is missing from the list. There are no results. No church-planting statistics, no numbers converted, no cities won. If a man today were asked to commend his ministry, this is not the document he would produce.

And that is exactly Paul’s point, aimed at a church that had begun assessing ministers the way the world assesses anyone. His credential is not what he has achieved but what he has absorbed and not quit.

There is a word here for the person whose service has produced very little that can be counted. The years in a small church that never grew. The teaching to eight children, six of whom moved away. The praying for a family member across two decades with nothing to show. On this list, none of that is failure. Endurance is the credential, and it is the one thing in Christian service that cannot be faked, borrowed, or produced quickly.

The Lord said the same to a church under pressure at Smyrna, promising nothing about outcomes and everything about the end: Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life (Rev. 2:10). Faithful, not successful. The two are frequently confused, and only one of them is ever commanded.

verseByVerse.quote: by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; by truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;
verseByVerse.commentary:
by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; by truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;

The list continues, and it turns inward. Paul has said what has been done to him; now he says what has been produced in him. This is the more searching half, because a man can endure a great deal and remain unpleasant.

Purity heads it — cleanness of motive, the state of a man with nothing to keep out of sight. Knowledge is not cleverness but the true understanding of God and his gospel; warmth without content is no credential. Patience is makrothymia, literally long-temperedness: the fuse that takes a very long time to burn. It is used of God himself, and it means the ability to be wronged by the same person repeatedly and not retaliate.

Kindness is the practical, unglamorous form of love — the useful act, the small mercy. It is possible to be doctrinally impeccable and unkind, and this list forbids it.

Then, in the middle of a list of virtues, something that is not a virtue at all: the Holy Spirit. Paul does not explain the intrusion, and the absence of explanation is the point. None of the qualities on either side of him is native to a human being. He is named among them because he is the one producing them.

Genuine love — literally love without hypocrisy, love that is not acted. The word for hypocrite was the word for a stage player. There is a way of doing all the right things for people while performing, and everybody can eventually tell.

Then two more: truthful speech, the word of truth, saying what is so; and the power of God, without which the whole list is a moral programme and not a ministry.

And finally the image that gathers them up: the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left. A Roman soldier carried the sword in the right hand and the shield on the left. So this is armament for attack and for defence — and the material of both is righteousness. It is one of Paul’s recurring pictures; he will give it in full to the Ephesians, where the belt is truth and the shield is faith (Eph. 6:13–17).

Take the picture seriously and it changes how a Christian handles opposition. When you are misrepresented, the instinct is to defend yourself by the means being used against you — the counter-story, the quiet word to the right person, the version that puts you in a better light. Paul says the shield in the left hand is righteousness. Not cleverness, not the better argument, not a well-placed friend. You defend yourself by continuing to live rightly, and you attack by the same means, and there is nothing else in either hand.

It is slower than the alternative and it is very much harder. It is also the only defence that does not have to be maintained, because a life is a great deal more difficult to answer than an argument.

verseByVerse.quote: through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;

Now the paradoxes begin, and they are among the most compressed things Paul ever wrote. Each one has the same shape: what people see, then what is actually so.

First the pairs that come at him from outside. Honor and dishonor. Slander and praise. Note that he does not say he receives one and not the other; he passes through both. In the same week a man may be admired in one town and vilified in the next, and both reports concern the same person doing the same work.

That is worth holding on to, because most people are governed by these two more than they know. We adjust ourselves, often without noticing, toward whatever produces praise and away from whatever produces criticism, and after twenty years of small adjustments a life has been shaped by other people’s opinions. Paul walks through both without changing direction, which is only possible for a man who is expecting to give his account somewhere else (5:10).

As impostors, and yet are true. The word means a deceiver, a fraud — someone pretending to be what he is not. This was actually being said about him. And his answer is not an argument; it is a fact: and yet are true.

As unknown, and yet well known. Nobody in Rome had heard of him. He was a provincial of no standing, and in most rooms he entered he would have had to explain who he was. And he is well known — the same verb used of God knowing his people. He is known where it counts. There is real comfort here for anyone who has spent a life doing something no one notices. The question is never whether you are known; it is only ever by whom.

As dying, and behold, we live. The behold is a note of astonishment — he is surprised himself. By every reasonable assessment he should be dead: the stoning at Lystra, the night and day adrift at sea, the affliction in Asia. And here he is, writing.

As punished, and yet not killed. The word carries the sense of being disciplined or corrected. Behind it lies a psalm Paul knew well: The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death (Ps. 118:18). The floggings had not been random cruelty only; a Father had been at work in them, and had set the limit himself.

Which is the thread running through all four. The world’s assessment of a Christian is not merely unkind; it is working with incomplete information. It reads the visible half of the sentence and stops. And the second half, in every case, is supplied by a God who is not impressed by appearances and has never once mistaken one of his servants for a fraud.

verseByVerse.quote: as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.

Three more, and they go deeper than the four before them, because these are not about how others see him. They are about what is true inside.

As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. This may be the most useful sentence in the chapter for ordinary Christians, and it is regularly flattened by being read as though one cancels the other.

It does not say sorrowful, but cheering up. It does not say the sorrow was a misunderstanding to be corrected by better theology. Both verbs stand, and the second has always attached to it. Paul is describing a man who is genuinely grieving and genuinely rejoicing at the same time, in the same hour, about different things.

Anyone who has stood at a Christian funeral has seen it. The grief is not reduced; a real person is gone and the loss is exactly as large as it feels. And underneath it, not instead of it, there is something that will not go out — because the same person who is being buried is with the Lord, and the God who arranged that is still what he was last week. Two floors in one house. Paul says elsewhere, of the same reality, sorrowing yet always rejoicing is possible because Christian joy was never built on circumstances and therefore is not demolished when they collapse.

This liberates the believer from a cruel expectation. Christians are frequently made to feel that grief is a failure of faith, that a really trusting person would be at peace by now. That is not in the Bible. Jesus wept at a grave he was about to empty (Jn. 11:35). What the gospel promises is not the absence of sorrow but a joy that runs at a level sorrow cannot reach.

As poor, yet making many rich. Paul owned almost nothing — a cloak, some books, the parchments (2 Tim. 4:13). And whole provinces were made rich through him, in the only currency that survives. The pattern is his Lord’s: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (8:9), a sentence Paul is two chapters away from writing.

As having nothing, yet possessing everything. The last one is the largest. A man with no property, no security, no home and no legal protection says he possesses everything — and he is not being brave. He had already told this church why: all things are yours, whether the world or life or death or the present or the future — all are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (1 Cor. 3:21–23).

That is the arithmetic of the kingdom, and it is not consolation for people who have missed out. The one who owns everything gave himself to his people, and everything he owns came with him. There is no Christian anywhere, however little he has, who is not an heir of the world — and no one outside Christ, however much he holds, who owns anything he will still have in a hundred years.

verseByVerse.quote: We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.

The rhetoric stops. For the first time in the letter he uses their name — Corinthians — and it is the sound of a man dropping his voice.

We have spoken freely to you. Literally, our mouth is open to you. Nothing has been withheld, nothing said behind a hand. He has told them about the affliction in Asia, about despairing of life, about being unable to preach at Troas for anxiety. A man defending his authority has spent five chapters admitting weakness.

Our heart is wide open. The verb means widened, enlarged, made spacious. There is room in him for them; whatever they have done, they have not been shut out.

Then the diagnosis, and it is put with great delicacy: You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. The word for restricted means to be cramped, confined in a narrow space — it is the opposite of the widened heart. And the word for affections is splanchna, the inward parts. Hebrew and Greek alike located deep feeling in the gut rather than the chest, and the word is not decorative; it is the same one used of the Lord’s compassion when he saw the crowds.

So the trouble in this relationship is named exactly. It is not that Paul has withdrawn. It is that they have narrowed. There is a cramped place in them where he used to be.

Anyone who has been on either side of a cooled relationship knows how precisely this describes it. Nothing is formally wrong. The greetings still happen. But something has closed, and the person on the outside can feel the reduced room without being able to point to a moment.

Notice how Paul handles it. He does not accuse them of sin, though something is wrong. He does not demand an explanation. He describes what is true — his heart open, theirs narrow — and leaves it in front of them. That is remarkably hard to do. The instinct is either to pretend not to notice or to make an accusation that forces a defence, and both close the door further.

And the deeper point: constriction of heart is a real spiritual condition, not merely a social awkwardness. A narrowed heart cannot receive much, which is why the Corinthians could not take in what Paul was giving them. Their capacity had shrunk. Suspicion does that; so does resentment held for a long time; so does the quiet decision to protect yourself after being hurt once. It always feels like prudence and it always costs the same thing — the ability to be loved.

Which is worth turning on yourself. Where has your heart narrowed? There is usually a name attached to the answer, and there is usually a good reason, and the reason has never yet made anybody less confined.

verseByVerse.quote: In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.

The whole appeal comes to one request, and there is not a trace of authority in it.

He could have commanded. He is an apostle; he founded this church; he has just spent ten verses laying out what it has cost him. Instead: widen your hearts also. The same word as verse 11 — make room, open up, be enlarged.

It is one of the most exposed moments in Paul’s letters. He is asking to be loved, by people who have not been loving him, and he is asking without leverage. Anyone who has done this knows the risk: a request for affection can be refused, and the refusal costs more than never having asked.

Then the parenthesis, and it is doing careful work: (I speak as to children). Two things at once. It is affectionate — he is their father in the faith, as he told them plainly in the earlier letter (1 Cor. 4:15), and a father may say things to his children that a colleague could not say. And it is a small, deliberate reduction of the pressure. By flagging that he is speaking as a parent speaks, he lets them off the formality of an adult negotiation. He is not building a case. He is asking.

Notice also what he is not asking for. Not an apology. Not agreement about the past. Not for the offenders to be dealt with. Only for room in their affections.

There is a lesson here for anyone in a damaged relationship, and it works in families as well as churches. We tend to make the reopening of a relationship conditional on settling the history: who was right, what was said, who should speak first. Paul, who had by any reckoning the stronger case, sets all of it aside and asks for the one thing that would actually change anything. Widen your heart. The record can be sorted out later, or never; a heart that has opened usually finds the record matters less than it did.

And observe that the widening is something he asks them to do. A heart does not enlarge by itself, and it does not enlarge by waiting to feel differently. It is an act — the visit made, the message sent, the deliberate refusal to run the grievance through your mind one more time, the choice to think the better explanation of what they did.

Behind it all is the pattern that made Paul’s heart wide in the first place. He had been the enemy. He had watched Stephen die and gone looking for more. And the room made for him in the church of God was not made because he apologised his way in; it was made by the one whose heart was so wide that it took in the man who was hunting him. Nobody who has been received like that can plead a shortage of room.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–7:1 — Do Not Be Unequally Yoked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The command “do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (v. 14, mē ginesthe heterozygountes apistois) draws on the Old Testament prohibition of yoking an ox and a donkey together (Deut. 22:10) — animals of different strengths and stride that cannot pull together. In the new covenant context the yoke is spiritual: a binding partnership that requires a shared direction with those opposed to Christ. What is not in view is ordinary friendship, employment or neighbourliness, and it is never a reason to leave a marriage already entered — Paul is explicit on both points elsewhere (1 Cor. 5:9–10; 7:12–13).

Paul supports the command with a sequence of rhetorical questions: what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? What fellowship has light with darkness? What accord has Christ with Belial (v. 15 — a name for Satan in Jewish apocalyptic, from a Hebrew word meaning worthlessness, so that the comparison is between everything and a name meaning nothing)? What has a believer in common with an unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols? The final question is the key: the Corinthians are the temple of the living God (v. 16) — the dwelling place of God himself, who says he will make his dwelling among them and walk among them. What a believer joins himself to is therefore never a private matter of preference; Someone is already resident.

The passage closes with a chain of Old Testament citations (Lev. 26:12; Ezek. 37:27; Isa. 52:11; 2 Sam. 7:14; Jer. 31:1) that together describe the new covenant community as the people among whom God dwells. Verse 17 calls them to go out, be separate, and touch no unclean thing — a separation not from people but from defilement, as the exiles leaving Babylon were told not to carry Babylon home — and adds the promise “then I will welcome you.” Verse 18 crowns the chain by handing the church the charter of the house of David: “I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty,” with 2 Samuel’s singular “son” deliberately widened to sons and daughters. The cleansing from “every defilement of body and spirit” (7:1) is the practical application: knowing these promises, make holiness complete.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage has been applied to several specific situations: (1) Marriage between believers and unbelievers — the most common application, supported by the principle if not the primary context. 1 Cor. 7:39 (she is free to marry “only in the Lord”) is the direct marriage prohibition. (2) Formal religious partnerships — interfaith worship, ecumenical agreements that require treating fundamental doctrinal differences as unimportant. (3) Business partnerships that require ethical compromise. The principle is: any relationship of primary spiritual allegiance that requires pulling in the same direction as one who is opposed to Christ creates an incompatible yoke. Ordinary friendship, working relationships, and engagement with unbelievers are not in view — Paul explicitly says in 1 Cor. 5:9–10 that he did not mean to avoid all contact with the immoral of the world.
verseByVerse.examples: A senior pastor receives an invitation to co-host a community prayer service with leaders from several faiths, including those who explicitly deny the Trinity and the uniqueness of Christ as Saviour. He must decide whether this is a civic engagement (speaking to the community) or a spiritual partnership (worshipping together). This passage suggests the distinction matters: representing the church’s concern for the community is different from implying that all faith traditions are pulling the same spiritual yoke toward the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?

The subject changes abruptly, and the abruptness has led some to think this paragraph was originally somewhere else. But the connection is there. He has just asked them to widen their hearts toward him; now he tells them there is one direction in which the heart must not be opened. A church that has room for everything has room for nothing in particular.

The image comes from farming. Heterozygountes is built from different and yoke, and behind it stands the old law: You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together (Deut. 22:10). The reason is practical rather than ceremonial. Two animals of different height, strength and stride, fastened to the same beam, cannot work. Each is pulled off its line by the other, the furrow wanders, and both are injured by the harness. It is not that the donkey is wicked. It is that they cannot pull together.

So what is being forbidden? The word is about a shared yoke — a binding partnership with a common direction. And it is important to be precise, because this verse has been used to justify things Paul explicitly refused.

It does not mean avoiding unbelievers. Paul had already had to correct exactly that misunderstanding in his earlier letter: he had told them not to associate with the immoral, not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world … since then you would need to go out of the world (1 Cor. 5:9–10). Friendship, employment, neighbourliness, hospitality, business dealings, marriage to an unbeliever already entered — none of these is in view, and a Christian who withdraws from the world has misread the whole New Testament and disqualified himself from the ministry of chapter 5.

What is in view is a yoke: a binding of your direction to someone whose direction is opposed to Christ, in a way you cannot easily undo. The clearest applications are the obvious ones — a Christian choosing to marry someone who is not one (he gives the rule elsewhere: she is free to marry, only in the Lord, 1 Cor. 7:39); a partnership that requires you to serve two masters; a formal religious alliance that treats the identity of God as a detail.

And a word must be said straight to the person for whom this is not a decision but a situation. If you are already married to someone who does not believe, this verse is not about you, and no one should be allowed to use it against you. Paul’s instruction in that case could not be plainer: do not leave. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him (1 Cor. 7:13), and the reason he gives is hope — how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? The command here is about yokes you are choosing. It is never a reason to break one you are already carrying, and God has used a great many such marriages to save the other half of them.

Then the two questions, and they are not really questions. What partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? What fellowship has light with darkness? The second answers itself in a way anybody can test. Light and darkness do not negotiate, and they do not blend. One of them simply ends where the other begins.

verseByVerse.quote: What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?

The questions keep coming, and this one is sharper than the rest, because Paul now names the opposition.

Belial is a Hebrew word, and it is not really a name to begin with. It means worthlessness — something with no profit in it, a thing that yields nothing. The Old Testament uses it as a description: the men of Gibeah who surrounded the house were sons of Belial, worthless men (Judg. 19:22). By the time of Paul, Jewish writers had turned the word into a title for the chief adversary. It is the only place the New Testament uses it.

He could have written Satan, as he does elsewhere in this letter. He chose the word that means worthless, and the choice is doing something. Set the names side by side: Christ, the Anointed One, in whom every promise of God is Yes — and Belial, the one whose entire estate is worth nothing. That is the actual comparison. It is not two powers of comparable weight dividing the world between them. It is everything, against a name that means nothing.

What accord — the word is the one behind our symphony: sounding together, in tune. Christ and Belial do not make a chord. Anything that tries to hold both will be, quite literally, discordant, and everybody listening will hear it.

Then the last question, and it is put in the plainest terms of the five: what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever? The word portion is a word for an allotted share — the piece of land a family received in Israel, what falls to a person by right. It is about what you have in common at the deepest level.

And here the honest reader must be careful not to hear more than is said. Paul is not saying believers and unbelievers have nothing in common; they share a world, a workplace, a street, a humanity, and Christians who forget that become insufferable. He is saying that at the level of ultimate allegiance — what your life is finally for — there is no shared portion. Two people can share a house and a mortgage and thirty years of affection, and still be walking in opposite directions on the one road that goes anywhere.

Which is why the yoke matters and why the question is worth putting to yourself about the partnerships you are actually in. Not is this person pleasant? They often are. Ask instead: if this arrangement is pulling in a direction, where does the direction go, and am I free to stop?

And take the comfort in the name he chose. Whatever is on the other side of the yoke, it is not a rival to Christ. It is Belial — a name meaning nothing at all, wearing the borrowed authority of an age that is passing. He has already been judged, and the one who judged him is the one every believer is joined to.

verseByVerse.quote: What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

The last of the five questions arrives, and it turns out to be the one the others were climbing toward. The reason a believer cannot be yoked to the darkness is not chiefly a rule about company. It is a fact about what he now is.

We are the temple of the living God. Stop and take that in, because the Corinthians would have heard it against a skyline. Corinth had temples — to Apollo, to Aphrodite on the height above the city, to half a dozen others. A temple was a building, and what made it a temple was that the god was understood to live there.

Paul says the temple is the congregation. Not the building they met in; there was no building. The people. God has moved out of architecture and into a group of former idolaters, dockworkers and freedmen in a Greek port.

Then he supports it with the Old Testament, and it is worth seeing what he does. The quotation is a weave of several promises — Leviticus 26:12, where God says he will walk among his people; Ezekiel 37:27, the promise of a dwelling in the middle of them; Jeremiah’s new covenant refrain that they shall be his people. Every one of those was given to Israel, about a tabernacle and a temple and a land. Paul says they have landed here.

And the words themselves repay slowing down. I will make my dwelling among them — the verb is built from the word for a tent, the same root as the tent of chapter 5, and the same word John uses when he says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (Jn. 1:14). God pitches his tent in the camp.

And walk among them. Not visit. Walk about among them, at home, as he walked in the garden in the cool of the day before anything went wrong.

Now the practical force of it, which is what Paul is after. If you are the place where God lives, then what you join yourself to is not a private matter of preference. You are not deciding what to do with your own life; you are deciding what to bring into his house. That is why the questions have been getting steadily more serious. It is not that idols are intellectually silly. It is that there is Someone already resident.

And there is a comfort in it larger than the warning. The whole story of the Bible has been God working out how to live with people who could not survive his presence — a garden lost, a tent in the wilderness with a curtain across it, a temple with a room nobody could enter but once a year with blood. Then a body, and the curtain torn from the top. And now, an ordinary congregation of unremarkable people, and the living God at home in the middle of them, walking about. He has wanted this from the beginning, and he paid what it cost to have it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,

The quotation continues, now from Isaiah 52:11 — words originally spoken to the exiles as they left Babylon, carrying the vessels of the temple home. Paul applies them to a church living inside a pagan city.

And the first thing to establish is what they cannot mean, because this verse has done a great deal of damage in the hands of people who wanted a reason to withdraw.

They cannot mean physical separation from unbelievers. The same apostle wrote that avoiding the immoral of this world would require going out of the world altogether (1 Cor. 5:10), and the same Lord prayed for his disciples not that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one (Jn. 17:15). The Christian is not withdrawn from society; he is planted in it, as light is planted in a dark room. Every retreat into a Christian enclave, every version of the faith that measures holiness by how few outsiders you know, has misread this sentence.

What then is being commanded? Look at the third phrase, which controls the other two: touch no unclean thing. It is not people who are to be avoided but defilement. The exiles leaving Babylon were not told to hate Babylonians; they were told not to carry Babylon home with them.

So the separation is real and it runs along a different line from the one we usually draw. It is not a line between us and them. It is a line through the middle of your own life, and it falls at every point where the surrounding culture would make itself at home in the temple of God — what you watch, what you are willing to laugh at, how you get money, what you do with your private hours, the ambitions you have absorbed without ever examining them.

That is a harder command than physical withdrawal, which is why physical withdrawal has always been the more popular option. It is entirely possible to live in a Christian bubble and be thoroughly Babylonian inside it, and possible to work in the least Christian environment imaginable and touch nothing unclean.

Then, at the end of the verse, the thing that turns a command into gospel: then I will welcome you. The verb is the word for taking someone in — receiving a guest, gathering someone to yourself.

Note the order, and do not get it backwards. This is not make yourself clean and then God may accept you; the whole letter has said the opposite, and chapter 5 ended with the righteousness of God given to people who had none. The welcome is what God does for his own. But he says it here because a life divided between two houses does not feel welcomed, whatever is true of it — and the way back into the enjoyment of what you already have is to stop carrying Babylon into the room where he lives.

verseByVerse.quote: and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”

The chain of quotations ends here, and Paul has saved the greatest for last.

The words come from 2 Samuel 7:14, and it is worth knowing exactly who they were spoken to. David wanted to build God a house. God refused, and turned the whole thing round: David would not build him a house; he would build David one. And of David’s son he said, I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son.

That promise belonged to the royal line. It was the charter of the house of David, the sentence that stood behind every king of Judah and finally behind the Messiah himself. It was not a promise for the general population, and it was certainly not a promise for Gentiles in a port city on the far side of the Aegean.

Paul hands it to them.

And notice the one alteration he makes, because it is not carelessness. Where 2 Samuel says a son, singular, Paul writes sons and daughters. The promise made to one royal heir has become a promise to a family, and the family includes women — which needed saying in a world where inheritance ran through sons. In Christ, a slave woman in Corinth stands in the sentence that was spoken over the throne of David.

How can that be? Only one way. The Son to whom the promise properly belonged took his inheritance and shared it. He is the firstborn among many brothers (Rom. 8:29), and everyone joined to him is inside his standing. This is why the Christian may say Father at all, and it is why the word is not a metaphor: see what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are (1 Jn. 3:1).

Then the title Paul chooses for God in the same breath, and the collision is deliberate: says the Lord Almighty. The word renders the Hebrew Lord of hosts — the God of armies, commander of everything that exists. That is the one who has just said he will be your father.

Hold the two together and do not let either soften the other. A father who is not almighty can love you and be unable to help; an almighty God who is not a father can help and have no particular interest in doing so. Here is one Person who is both, saying so under his own name.

And this is where the argument about yokes has been going the whole time. Paul is not fencing them in. He is telling them what they would be trading, and who they belong to. The Lord of hosts has taken the promise he made to a king and given it away to fishermen and slaves and idolaters who came in late, and he calls them sons and daughters, and he means it.
