7.title: Godly Grief and the Joy of Reconciliation
7.overview:
Chapter 7 completes the autobiographical section of the letter (chs. 1–7) with Paul’s account of his reunion with Titus and the report of the Corinthians’ response to the severe letter. Having urged the Corinthians to open their hearts (6:13), Paul returns to the theme of his own joy in them. Despite the afflictions in Macedonia — external conflicts and internal fears — God comforted him by the coming of Titus, who brought news of the Corinthians’ longing to see Paul, their mourning over the situation, and their zeal for him. Paul’s heart is full of joy.

The theological centrepiece of the chapter is the distinction between godly grief and worldly grief (vv. 9–11). The severe letter caused the Corinthians grief — but it was godly grief, and godly grief produces repentance leading to salvation. Worldly grief, by contrast, produces death. The fruits of godly grief in the Corinthians are then listed: earnestness, eagerness to clear themselves, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, punishment. In every way they demonstrated themselves to be innocent in the matter. Paul insists that his letter was not written for the sake of the one who did wrong or the one who was wronged, but to reveal to the Corinthians their own earnest care for Paul before God.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.

Everything hangs on the first three words. Since we have these promises — the ones just quoted: I will dwell among them, I will be their God, I will be a father to you, you shall be sons and daughters. The command that follows is not the condition of the promises; it is the consequence of them.

Get that order wrong and the Christian life becomes unbearable. Read as cleanse yourself and then God will dwell in you, this verse turns holiness into a probation with no visible end. Read as Paul wrote it, holiness is what a person does because the promises are already his and the house is already occupied.

Note also the word beloved, dropped into the middle of a command. He is not haranguing them. This is the one place in the letter he uses it.

Then the work itself: let us cleanse ourselves. Two things are worth noticing. First, let us — he includes himself. There is no holiness plateau from which an apostle issues instructions. Second, ourselves. This is something a Christian does, actively. It does not contradict the earlier chapters, where all the verbs had God as their subject; both are true and Scripture holds them together without embarrassment. God works in you, and you work — work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Phil. 2:12–13).

From every defilement of body and spirit. Both. Corinth would have understood the first easily — a city with a reputation for it. The second is the one religious people forget. Defilement of the spirit is the sin that leaves no mark on the body at all: the settled contempt, the appetite for other people’s failures, the ambition that would step over someone, the private rehearsal of grievances. A man can keep his body scrupulously clean and be filthy in a place nobody can see, and Paul refuses to let the categories be separated.

Bringing holiness to completion. The verb means to finish, to carry through to the end. It is a process with a direction, which is honest about the pace. Nobody is finished. But a Christian ought to be able to name something he is further on with than he was five years ago, and if he cannot, the verb is worth thinking about.

And the atmosphere it is done in: in the fear of God. Not the terror of a God who might reject you — Paul has spent six chapters removing that. It is the awe of someone who has grasped who is living in the house. Nobody has to be told to be careful in a room they know is occupied by someone they love and revere.

Which is the whole logic of the verse in one picture. If God has come to live in you, the question is never whether you are permitted to keep the defilement. It is what on earth it is still doing in his house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–16 — Godly Grief, Worldly Grief, and Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul picks up from 6:13 (“widen your hearts also”) with the resumed appeal: “Make room in your hearts for us” (v. 2). He insists on his integrity: he has wronged no one, corrupted no one, taken advantage of no one — three charges that were evidently in circulation. He is not saying this to condemn them (v. 3) but out of the abundance of his love — they are in his heart, to die together and to live together, the order of the verbs putting death first. He boasts about them; he has great confidence in them; he is filled with comfort and overflowing with joy in all his affliction (v. 4).

The account of meeting Titus in Macedonia (vv. 5–7) is a rare glimpse into Paul’s interior life: the afflictions were external (fighting without) and internal (fear within). He was genuinely anxious. God comforted him — under the title “God, who comforts the downcast” — and he did it not by a vision but through the ordinary means of a trusted friend’s arrival. The comfort was not merely that the situation was resolved but that their longing, mourning, and zeal for Paul himself were real. He was not alone.

Verse 8 is one of the most human sentences in the New Testament: Paul does not regret the severe letter — though he did regret it, during the weeks of waiting, and says so in writing. The regret ended when he saw what the letter had done. The grief it caused was real, severe, and temporary.

The theological distinction of vv. 9–11 is one of the most practically important in the New Testament. Paul is glad not merely that the Corinthians grieved but that they grieved in a godly way. Godly grief is the grief that responds to the truth about one’s sin and produces repentance leading to salvation — a repentance “without regret.” Worldly grief is the grief that focuses on consequences, social shame, and the emotional discomfort of the situation — it produces death because it never reaches genuine repentance. The test of grief is its direction: toward God or toward self? Verse 11 then supplies seven visible marks of the real thing: earnestness, eagerness to clear themselves, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, and punishment actually carried out.

Verse 12 gives the letter’s true purpose, and it is not the one anyone would guess: not for the offender’s sake, nor for the sake of the one wronged (which is Paul himself), but that their own earnestness might be revealed to them, in the sight of God. The crisis did not create their love; it brought it out where they could see it.

The chapter closes in a place chapter 2 could not have predicted (vv. 13–16). Paul is comforted, and rejoices still more at the joy of Titus, whose spirit was refreshed by them. The boasts Paul had made about the Corinthians before Titus went — made when the evidence was thin — proved true, and he was not put to shame. Titus’s affection for them has grown; they received him with fear and trembling, handling the conflict at the altitude it deserved. And the last word of the chapter, addressed to the church of the factions and the lawsuits, is “complete confidence.”
verseByVerse.theology: The distinction between godly grief and worldly grief is pastorally crucial. Worldly grief (hē tou kosmou lypē) can look like repentance: tears, distress, self-accusation. But its focus is on the pain caused to oneself (loss of reputation, loss of relationships, loss of comfort) rather than on the offence against God. Judas displays worldly grief — he is distraught over what he has done, even returns the money, but cannot receive forgiveness; he destroys himself. Peter displays godly grief — the same tears, the same self-accusation, but directed toward the face of Jesus, resolved by Jesus’s restoration. The direction of the grief determines its outcome.
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor is confronted with evidence of long-term financial dishonesty. He weeps, expresses remorse, describes how devastated he is — by the damage to his reputation, the pain to his family, the end of his ministry. He never directly addresses the harm done to those he stole from, or the offence against God. His leadership team recognises, with the categories of this passage, that they are witnessing worldly grief — real grief, but pointed in the wrong direction. Genuine repentance would ask different questions: not “what have I lost?” but “against whom have I sinned, and what must I do to make it right?”

verseByVerse.quote: Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.

He picks up exactly where he left off at 6:13 — widen your hearts, now make room. The subject never really changed; the paragraph about yokes was a necessary detour, and here is the appeal again.

Then three denials, and they are worth hearing as answers to charges that were actually being made. We have wronged no one — nobody has been treated unjustly. We have corrupted no one — the word means to ruin or spoil, and it may point at the accusation that his teaching damaged people. We have taken advantage of no one — this is the money charge, the same verb used in 2:11 of Satan swindling someone; the suggestion that the collection was a scheme. He will have to answer that one at length in chapter 12.

Three flat denials, no explanation, no evidence produced. There is a kind of accusation that cannot be disproved and should not be dignified with a defence, only with a plain contradiction and a life that goes on being what it is.

And then, immediately, the sentence that shows what kind of man is speaking: I do not say this to condemn you. He has just been forced to deny that he is a fraud, and his first concern is that they should not feel accused by his denial.

Anyone who has been on the wrong end of a false rumour will recognise how rare that is. The natural motion, once you finally get to speak, is to make somebody pay for the months of silence. Paul closes that door before it opens.

Then the reason he can afford to: you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together. This is covenant language — the promise Ruth made to Naomi, the bond David and Jonathan swore. It means: there is no circumstance in which I stop being yours. Not if you believe the rumours. Not if you never apologise.

Notice the order of the two verbs, because it is not the natural one. We would say live and die together; Paul puts dying first. He is not describing an association that would survive death if it came to that. He is describing one that has already been through it — a relationship built by people who died with Christ and now live in him, and therefore cannot be ended by anything smaller.

That is the standard for Christian relationships, and it is a rebuke to how easily most of them are abandoned. Churches are left over a decision; friendships end over a comment; families divide over an estate and never recover. What Paul offers people who have been cool toward him for a year is a commitment that has no exit clause in it at all — and he offers it because it was offered to him first, by one who does not release anyone he has taken into his heart.

verseByVerse.quote: I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.

Four short statements, and they run in an order that is easy to miss.

Great boldness toward you. The word is parrēsia again, met at 3:12 — freedom of speech, the right to say everything. He is telling them there is nothing he is holding back, which is the natural companion of the wide-open heart of the previous chapter. A guarded heart produces guarded speech; an open one says what it means.

Great pride in you. Literally, much boasting about you. This is a startling thing to say about the Corinthians. He is not describing them as they were in the earlier letter; he is telling them how he speaks about them when they are not in the room, and it turns out he brags. Every person who has ever heard second-hand that someone spoke well of them knows what that does.

Then I am filled with comfort — the word from chapter 1, the whole letter’s theme, and now it is stated as an accomplished fact. Paul, who despaired of life itself in chapter 1, is filled.

And the last clause holds two things together that most people think are alternatives: In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.

Not after the affliction. Not in spite of it. In it. The verb means to superabound, to run over the top. The affliction has not been removed and is not being minimised; the news from Corinth has not made his circumstances any safer. Something else has been poured in until the container will not hold it.

Which points at where Christian joy actually comes from, and it is worth being concrete. Read the verse in context and the source is not mysterious. Titus arrived. He brought news that people Paul loved had turned the right way. That is what filled him — not a change in his health, his safety, his finances or his reputation, but the spiritual good of other people.

There is a searching diagnostic in that. Take an inventory of the last month and ask what actually lifted you and what actually sank you. For most of us the list is entirely circumstantial: money, health, weather, how things went at work, whether someone was pleasant. Paul’s list is other people’s repentance. A man whose joy depends on his own circumstances will be up and down for life, because circumstances are designed to move. A man whose joy is attached to what God is doing in other people has fastened it to something that tends in only one direction.

And that is why the affliction could not empty him. The things that were going wrong were all happening to Paul, and his joy was not being sourced from there.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn — fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,

Paul goes back and picks up the story he abandoned at 2:13. He had left Troas, unable to preach for anxiety, and crossed to Macedonia to find Titus. Now he tells us what that was like.

Our bodies had no rest. The word is the one he used at 2:13 of his spirit — no relief, no loosening. Now it is the body too. He is not sleeping.

Afflicted at every turn — fighting without and fear within. Two directions, and the second is the remarkable one. Fighting without we expect: opposition, hostility, conflict wherever he went. Fear within is an apostle admitting, in a public letter to a church that thinks him weak, that he was frightened.

He does not qualify it. He does not say he wrestled the fear down or that it was brief. He lists it beside the external conflicts as simply part of the account. Any Christian who has believed that fear is incompatible with faith should read this verse slowly. The man who wrote God gave us a spirit not of fear is the same man who says here that he had fears within, and the Bible puts both sentences in the canon without apology.

Then the turn, and it is one of the great turns in Paul: But God.

Take the title he chooses, because it is chosen. God, who comforts the downcast. The word is tapeinos — low, brought down, at the bottom. It is the word for humble in the Sermon on the Mount and the word for humiliated in ordinary Greek. Of all the titles available to him, Paul reaches for the one that describes what God does for people who are on the floor. This is not a general statement about the divine nature. It is a man saying: I was down there, and this is what he is like when you are.

And then how the comfort arrived. Not a vision. Not a voice. Not the third heaven, which he had had and which is not mentioned here. By the coming of Titus. A friend walked in the door.

That should be said plainly to anyone waiting for God to do something dramatic. The overwhelming majority of the comfort God gives his people arrives on two legs, with a face and a name. It looks like a visit, a meal left on a doorstep, a phone call from someone who did not know why they rang. Paul does not treat it as a lesser form of help; he calls it God comforting him, and the sentence has God as the subject and Titus as the instrument.

Which has a consequence for anyone who finds it easier to pray for a suffering friend than to go and see them. God has arranged the world so that the comfort of the downcast usually requires somebody to make the journey.

verseByVerse.quote: and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.

Follow the comfort as it moves, because this verse traces its whole route.

God comforted the Corinthians. The Corinthians comforted Titus. Titus, comforted, came to Macedonia and comforted Paul. Three links, and the chain runs exactly as chapter 1 said it would: comfort received is comfort passed on, and the supply at the head of the line is God.

Notice that Titus is not merely a messenger. He did not simply carry the information; he had been changed by his stay in Corinth, and it was the state of the man arriving, as much as the news he brought, that lifted Paul. That is worth knowing about how encouragement actually works. People rarely encourage others by transmitting facts. They do it by being visibly people to whom something good has happened.

Then three words describing what Titus reported, and each one is a mark of a church coming right.

Your longing. They wanted to see Paul. After a year of distance and rumour, the affection had come back on.

Your mourning. This is the strong word — the grief you feel at a death. They were not embarrassed about how the situation had been handled; they were grieved. There is a great difference between a church that regrets an episode and one that mourns it, and the difference shows up in whether anything changes.

Your zeal for me. The word is the root of our zealous: heat, intensity. Whatever coldness there had been was gone, and it had been replaced not by politeness but by warmth.

Take those three as a description of what genuine restoration looks like anywhere — in a marriage, between a parent and a grown child, in a friendship that went wrong. Not merely the end of hostilities. Longing, grief, and heat. If a reconciliation has produced nothing but a resumption of civil contact, it has not yet reached what Paul is describing.

So that I rejoiced still more. More than what? More than he had already rejoiced at the simple relief of Titus arriving safely. The news kept raising the level.

And behind all of it stands the quiet arrangement that makes the chain possible. God chose not to be the only one who comforts. He gives the comfort, then puts it into people, then sends those people to each other, so that the consolation of an apostle in Macedonia depended on the state of a church in Achaia and the journey of a friend in between. He could have done it directly and instantly. He preferred to do it through his people, and in doing so gave every ordinary Christian a share in the work of the God of all comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it — though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.

This is one of the most human sentences in the New Testament, and it is a great mercy that the Holy Spirit left it in.

Watch him change his mind twice inside a single line. I do not regret it — then, immediately, though I did regret it. The severe letter went off. Paul then spent the waiting weeks wishing he had not sent it. And now, knowing the outcome, he is glad he did.

Consider who is writing. This is an apostle, describing a letter written under the guidance of the Spirit for the good of a church, and he admits that after sending it he wished it back. He does not tidy this away. He does not present himself as a man of settled confidence who knew all along.

Anyone who has ever had to say a hard thing knows this exact sequence. You agonise over whether to speak. You speak. And then comes the awful stretch afterwards — the message sent and unanswerable, the conversation you cannot take back, the silence in which you rehearse every word and become certain you were too harsh, or too soft, or should simply have left it alone. That stretch is in the Bible. Paul lived in it.

And note what resolved it. Not a better argument with himself. Not a stronger conviction that he had been right. The outcome resolved it: for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while. The regret ended when he saw what the letter had actually done.

Which means that during the weeks of regret Paul was wrong, and the letter he wished unwritten was the right letter all along. That is worth holding on to, because the regret you feel after a hard conversation is not evidence about whether you should have had it. It is usually only evidence that you love the person and cannot see the end from here.

Then the last phrase, and it is the pivot of the passage: though only for a while. The grief had a term on it. It was real, it was severe, and it was temporary — because it was grief that led somewhere.

That is the difference between the wound of a friend and the wound of an enemy, and Proverbs had said so long before: faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Prov. 27:6). The friend’s wound hurts and heals. The flattery feels better and leaves the thing that was killing you exactly where it was.

So if you are still carrying the regret of something you had to say, this verse gives you two things: permission to have felt it, since an apostle did, and the reminder that you are not yet in a position to judge. Paul was only able to write this sentence because Titus came back.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.

Here is one of the most practically important distinctions in Scripture, and everyone who has ever wondered whether their sorrow over sin was the real thing needs it.

First, Paul’s care in verse 9: not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. He takes no pleasure in having hurt them. The grief was never the goal; it was the road. Anyone who enjoys the discomfort he causes in the name of correction is not doing what Paul did.

Then the two kinds of grief, and the difference between them is not intensity. Both hurt. Both produce tears. The difference is direction.

Godly grief is literally grief according to God — sorrow shaped by his view of the matter. It sees the sin as an offence against him first, and it moves toward him. The psalm every believer eventually says is the model: against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight (Ps. 51:4). That is a man who has wrecked several lives, and he says against you only — not because the others do not matter, but because he has seen who the offended party ultimately is.

Worldly grief is sorrow about consequences. It is real distress, and it is entirely about the self: what I have lost, how I am now seen, what happens to me next. It can be extremely convincing from the outside and even from the inside.

Scripture gives us the two men, and they were in the same room on the same night. Judas betrayed Christ, and then changed his mind, and threw the money back into the temple, and said I have sinned by betraying innocent blood — and went out and hanged himself (Matt. 27:3–5). Every visible mark of repentance is there: remorse, confession, restitution. And it ended in death, exactly as this verse says, because it never turned toward anyone. Peter denied Christ three times with oaths, went out and wept bitterly, and was restored over breakfast on a beach. The same night, the same failure of nerve, comparable tears — and one man’s grief took him to Christ while the other’s took him to a rope.

So here is the test, and it can be run on yourself in about a minute. When you are sorry for something, listen to the sentences in your head. If they are mostly about how this looks, what it will cost you, and how you will get out of it, that is the sorrow of the world, and it will not save anyone. If they are about God — that you have grieved someone who loves you, that this is what you are and you need him to deal with it — that is godly grief, and it is already carrying you in the right direction.

And notice how Paul describes where it ends: a repentance that leads to salvation without regret. Nobody who has ever come to Christ in genuine sorrow has looked back and wished he had not.

verseByVerse.quote: For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.

Having defined godly grief, Paul now shows what it looked like when it landed. This is the most concrete description of repentance anywhere in the New Testament — seven marks, and they can be laid against a life.

Earnestness. Literally speed, urgency. Repentance that is real is in a hurry. It does not put the matter down to be dealt with when convenient, which is the surest sign that nothing has happened.

Eagerness to clear yourselves. Not self-justification — they had just admitted they were wrong. It is the desire to put right what they were rightly blamed for, so that the charge no longer stands against them because the thing itself has been dealt with.

Indignation. Anger. At the sin, at the situation, at themselves for tolerating it. Repentance without any heat in it is usually just embarrassment. A man who is genuinely done with something is angry about it.

Fear. A proper seriousness about God, whose name had been dishonoured in the whole affair.

Longing. For the restoration of what was broken — in this case, for Paul. Sin isolates; real repentance wants back into the room.

Zeal. Heat again, but now positive: energy for what is right, where before there had been indifference.

Punishment. They acted. Discipline was actually carried out — the punishment of 2:6 that Paul then told them was enough. This is the mark most often missing today, and its absence is why so much apparent repentance changes nothing. Nothing was done.

Lay the list against the usual modern article. We tend to be satisfied with the first minute of it: an apology, some evident distress, a request to move on. Paul’s list has urgency, anger, fear, longing, energy and action in it. The apology is not even mentioned.

Which gives an unusually practical test, and it works both ways. If you are wondering whether your own repentance over something is real, walk the seven and ask which are present. And if you are on the other side, trying to judge whether someone who has wronged you has genuinely turned, this is a far better instrument than reading their tone of voice — because six of the seven are things that can be seen from outside.

Then the verdict: at every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter. He is not saying they were never guilty. He is saying the matter is closed. That is what God does with a repentant person, and it is what a church must learn to do: not a probation, not a permanent asterisk, but a case fully and publicly shut.

verseByVerse.quote: So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.

Paul now tells them why he really wrote, and the answer is not what anyone would have guessed.

Not for the offender’s sake, though the man has been dealt with and forgiven. Not even for the sake of the one who was wronged — which, since the wrong was done to Paul himself, means not for my own sake. He is stating that the letter was not written to get himself vindicated, which was precisely what his critics were saying about it.

So what was it for? That your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.

Read the last part slowly, because two small phrases carry the whole verse. Revealed to you — not to Paul, not to the neighbouring churches. To themselves. And in the sight of God — with him as the one before whom the revealing takes place.

The Corinthians did not know what they were. They had grown cold, listened to rumours, and let their affection for Paul narrow into a cramped little space, and they would have said, if asked, that this was simply how things now stood. The severe letter did not create their earnestness. It brought it out where they could see it. The love was still there under the resentment, and it took a crisis to prove it — to them.

That is a genuinely important thing to know about how God works. He very often puts his people into a situation whose purpose is not to change them but to show them what he has already done in them. The trial arrives and you discover you did not let go, and the discovery is the point; it is what the whole thing was arranged for. Moses said as much about the desert years: God led Israel forty years in the wilderness that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart (Deut. 8:2) — and God, of course, already knew.

Which reframes the hardest seasons in a Christian life. You may never be told what a particular stretch of suffering accomplished for anyone else. It is entirely possible that a large part of what it was for was that you should find out what you actually believe, in the sight of God, where the finding-out counts.

And notice what Paul assumes about them in order to write the sentence at all. He assumes the earnestness was there to be revealed. He has never at any point believed that these people had stopped loving him. He believed the affection was buried and wrote a letter to dig it up — which is what a father does, and not what an offended colleague does.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.

Therefore we are comforted. The word closes the circle opened in the first paragraph of the letter. The God of all comfort has done in Paul’s own case exactly what chapter 1 promised, and it took a year, a painful visit, a letter written in tears, and a friend crossing a sea.

Then something easy to hurry past: we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus. Paul’s own comfort is not the peak of his gladness. What lifted him higher was watching somebody else be happy. That is a rare and unmistakable mark of a man who has genuinely stopped living for himself (5:15).

His spirit has been refreshed by you all. The verb means rested, given relief — the same idea as a field left fallow. Titus had gone to Corinth carrying a letter that might have provoked a riot; he came away rested. It should be said that a congregation can do this to the people who serve it, in either direction. There are churches that send their workers away refreshed and churches that send them away hollow, and the difference is almost never about size or resources.

Then Paul admits something rather charming. He had bragged about the Corinthians to Titus before Titus went — told him they were a good people, that they would come right — and then had to wait to see whether he had made a fool of himself. I was not put to shame.

Consider the risk in that. He talked them up when the evidence was thin. And notice the logic he draws out of it: just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true. His truthfulness to them and his praise of them behind their backs are of a piece. A man who tells you the hard truth to your face and speaks well of you elsewhere is doing the same thing twice; both are honesty, and neither is flattery.

There is a practical wisdom here worth taking. Paul’s confidence went ahead of their performance, and it very probably helped produce it. Titus arrived expecting to find a church that would respond, and treated them accordingly, and they responded. This is not manipulation — Paul genuinely believed it. But it works, and it is the opposite of how difficult people are usually handled. We approach the awkward member expecting the worst, and communicate the expectation without saying a word, and are then proved right.

Somebody has to go first in believing the best. Paul did it here, at the risk of public embarrassment, because it had been done for him first: he was brought to the apostles by a man who vouched for him when nobody else would.

verseByVerse.quote: And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.

The chapter ends, and it ends in a place nobody could have predicted from chapter 2.

His affection for you. The word is splanchna again — the inward parts, where 6:12 said the Corinthians had gone narrow. Titus’s are the opposite: enlarged, and growing. Something in that visit expanded the man.

The obedience of you all. Not most of them. All. Whatever divisions had run through that congregation, on this they moved together.

How you received him with fear and trembling. The phrase is not about being frightened of Titus. It is Paul’s standard expression for a proper seriousness before God in a weighty moment — he uses it of working out your own salvation (Phil. 2:12). They knew that what was happening in that room was not merely a difficult meeting with a visiting delegate. God was in it, and they behaved accordingly.

That is worth naming, because most church conflict is handled at exactly the wrong level. It is treated as a matter between people, to be managed with tact, patience and the right procedure — all of which are good and none of which reaches the actual altitude. The Corinthians handled theirs with fear and trembling, and the outcome was not merely a settlement but a restored church, a refreshed messenger and an apostle overflowing with joy.

And then the last line, which ought to be read against everything that has gone before: I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.

This is the church of the factions, the lawsuits and the drunkenness at the Lord’s table. This is the congregation that sat still while its founder was publicly humiliated, that compared him unfavourably with smoother men, that had gone cold on him for a year. And the last word of the chapter is complete confidence.

Nobody should read that as a verdict on how good they were. Paul is about to spend chapters 10 to 13 dealing with the opposition still active among them; he is not naive. His confidence is of the same kind as the unshaken hope of 1:7 — resting not on their record but on what God does with people he has begun with.

And that is the only ground on which anyone has ever been able to hope for a difficult church, a difficult family, or himself. The God who did this in Corinth — who took a wrecked relationship, a humiliated apostle and a letter written in tears, and produced longing, mourning, zeal and complete confidence — has not changed his methods or lost his touch. He has never yet been handed a situation past mending.

We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one.<sup>3</sup>I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.<sup>4</sup>I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort.
