8.title: The Grace of Giving: Christ Became Poor
8.overview:
Chapters 8–9 form a unit on the collection for the Jerusalem church — but they are far more than a fundraising appeal. They are a sustained theology of Christian generosity, grounded in the gospel and illustrated by the example of the Macedonian churches. The collection was Paul’s great ecumenical project: a voluntary gift from the Gentile churches to the poor Jewish Christians in Jerusalem, intended to demonstrate the unity of Jew and Gentile in Christ and to fulfill Paul’s commitment to the Jerusalem pillars (Gal. 2:10).

Chapter 8 opens with the astonishing example of the Macedonian churches (Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea) — churches in severe affliction and extreme poverty who gave beyond their means, begging Paul earnestly for the favour of participating in the collection. Their giving was not extracted; it was given. It was not from surplus; it was from poverty. And it was not merely financial; they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to Paul. This is the model Paul holds before the Corinthians.

The theological ground of all Christian generosity is then stated with precision: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.” This is the incarnation described in economic terms — the ultimate act of voluntary self-impoverishment for the enrichment of others, setting the pattern for every act of Christian generosity.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Macedonian Example and Christ Who Became Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Macedonian churches gave in extreme circumstances (vv. 1–2): severe affliction (en pollē thlipsei) and extreme poverty (hē kata bathous ptōcheia — deep-level poverty, poverty to the depths). These were not comfortable churches making comfortable gifts; they were suffering churches making sacrificial gifts. And the combination produced — paradoxically — an overflow of joy (perisseia tēs charas). Affliction + poverty + joy = overflowing generosity. This is not natural; it is supernatural, which is why Paul heads the whole account with the words “the grace of God that has been given.”

They gave according to their means and beyond their means, of their own accord (v. 3), and then did the thing that reverses every appeal ever made: they begged Paul for the favor of being allowed to take part (v. 4). The explanation is in v. 5, and it is the key to both chapters: “they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.” The money was not the transaction; it was the receipt. Accordingly Titus, who had begun the collection in Corinth a year before, is urged to return and complete it (v. 6).

Paul wants the Corinthians to “excel in this act of grace also” (v. 7) — placing generosity alongside faith, speech, knowledge, all earnestness, and love as one of the spiritual graces in which Christians are to grow. Giving is not merely a financial transaction; it is a spiritual grace to be cultivated and exercised. He is explicit that he is not commanding it (v. 8) but testing the genuineness of their love by the example of others — and it is worth noticing that in the longest treatment of giving in the New Testament he never once names a percentage.

The Christological ground of generosity (v. 9) is the most important verse in the chapter: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.” The pattern of self-impoverishment for the enrichment of others is the pattern of the incarnation and cross, and therefore the pattern of Christian generosity. The believer gives because Christ gave; the measure is Christ’s own self-giving.

From there Paul turns practical, and the second half of the section is as important as the first. He gives his judgment rather than a command (v. 10), reminding them that the desire was theirs first, a year ago — and asks that their readiness in desiring be matched by their completing it out of what they have (v. 11). The standard is not achievement but proportion: if the readiness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have (v. 12) — the verse that frees every small giver from comparison.

He is not asking that others be eased and they burdened (v. 13) but that present abundance should supply present need, in either direction, so that there may be fairness (v. 14). And he seals it with the manna (v. 15; Ex. 16:18): whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack — God’s own arrangement of sufficiency, in which the surplus was never the gatherer’s to keep.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is one of the key NT texts for the kenosis of the incarnation (alongside Phil. 2:5–8 and John 1:1–14). “Though he was rich” describes the pre-incarnate state of the Son — possessing all the resources of divine glory, honour, and power. “He became poor” (eptōcheusen — an aorist of decisive action, choosing poverty) describes the incarnation and more specifically the cross: the Son laid aside the exercise of divine prerogatives and took on the condition of creaturely poverty, ultimately the poverty of crucifixion and cursed death. “That you by his poverty might become rich” — the result is the enrichment of believers: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, the inheritance of the new creation.
verseByVerse.examples: A church board is considering its annual budget and the portion allocated to mission outside its own walls. One member argues that they should ensure their own facilities and staff are well-funded before giving generously abroad. This passage holds before him the Macedonian model: churches in deep poverty begging to give. And the Christological ground: the Son of God did not ensure his own comfort before giving to others. The board’s question is not merely financial but spiritual: does this budget reflect the grace described in v. 9?

verseByVerse.quote: We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.

Paul is about to ask the Corinthians for money, and he begins in a way no fundraiser would. He does not describe the need. He describes what God has been doing several hundred miles away.

Notice the word he puts over the whole subject: the grace of God that has been given. Not the generosity of the Macedonians. Their giving is described as something God did to them. That word — charis, grace — will run through these two chapters like a thread; it turns up in verse 4, verse 6, verse 7, verse 9, verse 19, and again in chapter 9. Giving, in Paul’s mind, is not first a duty discharged. It is a grace received.

Then the equation, and it is worth setting out as an equation because it does not work.

A severe test of affliction. The Macedonian churches — Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea — had been through it. Read Acts and the letters and you find riots, a jailing, believers dragged before magistrates, a congregation Paul had to leave by night. They were under pressure and it was not brief.

Their extreme poverty. The Greek is stronger than the English: poverty down to the depths, rock-bottom, the beggar’s level. Macedonia had been stripped by Rome — its mines confiscated, its wealth taxed away.

Affliction plus destitution. Any reasonable person could predict the result: nothing. No capacity, no surplus, nothing to spare, and every excuse in the world.

And what came out was an abundance of joy and a wealth of generosity. Both words are the language of overflow — something running over the top of the container. From people who by every measure had nothing to overflow with.

This is one of the plainest pieces of evidence in the New Testament that something other than human nature is at work in the church. Poverty makes people tight; that is not cynicism, it is observation, and it is a perfectly rational response to having little. Affliction makes people inward. Put the two together and you get a closed hand, every time — unless something has got in underneath.

Which is why Paul calls it grace rather than character. He is not holding the Macedonians up as heroes to shame the Corinthians into competing. He is showing them what God does in people, and saying in effect: he is doing this over there, and he can do it here.

There is a searching question in it for anyone who has ever waited for the right season to become generous. Most of us have a threshold in mind — when the mortgage is down, when the children are through, when there is something spare. The Macedonians never reached it. They gave out of the depths, and the joy was not the reward for giving; the joy and the generosity overflowed together, out of the same well.

verseByVerse.quote: For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints —

Paul now describes the giving itself, and every phrase in the sentence removes another of the usual explanations.

According to their means. They gave proportionately, which is the normal biblical standard, and it is already more than most people do.

And beyond their means. Literally beyond power — past what they could actually afford. They did not calculate what was reasonable and give it. They went over.

Paul knows this is a large claim, so he inserts himself as a witness: as I can testify. He was there. He watched it happen and he is prepared to swear to it.

Then the phrase that shuts the last door: of their own accord. Nobody asked them. There was no appeal, no target, no pressure applied by an apostle who wanted the collection to succeed. In fact the pressure ran the other way, which is the astonishing part of verse 4.

Begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part. Read that slowly, because it is the exact reverse of every appeal for money you have ever heard. Paul is not begging them to give. They are begging him to be allowed to. He was evidently reluctant — one does not take a collection from destitute people — and they pressed him until he agreed.

And the word they used for what they were asking is charis again, which the ESV renders favor. They regarded being permitted to give as a privilege granted to them.

Set that beside the way giving is usually felt in a church, where the offering is the awkward part of the service and the annual appeal is something to be endured. Somewhere along the line we came to think of giving as money leaving. The Macedonians thought of it as being let in.

Then the last words: taking part in the relief of the saints. The word for taking part is koinōnia — fellowship, partnership, having something in common. This is the same word used of the fellowship believers have with the Father and the Son. Money given to brothers they would never meet was, to these people, a way of being in fellowship with them.

It is worth asking what makes a person want that. Not guilt, which produces a payment and then resentment. Not obligation, which produces a calculation. The only thing that produces begging to be allowed to give is having grasped what you have already been given — and Paul is one verse away from naming it.

verseByVerse.quote: and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.

Here is the explanation, and it is the key to everything the two chapters say about money.

Not as we expected. Paul admits he was taken by surprise. He had hoped for something; what happened was of a different order. And when he goes looking for the reason, he does not find it in their circumstances or their temperament.

They gave themselves first to the Lord.

That is the whole thing. Before any money moved, they had handed over the people the money belonged to. The financial gift was not the transaction; it was the receipt.

Notice the word first. It is an order, not a coincidence. And the order explains why so much Christian teaching about money produces so little. We address the wallet directly — better principles, clearer proportions, a stronger appeal — and it works for about a fortnight, because the wallet was never the problem. A man who has not given himself to God will find reasons not to give his money, and he will find good ones. A man who has given himself has already given everything else; what remains is bookkeeping.

Which supplies a test that is more searching than any percentage. Do not ask first am I giving enough? Ask have I given myself? The first question can be answered with a calculation and leaves you exactly where you were. The second cannot be answered with money at all.

And there is a comfort in this order as well as a challenge, because it means the person with almost nothing to give is not at a disadvantage. The Macedonians were destitute. Whatever they put in that bag would have been unimpressive next to a Corinthian merchant’s contribution. It is not what God was measuring. He had already received the thing he was actually after.

And then by the will of God to us. A second surrender, and it is not an afterthought. Having given themselves to the Lord, they gave themselves to Paul — that is, to the work, to the mission, to the church. The two go together and always have. There is no giving yourself to God in the abstract; it lands on people, and usually on the nearest inconvenient ones.

And observe that Paul calls even that the will of God. Their availability to a missionary enterprise they would never see the results of was not enthusiasm. It was obedience, and God arranged it.

This is what it looks like when the gospel has actually landed in a person. He does not negotiate about what portion of himself God may have, because that was settled at the start — the day he understood that he was not his own, having been bought with a price (1 Cor. 6:19–20). Everything after that is detail.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.

Having described the Macedonians, Paul turns to the practical arrangement. Titus, who had already begun the collection in Corinth on an earlier visit, is being sent back to finish it.

The verb urged is parakaleō once more — the word that has run through the whole letter as comfort, and here in its other sense: to appeal, to press someone. Even with a trusted colleague, Paul asks rather than orders.

Then the phrase this chapter keeps returning to: this act of grace. In the Greek it is simply this grace — the same word again. The English needs a noun to hang it on and supplies act, but the bare word is the point. The collection for the poor in Jerusalem is charis. God’s grace comes down into a church; the same word describes it going out again as money to strangers.

That is a striking thing to have noticed about the shape of Christian giving, and it is worth holding on to. Grace is not a substance that stops when it reaches you. What God gives, he gives in order that it should keep moving — which is exactly what he said about comfort in chapter 1, and about the gospel in chapter 5, and now about money.

Then the word that carries the practical weight of the verse: complete. Titus is to finish what he began. And the reason this is in the letter at all is that the Corinthians had started, enthusiastically, a year earlier, and stopped.

There is nothing unusual about that and no need to be hard on them. It is the ordinary shape of religious enthusiasm. The appeal is made, the moment is genuine, the intention is real — and then the weeks pass, other things arrive, the sum that seemed straightforward in the meeting looks larger at the kitchen table, and the thing quietly lapses. Nobody decides against it.

Which makes this a good verse to stop at and be honest. What did you begin and not finish? A commitment made at a conference. A monthly amount you meant to set up. A person you said you would visit. A promise made at a graveside. Almost every Christian has a small graveyard of good intentions, and the reason they died is never a decision.

Notice that Paul’s remedy is not a rebuke but a person. He sends Titus. He does not write a sharper paragraph and hope; he puts a man on a boat, because he understands that good intentions do not need more motivation, they need somebody to come and help finish them. That is worth knowing about how churches actually change: exhortation is cheap, and presence is what completes things.

verseByVerse.quote: But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as you excel in everything — in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you — see that you excel in this act of grace also.

Paul now names the Corinthian strengths, and he does it generously before he says what is missing.

Faith, speech, knowledge, all earnestness, and their love. Anyone who has read the first letter will recognise the list — these were the things the Corinthians prized. They were an articulate, gifted, energetic church that thought rather well of its own understanding.

And Paul does not sneer at any of it. He says they excel in these things, and means it. The word is one he uses for abundance and overflow. Whatever else was wrong in Corinth, this was a church with real gifts.

Then the sentence turns: see that you excel in this act of grace also. Generosity is added to the list — placed alongside faith, speech and knowledge as one of the graces a Christian is expected to grow in.

That placement is quietly revolutionary and it ought to change how a church thinks about maturity. We readily accept that a believer should grow in his understanding of doctrine, in prayer, in self-control, in love. We do not usually think of a person as immature in giving in the way we might think of him as immature in patience. Paul does. He treats generosity as a spiritual capacity that can be developed or left undeveloped, and he assumes it belongs in the same sentence as faith.

Which raises an uncomfortable and useful question. It is possible to be genuinely advanced in several of these and entirely undeveloped in this one. A person can know his Bible thoroughly, speak well about it, be earnest, be warm toward the congregation — and give exactly what he gave ten years ago, when he had considerably less. The other graces have grown and this one has not been touched.

Notice also the verb: see that you excel. It is an imperative with attention in it — look to this, make sure of it. Paul does not expect it to happen by drift, and the Corinthians are the evidence, since drift is precisely what had happened to their collection.

And notice one more thing, easily missed. He is asking a wealthy church to learn something from a destitute one. The Corinthians had every material advantage over Macedonia and were being told to catch up. Gift, eloquence and knowledge do not automatically produce an open hand; if anything they can supply better arguments for keeping it shut. What produced it in Macedonia was not resources but grace, and grace is available on the same terms in a prosperous church as in a poor one.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.

Paul stops and makes something explicit, and the fact that he bothers tells us how carefully he is handling this.

Not as a command. He is an apostle. He could order it, and everyone reading knew he could. He declines. And the reason is not delicacy about money; it is that a commanded gift would prove nothing and change nobody. He wants a certain kind of giving, and that kind cannot be produced by an instruction.

This is the natural place to answer the question every reader of these two chapters actually has, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a silence. How much? Is a Christian required to give a tenth?

The honest answer is that the New Testament nowhere commands the tithe of believers, and Paul is the proof. Here he has two entire chapters on giving — the longest treatment of the subject in the New Testament, written to a church that had stalled and needed a clear standard — and he never names a figure. He had every opportunity and every reason to, and he did not.

What he gives instead is harder rather than easier. He gives proportion (according to their means, v. 3), readiness (v. 12), cheerfulness (9:7), and one supreme example (v. 9). A fixed percentage can be paid and forgotten; a proportion has to be thought about again every time the circumstances change, and it will not let you stop at ten if you have forty.

None of which makes the tenth useless. Christians who treat it as a floor rather than a ceiling are not being legalistic; they are being sensible, and they have a great deal of Scripture behind the instinct. But it is a benchmark, not a command, and it must never become the number that tells a rich man he has done enough or a poor man that he has failed.

Then the reason Paul refuses to command: to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine. The word for prove is the assayer’s word — testing metal to see whether it is what it claims to be.

And that is what money does. It is the most reliable test of love there is, because it cannot be faked and it costs exactly what it costs. Anyone can say they care about the poor in Jerusalem. Very few things reveal what a person actually values as accurately as where the money goes when nobody is watching, which is why the Lord put it so bluntly: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matt. 6:21). He did not say the heart directs the treasure. He said the treasure shows where the heart already is.

So the invitation here is not to be dutiful. It is to find out whether the love is genuine — and Paul is confident enough about them to let the test run.

verseByVerse.quote: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.

Paul has been arguing about a collection. In one sentence he goes to the incarnation, and this is the ground everything else in two chapters has been standing on.

You know the grace. He does not introduce it; they have it already. The whole appeal turns on something they were told the day they believed.

Though he was rich. The riches are not metaphorical. This is the Son before Bethlehem — the one who says to his Father, the glory that I had with you before the world existed (Jn. 17:5). He possessed everything, needed nothing, was worshipped without interruption, and had never in eternity known a moment of want.

He became poor. The verb is decisive and voluntary — he impoverished himself — and the word for poor is ptōchos, which is not modest means. It is the beggar with nothing, the man dependent on what other people put in his hand.

And the descent is traceable. He was born in a borrowed stable to a family that could afford only the two pigeons the law allowed the poor. He worked with his hands. As a grown man he said foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matt. 8:20). He was supported by the money of women who followed him. He rode into Jerusalem on a borrowed animal, ate his last meal in a borrowed room, and was buried in a borrowed grave. At the very end soldiers divided his clothing, which was all he had, and gambled for the one piece worth keeping. He died owning nothing at all.

And beneath the material poverty is the real one. On the cross he was stripped of the thing that had never been taken from him in all eternity — my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? That is ptōcheia. That is destitution.

So that you by his poverty might become rich. Not so that you might become comfortable. Rich. Forgiven, adopted, indwelt, given a righteousness that is not ours, made heirs of everything — all things are yours, he had already told this church (1 Cor. 3:21). The exchange is exact and it runs in both directions: his poverty for our wealth, as at 5:21 his being made sin was for our becoming righteousness.

Which is why Paul does not have to command anything. The argument is not give, because the Jerusalem church needs it, true as that is. It is: look at what was done for you, and then look at your bank account, and see whether the two can be held in the same mind.

And it is worth ending where the verse ends, without applying it. He was rich. He is the one by whom and for whom everything was made, and there was never anything he lacked. He looked at people who had nothing and could give him nothing, and he emptied himself out to the last coin and the last comfort and the last shred of the Father’s face — and he did it, the sentence says, for your sake. There is no accounting for that anywhere in heaven or earth except the word Paul uses for it: grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.

After the summit of verse 9, back to the practical business, and Paul handles it with great skill.

I give my judgment — not I command. He said in verse 8 he would not order this and he keeps his word. What he offers is considered counsel from a man they have reason to trust.

Then a phrase easy to skate over: this benefits you. The advantage is theirs. Paul does not say the collection benefits Jerusalem, though obviously it does. He says the giving will do the Corinthians good. That is not sales talk; it is the settled New Testament view that a generous person is the one who gains most from his own generosity, and that a closed hand damages the one it belongs to before it damages anyone else.

Then he does something worth watching, because it is one of the wisest pastoral moves in the letter. He reminds them what they themselves wanted.

A year ago you started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. Note the order — they did not merely begin the task, they wanted it. The enthusiasm was genuine and it was theirs. He is not importing a burden from outside; he is handing them back something they laid down.

That is a far better instrument than pressure, and it works because it is true. The most powerful motivation available to any of us is not somebody else’s expectation but our own earlier and better intention, recalled gently. You wanted this. You still do. Finish it.

So now finish doing it. The whole weight of the verse is on completion, and Paul then defines what completion means with two careful phrases.

So that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it. The desire and the deed are to be the same size. This is the standard, and it is uncomfortably precise: not that you should do great things, but that what you actually do should correspond to what you actually meant.

Most of us live with a permanent gap there, and it is the quietest form of self-deception in the Christian life. We feel the intention and count it as though it were the act. We are moved by the appeal and file the feeling as a response. The intention is real; it simply never becomes anything, and after some years a person can have a rich interior life of good desires and very little to show.

Out of what you have. And there is the relief attached to the demand. Not out of what you wish you had, not out of what the Macedonians managed. Out of what is actually in your hand. That is the whole requirement, and it is within reach of everyone reading it this afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.

This is the verse to hand to anyone who has ever felt that their giving is too small to matter.

Three things are settled in one sentence.

If the readiness is there. Willingness comes first — the same order as verse 5, where they gave themselves before they gave anything else. God is after a willing giver, and without that the sum is irrelevant in either direction. A large gift from a reluctant heart and a small one are equally beside the point.

It is acceptable. The word means well-received, welcome. Not tolerated. Not graciously overlooked. Welcomed.

According to what a person has, not according to what he does not have. And there is the liberty. The measure is your actual resources. Not the giving of the person beside you in the pew, whose circumstances you do not know. Not what you could have given had life gone differently. Not the figure in the appeal letter. What you have.

Sit with how much that removes. A great deal of Christian unhappiness about money is really comparison, and it runs in both directions. The person of modest means feels his contribution is negligible beside the large gift that funded the roof, and quietly concludes that generosity is a rich man’s virtue. The person with more looks at the sacrificial giving of someone with less and cannot work out whether he is doing anything at all. This verse dismantles both, because it makes the measure personal and relative rather than absolute.

And the Lord had already made the same point in the most memorable way possible. He sat down opposite the temple treasury and watched people putting money in — large sums from the rich — and then a widow put in two small copper coins, the smallest in circulation. And he called his disciples over to say that she out of her poverty has put in everything she had (Mk. 12:44). The largest gift given that day, by his accounting, was worth less than a penny.

Which means the accounting in heaven is not the accounting in the ledger. There will be people at the end who are found to have given more than wealthy benefactors whose names are on buildings, and they will be as surprised as anyone.

So if your gift is small, this verse says two things and neither is a consolation prize. It is acceptable — genuinely welcomed by God, not merely permitted. And it is measured by a standard you can actually meet, which no one else’s giving can raise or lower. Nobody has ever been asked for what he does not have.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.

Paul now heads off a suspicion before it forms. He is not proposing that the Corinthians be squeezed so that Jerusalem can relax.

Eased and burdened — one party comfortable at the other’s expense. That is not the arrangement, and he says so plainly, which tells us somebody in Corinth had probably said it was.

The word he uses instead is isotēs — equality, fairness, an even balance. It occurs twice in the sentence, opening and closing it.

Now be careful here, because the word has been made to carry a great deal it will not bear. Paul is not proposing that all Christians should hold the same amount, nor that anyone should compel a transfer. Every element of this collection has been voluntary — of their own accord, not as a command, if the readiness is there. Whatever this is, it is not enforced.

What is it, then? Look at the two words he attaches to it: your abundance at the present time. Both halves matter. Abundance is surplus — what is over and above need. And at the present time makes it a snapshot rather than a permanent classification. Corinth has more today; Jerusalem has need today. Neither of those is guaranteed to be true in five years, and Paul says so: so that their abundance may supply your need.

So the picture is not redistribution but circulation — a body in which resources move to wherever the lack currently is, in whichever direction that happens to be. The aim is not that everyone should have the same but that no one should be in want.

And notice the assumption underneath it, which is the genuinely radical part. Paul takes it for granted that a Gentile church in Greece is responsible for Jewish believers in Judea whom they have never met, will never meet, and who differ from them in language, diet, culture and temperament. There is no natural bond there at all. There is only the one thing they have in common, and Paul treats it as sufficient.

Which puts a question to any congregation with a surplus. It is easy to feel that the money raised here should stay here — the building needs work, the staff need paying, the local needs are visible and the distant ones are not. Paul’s categories do not really allow the question to be settled locally. If the church is one body, then a need in another part of it is not somebody else’s problem being brought to our attention. It is our need, currently being felt somewhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”

Paul reaches for one line of Scripture to settle the whole argument, and it is a surprising choice: a sentence about breakfast in a desert.

The quotation is from Exodus 16. Israel is a month out of Egypt, in a wilderness with no food, and God begins sending bread every morning. The instructions are specific: gather what you need for the day, an omer a person, and no more. And then the detail Paul is quoting: when they measured it, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack (Ex. 16:18).

Stage it, because the picture is what carries the point. Some men were strong and worked fast; some were old, or ill, or had small children slowing them down. They came back to the camp with visibly different amounts in their baskets. And when it was measured out, everyone had exactly enough. The industrious man had no surplus to store and the slow man had no shortfall. Effort had made no difference to the outcome at all.

Two things follow, and Paul is leaning on both.

First, this is how God provides for his people — sufficiency for each, without regard to capacity. Nobody starved because he was weak, and nobody got ahead because he was quick. That was the arrangement in the wilderness, and Paul says the church is meant to look like it. The difference is only in the mechanism: in Exodus God did it directly with a miracle, and in Corinth he does it through the offering plate. The surplus of the strong ends up meeting the need of the weak either way.

Second, and it is the sharper point, the man who gathered much never actually owned the surplus. It was not his to keep — and if he tried, as some did, it bred worms and stank by morning. Manna could not be hoarded. It was given daily, for use, and it rotted the moment it was treated as property.

That is a very old lesson and it has never stopped being needed. What you have beyond your need was not given to you to store. It is not a reward for having gathered faster; the whole story is designed to disprove that. It is manna, and manna keeps badly.

Which is worth holding beside the way most of us actually think about a surplus — as margin, as security, as evidence that things have gone well. Paul, quoting Moses, says the surplus in your basket this morning has somebody else’s name on it, and that the God who arranged the imbalance did it deliberately, so that his people would have to become the means of each other’s supply.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Titus and the Brothers; Transparency in Giving
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul describes the arrangements for the collection. He begins by thanking God — not Titus — for putting into Titus’s heart the same earnest care he has himself (v. 16), and notes that Titus both accepted the appeal and was already going of his own accord (v. 17); the request did not create the willingness, it met it. With him travels a brother famous among all the churches for his preaching (v. 18), who has been appointed by the churches themselves — not by Paul — to travel with the gift, for the glory of the Lord himself (v. 19).

Paul is meticulous about the handling of the money: he takes this course so that no one should blame him about the gift being administered (v. 20), aiming at what is honourable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of men (v. 21). He wants no accusation of mishandling the large sum; the financial transparency is itself an act of integrity, and it is arranged before any accusation exists, which is the only time such arrangements can be made without looking like a reaction.

A third man is added (v. 22), commended not for gifting but for having been often tested and found earnest in many matters — trust built slowly, in small things, before responsibility was given. Paul then introduces the three formally (v. 23): Titus is his partner and fellow worker; the brothers are messengers of the churches, and — astonishingly, of men currently employed as couriers of a charitable fund — “the glory of Christ.” The chapter closes with a single plain instruction (v. 24): give proof, before the churches, of your love and of our boasting about you. Paul has vouched for them publicly, and says so.

The principle of v. 21 — ensuring integrity both before God and before men — is a foundational principle for all Christian financial administration. The desire to be above reproach in financial management is not the same as treating financial transparency as the primary accountability; it is recognising that financial integrity in the sight of men is a necessary expression of integrity before God.
verseByVerse.theology: The principle of handling ministry finances with transparent accountability applies directly to all Christian organisations. Paul, who could have simply trusted his own integrity, insists on multiple overseers and transparent processes — because the integrity of the ministry is at stake not only in God’s sight but in the sight of the watching world. Financial scandal in Christian ministry has consistently damaged the gospel’s credibility; Paul’s instinct to “take every precaution” (v. 20) is prophylactic wisdom.
verseByVerse.examples: A mission organisation implements a new policy requiring two-signature approval for all expenditures over a certain threshold, and annual independent financial audits reported to the whole organisation. Some staff feel this implies distrust. This passage gives the theological rationale: the precautions are not about distrust of individuals but about protecting the honour of the Lord and the integrity of the ministry in the sight of those who would use any irregularity to attack the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.

The argument about money pauses, and Paul does something small and very characteristic: he thanks God for a person.

And notice what exactly he thanks him for. Not that Titus agreed to go. That God put into the heart of Titus the same care Paul had. He traces a colleague’s affection back past the colleague to its source.

That is worth pausing on, because it is a habit most of us do not have. When someone shows us real kindness we thank them, which is right. Paul thanks God, because he assumes that the love one Christian has for another did not originate in that Christian. Somebody put it there.

Which has a practical use. Think of the person who has stood by you — the friend who kept turning up, the older believer who prayed for you for years, whoever it was that noticed. You have probably thanked them. Have you thanked God for the fact that they wanted to? That is not sentimentality; it is accuracy about where affection comes from.

Then verse 17, and it is finely balanced. He not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.

Both halves are true at once. Paul asked him — there was a genuine appeal, and Titus accepted it. And he was already going anyway, of his own accord, out of his own eagerness. The request did not create the willingness; it met it.

The phrase of his own accord is the same one used of the Macedonians in verse 3, and its reappearance is not accidental. Everything in this chapter that God is doing, he is doing through people who chose it freely and would tell you it was their own idea. Both things are being said in the same paragraph without embarrassment: God put it in his heart, and he is going of his own accord.

That is the ordinary pattern of the Christian life and it is a great relief to see it stated so plainly. You are not a passenger. Nothing in this passage suggests Titus was moved about like a piece on a board; he was eager, and the eagerness was his. And behind it, quietly, was Someone who had arranged it, which is why the paragraph opens with thanks rather than congratulation.

And notice, finally, what Titus was eager about. Not a preaching tour. He was volunteering to go and organise a collection in a church that had been difficult, and to handle other people’s money in a situation where he could easily be accused. That is the kind of enthusiasm only God puts in a heart.

verseByVerse.quote: With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.

A second man joins the party, and Paul does not tell us his name.

The guesses have been made for nineteen centuries — Luke, because he was with Paul and wrote a gospel; Barnabas; Apollos; Silas. There is no way to decide, and the anonymity may well be deliberate. This is a letter about money that will be read aloud in every church in the province; naming the man who is coming to collect it would make him a figure rather than a servant, and would look uncomfortably like Paul commending his own choice.

What we are told about him is two things, and they are the two things that matter.

He is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. A man of real standing, known everywhere, whose reputation was made in the pulpit and not in administration. And he is being sent to help carry a bag of money four hundred miles.

There is a quiet rebuke to a certain kind of ministry ambition in that. Nobody is too senior for the practical work. The best-known preacher in the Aegean is spending months of his life as a courier and an auditor, because the money has to be handled properly and somebody trustworthy has to do it.

Then the crucial detail: he has been appointed by the churches. Not chosen by Paul. The congregations themselves selected him — the verb suggests a formal choice, a hand raised or a vote taken. So the man overseeing the funds is not the apostle’s appointee but the churches’, and he answers to them.

Paul is building a structure here, and he is building it deliberately: multiple men, chosen by the donors, travelling with the gift. He, who could have said with complete honesty that his own integrity was sufficient, arranges things so that it does not have to be taken on trust.

Then the aim of the whole exercise, and it lifts the accounting into another register: for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will. A collection for hungry believers, carefully audited and honestly delivered, is done for the glory of the Lord.

Which is worth saying to everyone who has ever felt that the practical end of church life is the unspiritual end — the treasurer, the person who counts the offering, the one who checks the invoices and is never thanked. Paul puts that work and the glory of God in the same sentence, because a church whose money is handled honestly is telling the truth about its God, and one whose money is handled loosely is telling a lie about him with every receipt.

verseByVerse.quote: We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.

Here is the reason for all the arrangements, stated flatly, and it is one of the most practically useful principles in the New Testament.

So that no one should blame us. The verb means to find fault, to bring a charge. Paul is taking precautions against an accusation that has not yet been made, about a sum of money that has not yet been collected.

That is worth noticing. He is not responding to a scandal. He is arranging matters so that a scandal cannot be manufactured — which is the only time such arrangements can be made, since after the accusation they always look like a reaction.

Then the principle: we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man. Two audiences, and both are taken seriously.

The first is obvious and is where Christians usually stop. God sees; my conscience is clear; he knows my motives. All true. And Paul says it is not enough.

The second audience is the watching world, which cannot see motives and must judge by arrangements. And here is the point that so many sincere people miss: it is not sufficient to be honest. Where other people’s money is concerned, you must be visibly, checkably honest, in a way that does not depend on anyone believing you.

This cuts against a common and rather pious instinct. A man of genuine integrity finds oversight faintly insulting — the second signature, the audit, the receipts, the rule that he may not authorise his own expenses. It feels like being suspected. Paul, whose integrity nobody should have doubted, built the structure himself and volunteered for it, and he did it precisely because he was trustworthy. It was not about him.

The reason is that the reputation of a ministry is not the private property of the person carrying it. It belongs to the gospel. And nothing in the last century has damaged the credibility of the church in ordinary people’s eyes as reliably as money — the ministry whose accounts nobody sees, the appeal that funded a lifestyle, the collapse that made the evening news and gave a hundred thousand people a reason never to listen again. Every one of those started as a good man who did not think the precautions applied to him.

So the application is not complicated, and it reaches beyond churches. Two people count the offering. Nobody handles a fund alone. The accounts are open to the members. The person who decides the spending is not the person who signs the cheque. None of it implies distrust; all of it removes a stone from the road (6:3), which is the whole reason Paul is doing it.

verseByVerse.quote: And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.

A third man, also unnamed, and the way Paul describes him is worth attention.

He does not say the man is gifted or well known. He says he has been often tested and found earnest in many matters. This is a reputation built slowly, in a series of small situations, over years. Somebody kept giving him things to do and he kept doing them.

That is how trust is actually acquired, and it is worth saying in a church culture that tends to be impressed by the newly arrived and the obviously able. The man Paul will trust with a large sum of money is the man who has been reliable in a lot of unremarkable matters, and the reliability was demonstrated before the responsibility was given, not after.

And then the reason he is keener than ever: because of his great confidence in you. Titus went to Corinth and came back with a good report, and it has evidently made an impression on this man, who now wants to go himself. A church that comes right does not merely settle its own trouble; it energises people who have only heard about it.

Then Paul introduces the three of them formally, and the titles rise as he goes.

Titus is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit.Partner is koinōnos, the man who shares the enterprise — not an assistant, a colleague with a stake in it.

Our brothers are messengers of the churches. The word is apostoloi — sent ones. Not apostles in the sense Paul is, but men formally commissioned and sent by congregations, carrying their authority.

And then the last phrase, dropped in without explanation, and it is the largest thing in the verse: the glory of Christ.

Of these two men — one unnamed, one described only as reliable, both currently employed as couriers of a charitable fund — Paul says that they are the glory of Christ. That is what he calls them. Not they bring glory to Christ, though they do. They are his glory.

It is the same astonishing claim as chapter 3, where the Corinthians were the letter, and chapter 4, where the treasure is in clay. Christ has arranged that his glory in this world should be visible in people — in ordinary, unnamed, tested, faithful people carrying out unglamorous work for churches they will never be famous in. He is not ashamed of the arrangement. He chose it.

verseByVerse.quote: So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.

The chapter ends with a single instruction, and after everything that has gone before it is almost startling in its directness. Give proof.

The word means to demonstrate, to show the reality of a thing. Paul has spent twenty-three verses on grace, on the Macedonians, on Christ becoming poor, on readiness and proportion and transparency. And it comes down to this: when the three men arrive, put something in the bag.

That is not a descent from the theological heights. It is where the theological heights were always going. This is a letter, not a lecture, and the love that has been discussed has to be demonstrated to actual people arriving on an actual day.

Proof of your love. Back to verse 8, where the point of the exercise was to prove whether their love was genuine. Love that cannot be demonstrated has not yet been shown to exist. John put it as bluntly as it can be put: if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him? Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth (1 Jn. 3:17–18).

And of our boasting about you. There it is again — the thing Paul has been risking all through these chapters. He has told the Macedonians that Corinth would come through (9:2 will say so explicitly). He has told Titus they were a good people and was not put to shame (7:14). Now he tells them, in writing, that his reputation is attached to what they do next.

He could have kept that quiet. Instead he says it out loud, which is either reckless or a deliberate act of trust, and given how carefully he has handled everything else in this chapter it is plainly the second. He is telling them: I have vouched for you. That is a form of love, and it makes a demand precisely because it was given before it was earned.

Before the churches. The demonstration is public. Other congregations are watching, and Paul does not pretend otherwise.

So the chapter closes where it opened, with churches looking at each other and being provoked to something better. It began with Macedonia’s example held up to Corinth; it ends with Corinth’s response held up to everyone. That is not manipulation — it is the ordinary way God has always spread generosity through his people, one congregation catching it from another, and every one of them catching it, in the end, from a Lord who was rich and became poor for their sake.

9.title: Sowing Generously: The Cheerful Giver
9.overview:
Chapter 9 continues the appeal of chapter 8, adding two further theological foundations for generous giving: the agricultural principle of sowing and reaping, and the character of God as the one who loves a cheerful giver. Together they move the discussion of giving from mere duty to delight — from the obligation of the generous to the freedom and joy of those who have understood who God is and what giving does in the world.

The chapter is framed by two great theological statements. The first (v. 6) states the sowing principle: whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. This is not a prosperity gospel guarantee but an agricultural reality applied to spiritual generosity: what is given away is not lost but invested. The second (v. 15) closes the chapter with an exclamation of wonder at the “inexpressible gift” of God — which is both the grounds for human generosity (we give because we have received) and the ultimate standard against which all giving is measured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Sowing and Reaping; the Cheerful Giver; the Inexpressible Gift
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul begins by saying it is superfluous to write about the collection at all (v. 1), and then discloses why he is writing: he has been boasting about the Corinthians’ readiness to the Macedonians, and their zeal has stirred up most of them (v. 2). Each church has been provoked by the other, and Paul has been carrying the news back and forth. He now sends the brothers ahead (v. 3) so that the boast does not prove empty and so that they are genuinely ready — sparing both him and them the humiliation of a Macedonian delegation arriving to find nothing prepared (v. 4).

The reason for the timetable is stated in v. 5, and it is the governing concern of the whole chapter: the gift is to be ready as a willing gift (eulogia, a blessing), not as an exaction (pleonexia, grasping). The same sum arriving in the same bag is either a blessing or a shakedown, and the difference is whether it was freely given. Paul deliberately builds the arrangement that removes the pressure he could most easily have applied.

The sowing principle (v. 6) reflects an agricultural reality: you cannot reap more than you sow. The application to giving is that generosity is an investment, not merely an expenditure. Verse 7 then settles the manner: each one is to give as he has decided in his heart — a settled decision made in advance, not a reaction to an appeal — not reluctantly or under compulsion, “for God loves a cheerful giver.” The word hilaron (cheerful, joyful, even hilarious — from which English “hilarious” derives) describes the quality of the giver that God loves.

Verse 8 makes the theological ground explicit: “God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.” The giver is not depleted by giving; God replenishes so that the giving continues. Verse 9 supports it from Psalm 112:9, where open-handedness is listed among the identifying marks of the man who fears the LORD, and where the righteousness — unlike the money — endures forever. Verse 10 distinguishes the two things God supplies, seed for sowing and bread for eating, and promises to multiply the seed; and v. 11 states the purpose for the third time in four verses: enriched in every way in order to be generous in every way. The promise is never allowed to stand on its own for a single sentence.

The chapter closes with a doxology (vv. 12–15): the ministry of this service does more than supply the saints’ needs — it overflows in thanksgivings to God (v. 12), it proves to sceptical Jewish believers that the Gentile confession of the gospel is real (v. 13), and it sets the recipients longing and praying for the givers because of the surpassing grace of God upon them (v. 14). And the ultimate exclamation: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!” (v. 15) — the gift of Christ himself, the one who became poor so that we might become rich, which is the inexhaustible motivation for every act of Christian generosity.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sowing-reaping principle in v. 6 must be held in tension with the warning against prosperity theology, and the passage itself supplies the correction three times over. Paul is not promising that generous financial giving will result in financial wealth. The reaping he describes is named in v. 10 as “the harvest of your righteousness” — moral integrity and fruitfulness in God’s sight. The supply God gives in that same verse is “seed for sowing and bread for eating” — resources to live on and resources to give again — and it is the seed, not the bread, that he undertakes to multiply. Verse 11 then adds that the enriching is “in order to be generous.” The giver is not made wealthy; he is kept supplied so that generosity can continue. The decisive counter-example is in the previous chapter: the man held up as the supreme giver at 8:9 became poor.

Verse 9 quotes Psalm 112:9. The psalm is a portrait of the man who fears the LORD, and it places distributing freely and giving to the poor among his identifying marks, alongside steadiness and courage — generosity as a feature of godliness rather than an optional extra of temperament. The clause Paul is after is “his righteousness endures forever”: the money is gone and cannot be pointed to, and what it produced does not go anywhere.

“God loves a cheerful giver” (v. 7) comes from the Greek Old Testament at Proverbs 22:8, which carries a line the Hebrew text does not — a blessing on the cheerful and generous man. Paul’s citation focuses the divine pleasure on the disposition of the giver: the motivation and the manner of giving are as important to God as the amount.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation uses a pledge campaign with carefully designed giving targets and social dynamics (recognising top givers, publishing goals) that effectively apply social pressure to giving. Many give generously as a result. But the pastor wonders whether the giving is cheerful or compelled. This passage challenges not the amount raised but the mechanism: “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (v. 7). The goal is not merely generous giving but the formation of cheerful givers — people who give because they have been gripped by the inexpressible gift of God and cannot hold back.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.

Paul has just spent a chapter on the collection, and he opens the next one by saying there is no need to write about it. The touch is very light and entirely deliberate.

Superfluous. Unnecessary, surplus to requirements. It is a courtesy, and everyone knew it — he is about to write fourteen more verses on the subject. But the courtesy is not empty. He is telling them that he is not addressing a delinquent church. He is addressing people whose willingness he takes for granted and whose reputation he has already staked.

Then the disclosure: I boast about you to the people of Macedonia. He has been going round northern Greece telling the poorest churches in the empire that Achaia was ready a year ago.

Notice the extraordinary circularity of what has been happening. In chapter 8 the Macedonian example was held up to shame Corinth into action. Now we learn that the Corinthian example was what stirred the Macedonians in the first place. Each church has been provoked by the other, and Paul has been carrying the news back and forth between them.

That is not manipulation, and it is worth saying why. He has not told either church anything untrue. The Corinthians really had begun eagerly; the Macedonians really did give beyond their means. He is simply refusing to let two congregations two hundred miles apart remain ignorant of what God is doing in the other, and the result is that each one catches something from the other.

The word for it here is zeal — heat, intensity — and the verb is that it stirred up most of them. Enthusiasm turns out to be contagious across provinces.

Which is a reason for churches to talk to one another, and a reason for the report from another congregation to be treated as more than a slot in the notices. A church quietly convinced that giving on any serious scale is unrealistic will go on believing it indefinitely if it never hears what a poorer church down the road has just done. The single most effective thing Paul does in these two chapters is carry news.

And there is a quieter warning in it too. Your church’s giving, or your own, is not a private matter with no downstream effects. Somebody is watching, and what they see either enlarges what they think possible or confirms them in what they already assumed. The Corinthians had stirred up a whole province without knowing it, a year before this letter — and would have gone on not knowing, had Paul not told them.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated — to say nothing of you — for being so confident.

Having said it was superfluous to write, Paul now says exactly why he is writing, and he is remarkably candid about it.

So that our boasting about you may not prove empty. He has made a claim in public and he does not want to be found to have overstated it. That is a plain admission of self- interest, and its plainness is part of the honesty.

But look at the order of the concern in verse 4: we would be humiliated — to say nothing of you. He names his own embarrassment first and theirs as an aside. He could have led with theirs, which would have applied more pressure; he does not. And the little parenthesis is generous rather than pointed — the sort of thing said quickly and moved past.

Then the practical arrangement, and it is the whole reason for the paragraph. Titus and the brothers are being sent in advance so the money is collected before Paul arrives with a Macedonian delegation.

Consider what he is avoiding. If nothing has been gathered when he walks in with visitors, there will be an appeal on the spot, in the room, with witnesses present, and money will be produced — of course it will. And every coin of it will have been given under social pressure, in front of an apostle, to avoid a humiliation. It would have looked like generosity and been nothing of the kind.

So Paul builds the timetable specifically to remove the pressure he could most easily have used. He is an apostle with a Macedonian audience and a year-old promise; he holds every card, and he arranges not to play them.

That is worth setting beside how appeals are often run. The technique of the moment — the emotional peak, the visiting speaker, the pledge cards handed round while the feeling is high, the totals announced from the front, the giving made visible — works, in the sense that it produces money. Paul’s judgment is that it produces the wrong thing, and he says so explicitly in the next verse.

There is also something here about the relationship between belief in people and structure for them. Paul genuinely expects the Corinthians to come through; he has said so publicly. And he does not simply expect it and wait. He sends three men and a timetable, because good intentions need infrastructure, and the leader who believes the best about people and provides them nothing to act on has left the believing half undone.

verseByVerse.quote: So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.

Here is the reason for all the arranging, and it turns on two words held deliberately apart.

A willing gift is, in the Greek, a blessing — eulogia, the word that gives us eulogy, meaning a good word spoken, and by extension a benefit freely bestowed. That is what Paul wants the money to be: a blessing, given as blessings are given.

Not as an exaction is pleonexia — greed, covetousness, the grasping that takes what is not freely offered. It is a hard word, and Paul uses it of what the collection would become if it were extracted rather than given. The same root turned up at 2:11 of Satan getting the better of someone in a transaction.

So the same sum of money, arriving in the same bag on the same day, is either a blessing or a shakedown, and the difference is not in the amount. It is in whether it was freely given.

That should be allowed to land on how churches actually raise money, because the mechanisms that produce compulsion are rarely crude. Nobody is threatened. But there is the giving made visible so that the level is known; the target announced with a thermometer on the wall; the appeal placed at the emotional peak of a meeting; the pledge card passed along a row where everyone can see who is filling one in; the quiet awareness that the treasurer knows. All of these work. All of them shift the reason a person gives from what is in his heart to what the room expects.

Paul’s instinct is to build the structure that makes freedom possible: give people notice, give them time, let them decide at home, and arrange to be absent while they do it. That is what arrange in advance means here. He is not making it easier to give; he is making it possible to give freely.

And notice what he assumes about God in all this. He is prepared to risk a smaller collection in order to have a genuine one. He evidently does not believe that God needs the money badly enough to accept it on any terms — which is exactly right, since the whole letter has been saying that the God in question owns everything and became poor on purpose.

There is a personal version of the same test. Before you give, it is worth knowing which sentence you are answering: I want to, or I would look bad if I did not. The second is not wicked, and God is not standing over anybody with a stopwatch. But Paul has gone to considerable trouble here to make sure the Corinthians could answer the first.

verseByVerse.quote: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.

Now the principle, and it is drawn from the one place everybody in the ancient world understood.

Stage it. A farmer walks out in autumn with a bag of seed and a decision to make, and the decision is genuinely painful, because the seed in that bag is food. He could eat it. His family can see it. And what he is being asked to do is throw it on the ground and cover it up, where it will do nobody any good for months. The more he keeps back to eat, the less goes into the ground, and the less comes up in the spring. Everyone farming knows this and it never stops being hard, because the eating is now and the harvest is later.

Giving works the same way, Paul says. What you release is not lost; it is planted. And the size of what comes back corresponds to what went in.

Now this verse must be handled carefully, because it has been made the foundation of one of the ugliest distortions of Christianity there is. The prosperity teacher quotes it and stops: sow generously into this ministry and God will return it to you multiplied, and the more you give the wealthier you will become. Money is thereby extracted from poor people by a promise God has not made, using a verse from a passage whose entire concern is that giving must not be extracted.

Three things in the passage itself take that reading apart, and none of them requires going outside the chapter.

First, look at what Paul actually says the harvest is. Not money. Verse 10 calls it the harvest of your righteousness. Verse 11 says you are enriched in order to be generous. Verse 12 says the yield is thanksgivings to God. The crop, named three times, is righteousness, further generosity, and worship.

Second, the supply in verse 10 is seed for sowing and bread for food — enough to live on and enough to give again. That is provision for a farmer, not a fortune.

Third, and most decisively, the man Paul has just held up as the supreme example of generosity in 8:9 became poor. If sowing bountifully guaranteed material return, the Lord Jesus Christ is the counter-example, and so is Paul, who wrote this while hungry.

What the verse does promise is real, and it is better than money. Nothing given away in God’s name is lost. It is seed in the ground, and there is a harvest attached to it that you will see. The only question the verse puts is the farmer’s question, and it is a hard one every autumn: how much are you willing to put out of your own reach, on the word of God that the ground is not a hole but a field?

verseByVerse.quote: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

One verse, and it settles the manner, the method and the motive of Christian giving.

Each one. Not the wealthy, not those who feel able. Everybody. There is no exemption here for the poor, which is why the Macedonians gave out of the depths.

As he has decided in his heart. The verb means to purpose, to determine beforehand — a settled decision, made in advance, not a reaction. This is the strongest argument in Scripture for planned giving. It is a decision reached in private, with the figures in front of you, before any appeal is heard — and once made, it takes the question out of the offering plate and out of the emotional temperature of a meeting. Paul told this same church to do it weekly and in advance, so that there will be no collecting when I come (1 Cor. 16:2).

Then the two things it must not be, and both are shrewdly chosen.

Not reluctantly — literally, not out of grief. Not with a pang. That is the giving that is genuinely done and quietly resented, and the resentment usually surfaces later as a complaint about how the money is spent.

Not under compulsion — not because you had to. The pressure need not come from outside; most of it does not. It is the calculation of what is expected, what others will think, what a person in your position ought to be seen to do.

And then the sentence itself, and the word behind cheerful is a delight: hilaros, the root of our word hilarious. Paul had it from the Greek version of Proverbs. It is not sober approval; it is something closer to laughter. God loves a giver whose giving is a pleasure to him.

Which is a genuinely startling thing to be told, because it means God is not primarily after the money. He owns the cattle on a thousand hills and has no shortage. What he loves is a particular kind of person: one for whom letting go has become a joy rather than a loss.

And that cannot be produced by trying. You cannot decide to find giving delightful, any more than you can decide to find a person attractive. It comes from somewhere else — from having grasped, somewhere below the level of argument, that you cannot out-give the one who has already given you everything, and that nothing you release was ever really at risk.

So if giving is currently a duty you perform with a small internal wince, the answer is not to give more grimly. It is to go back and look again at 8:9 until the arithmetic changes. Cheerful givers are made by contemplation, not by resolve.

verseByVerse.quote: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.

Paul now supplies the reason a person can afford to give freely, and the sentence is built out of totality. Count the words: all grace, all sufficiency, all things, all times, every good work. Five in one line. He is piling them up on purpose.

Begin where he begins: God is able. That is the ground of the whole thing. Not God will make you comfortable, but God is able — the question of capacity is settled, and it is his capacity, not yours.

To make all grace abound to you. Grace again, the word running through both chapters. And here it plainly includes the material, since the context is money; but it is not only material, and Paul’s vocabulary refuses to let it shrink to that.

Then the key word: sufficiency. The Greek is autarkeia, and it has a history worth knowing. It was a great word among the Stoic philosophers, and it meant self-sufficiency — the ideal of the wise man who has trained himself to need nothing from anyone, and is therefore untouchable. It was an admirable and rather cold aspiration, and it depended entirely on the strength of the individual.

Paul takes the word and quietly turns it inside out. The Christian has autarkeia — he lacks nothing — and it does not come from within him at all. It is supplied. He is not self-sufficient; he is God-sufficient, and therefore has the freedom the Stoic wanted without the self-reliance the Stoic required. Paul says elsewhere that he has learned this by experience in both directions: I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content (Phil. 4:11), a sentence written from prison by a man who had been both well fed and hungry.

And then the purpose clause, which is the part that gets left out when this verse is quoted on its own. Why does God supply all sufficiency at all times? So that you may abound in every good work.

Not so that you may be secure. Not so that you may relax. The sufficiency is given to free the hands. God keeps a giver supplied for the same reason a farmer is kept in seed — because there is more sowing to do.

Which turns the verse into a genuine and searching question about what you have. Everyone has some margin, however small: the money, the time, the room, the skill, the years. The verse says that the margin was supplied, and it names the purpose it was supplied for. If it has been quietly reclassified as security, something has gone wrong in the accounting — because a God who gives seed and gets no crop has not been dealt with honestly.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”

Paul reaches for a psalm, and the choice repays looking up.

It is Psalm 112, and the whole psalm is a portrait of a particular kind of man: the one who fears the LORD. It describes him as gracious, merciful, unafraid of bad news, steady when others panic — and right in the middle of the portrait, as one of the marks of the God-fearing man, is this: he has distributed freely, he has given to the poor.
