11.title: The Fool's Speech and the Catalogue of Suffering
11.overview:
Chapter 11 contains Paul’s most ironic and self-revealing writing. He embarks on the “fool’s speech” — boasting as the super-apostles boast, but turning the boasting itself into an exposure of their false standards. If they boast in impressive credentials, Paul will boast — in his sufferings and weaknesses, the very things the super-apostles would consider disqualifications.

The chapter opens with Paul’s jealousy for the Corinthians: he has betrothed them to Christ as a pure virgin; he fears they are being led astray from sincere and pure devotion to Christ, just as the serpent deceived Eve. The false apostles are preaching a different Jesus, a different spirit, a different gospel. Paul does not dismiss these as minor variations; he identifies them as satanic counterfeits, presented by false apostles who are servants of Satan disguised as servants of righteousness.

The chapter closes with one of the most remarkable personal disclosures in the NT: Paul’s catalogue of sufferings (vv. 23–29) — more imprisonments, more beatings, near death, five times forty lashes minus one, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, a night and a day adrift at sea — and the inner burden: “there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.” This is the resume of the authentic apostle, offered as the ultimate rebuttal to those who boast in impressive credentials and spiritual experiences.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Jealousy for the Corinthians and the False Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with a little foolishness (v. 1), and explains why he is willing to look ridiculous. His divine jealousy for them (v. 2, zēlō gar hymas theou zēlō — I am jealous for you with God’s jealousy) is rooted in his role as their spiritual father: he betrothed them to one husband, to present them to Christ as a pure virgin. The betrothal image is drawn from the Old Testament pattern of God as the husband of Israel (Isa. 54:5; Jer. 3; Ezek. 16), and the role Paul claims is the friend of the bridegroom, who guards the bride until the wedding day.

The comparison to Eve (v. 3) is striking: the serpent did not argue the Corinthians away from Christ with obviously false teaching. He was subtle (panourgia — crafty, cunning), and what Paul fears losing is not first their orthodoxy but their “sincere and pure devotion to Christ” — the singleness of heart that can be crowded out without anything ever being renounced. The false apostles are preaching a “different Jesus” (allon Iēsoun), a “different spirit” (pneuma heteron), a “different gospel” (euangelion heteron) (v. 4). The terms are precise: allos means numerically different (another of the same kind); heteros means qualitatively different (another of a different kind). The false gospel is not merely a variation; it is a different species of religious message entirely — and the sting of v. 4 falls on the church: “you put up with it readily enough.”

Verses 5–12 turn to the rivals themselves and to the strangest accusation in the letter. Paul coins a title for them — the “super-apostles” (v. 5) — and concedes the charge of 10:10 without a fight: he is idiōtēs, untrained in speaking (v. 6), though not in knowledge. Then the money. He preached free of charge (v. 7), supported by gifts from Macedonia (vv. 8–9), refusing to burden a wealthy church while the poorest churches in the empire paid for his work there. In a patron-client culture that read payment as the mark of a teacher’s worth, this was used against him — and he answers the misreading directly (v. 11): “Because I do not love you? God knows I do!” He will not change the policy (vv. 10, 12), because it is the one piece of evidence his rivals cannot copy without ceasing to be what they are.

The false apostles are not dismissed as misguided enthusiasts; they are identified with Satan (vv. 13–15): “such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.” The most dangerous spiritual deceptions are not the obviously false but the apparently luminous — the ones that look like the genuine article but have substituted a different Jesus, a different spirit, a different gospel. Their disguise of choice is “servants of righteousness,” and their end will correspond to their deeds.
verseByVerse.theology: The identification of false apostles as servants of Satan (v. 15) is one of Paul’s most severe theological statements. It raises the question of how to identify false apostles — since they come disguised as servants of righteousness. The test that Paul has been applying throughout the letter is: what is the content of the message? What is the character of the minister? Does the ministry bear the cruciform pattern of genuine apostolic suffering? Paul’s opponents fail all three tests: their message is a different gospel; their character is self-promotional; their lives show no evidence of the suffering that authentic ministry requires.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation is attracted to a visiting teacher who is eloquent, radiantly confident, and preaches a message of spiritual empowerment, prosperity, and supernatural experience — all framed in Christian language. The pastor is concerned but cannot point to an obviously heretical statement. This passage gives him the categories: the test is not merely whether Jesus is mentioned but which Jesus is being presented, which spirit is being invoked, which gospel is being preached. The angel-of-light disguise means the most dangerous false teaching often looks impressively spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.

Paul is about to do something he finds distasteful, and he apologises for it twice before he starts. Bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! The second sentence is almost a plea. He knows how what follows will sound.

Then he explains why he is willing to look ridiculous, and the reason is not wounded pride. I feel a divine jealousy for you. The Greek repeats the root for emphasis — literally, I am jealous for you with God’s own jealousy.

That word needs handling, because jealousy is a vice in most of its ordinary uses and a divine attribute in Scripture. The difference is what is being defended. Envy wants what belongs to someone else. Jealousy of this kind guards what already belongs to you and is being taken. A husband who feels nothing when his wife is being drawn away does not love her more than a jealous man; he loves her less. God calls himself jealous for exactly that reason — the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God (Ex. 34:14) — and it is the language of a marriage, not of a tyrant.

Which is precisely the picture Paul now draws: I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.

Stage it, because a Jewish betrothal is not a modern engagement. It was legally binding; only a divorce could end it. And there was a role in the proceedings Paul is claiming here — the friend of the bridegroom, who arranged the match, guarded the bride through the betrothal period, and finally presented her to the husband on the wedding day. John the Baptist described himself the same way and said his whole joy was to hear the bridegroom’s voice (Jn. 3:29).

So Paul is not the husband. He is the man who brought the bride to him, and who is responsible for her until the day arrives. That is why he is jealous. Something is happening to his charge on his watch.

Notice what it makes of the church, and it is worth pausing on. This congregation — divided, suspicious, easily impressed by the wrong men — is a bride being kept for a wedding. Everything she is now is provisional. What she is being prepared for is the day she is presented, and Paul’s hope is fixed on how she will look then, not on how she looks this year.

And that is a truer way to see the church than most of us manage. It is not first a society for religious improvement or an institution with problems. It is a woman under an engagement, and the one she is engaged to intends to present her in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27). He is coming for her, and he has never once changed his mind about the arrangement.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.

I am afraid. The apostle who has been telling this church he has complete confidence in them now says he is frightened for them, and the two are not a contradiction; a father can be sure of a child and lie awake about him in the same week.

Then the comparison, and it is the third time in this letter he has reached back to Genesis. As the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning.

Go back and look at how that deception actually worked, because everyone remembers the fruit and forgets the method. The serpent did not arrive denying God. He arrived asking a question: Did God actually say…? He did not begin by contradicting; he began by opening a small gap between what God had said and what God had meant. Then he offered a better reading of God’s motives — that the prohibition was self-protective, that God was holding something back. By the time he flatly contradicts (you will not surely die), the ground has already been prepared.

The word Paul uses for the method is panourgia: readiness to do anything, craftiness. It is the same root he used at 4:2 of the cunning he himself renounced. Deception of this order is not crude. It is patient, plausible, and it works with the grain of what the hearer already half wants to believe.

And notice exactly what Paul is afraid of losing. Not their orthodoxy in the first instance — their sincere and pure devotion to Christ. The word behind sincere is haplotēs, the singleness met at 1:12: being one thing rather than two. He is afraid they will become complicated.

That is a very precise fear and it is worth taking personally. The danger to a Christian is rarely that he will one day decide Christianity is false. It is that the simple attachment — the plain love of Christ that made everything else fall into place — gets crowded. Other loyalties arrive, and interests, and a growing sophistication about the faith that somehow leaves less warmth in it than there was at the beginning. Nobody renounces anything. The devotion simply stops being single.

The Lord said the same thing to the church at Ephesus, which was doctrinally impeccable, hard-working and patient, and had one thing wrong with it: you have abandoned the love you had at first (Rev. 2:4).

Which gives a test worth running honestly. Not do I still believe it? — you almost certainly do. Ask instead whether Christ is still simply and plainly the thing you love most, or whether he has become one item in a complicated arrangement. Eve did not stop believing in God. She stopped being single-hearted toward him, and the fruit came afterwards.

verseByVerse.quote: For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.

This is the most precise diagnosis of false teaching anywhere in Paul, and it repays being taken apart slowly.

Three things can be counterfeited, and he names them in order: a Jesus, a Spirit, a gospel. Notice that in every case the counterfeit keeps the word. Nobody arrived in Corinth announcing a new deity. They preached Jesus.

And the Greek marks a distinction the English cannot quite carry. For another Jesus Paul uses allos — another of the same sort, a second one. For the spirit and the gospel he switches to heteros — different in kind, another species altogether. Whether he intends the full weight of the distinction is debated, but the drift is unmistakable: a substituted Jesus produces a different spirit, and a different spirit produces a message that is no longer the same kind of thing at all.

So how would you know? The name is unchanged, the vocabulary is unchanged, and the man preaching is impressive. This is the practical question the verse exists to answer, and the whole letter has been supplying the tests.

Ask what this Jesus did. The real one was made sin for us and bore the wrath our sin deserved (5:21). A Jesus who is chiefly an example, a teacher, a life-coach or a source of personal power is a different Jesus, however warmly he is spoken of.

Ask what this Jesus asks. The real one calls people to die — no longer live for themselves (5:15). A Jesus who asks nothing that costs anything has been substituted.

Ask what the message does to the hearer’s sin. The genuine gospel names it, and then deals with it at the cross. A message that never mentions it is not a gentler version of the gospel; it is a different one, because it leaves the hearer with his actual problem untouched.

And ask what kind of ministers it produces. Paul’s test throughout: does the messenger bear the shape of the cross, or has he been made comfortable, admired and rich by the message he preaches?

Then the sting in the tail, and it is aimed at the Corinthians rather than the teachers: you put up with it readily enough. The tolerance is the crisis. A church that would argue for an hour about the seating plan sat quietly while the identity of its Lord was adjusted.

That is the abiding danger, and it is not solved by suspicion. It is solved by knowing the real one well enough that the substitute does not sound right — which is how bank clerks are trained to spot forgeries: not by studying counterfeits, but by handling the genuine note until anything else feels wrong in the hand.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.

These super-apostles. The word is Paul’s own coinage and it drips. Literally the extra-super apostles, the more-than-apostles. It is the tone of a man repeating a title other people use with a straight face.

Who were they? Not, on balance, the Jerusalem apostles — Paul has no quarrel with Peter and James here, and would not speak of them like this. These are the newcomers in Corinth, and the title is either theirs or the impression they had created.

Then the concession, and it is remarkable that he makes it: even if I am unskilled in speaking. The word is idiōtēs — a layman, an amateur, a man without professional training. It is where our word idiot comes from, though it did not mean that; it meant untrained.

He is granting the charge of 10:10. He was not a trained orator, and in a Greek city that was not a small thing. Public speaking was the prestige skill of the age, taught by paid professionals, judged by crowds who knew the technique. Against a man who had been taught to handle an audience, Paul evidently sounded ordinary.

And he lets it stand. He does not claim hidden eloquence or plead that his letters prove otherwise. He simply moves the contest to different ground: I am not so in knowledge.

What knowledge? Not cleverness in general. He means knowledge of God and of the gospel — the thing he has spent eleven chapters unfolding, from the new covenant to the great exchange. He is saying: I may not be able to hold a room the way they can, but I know what I am talking about, and they do not.

That distinction is worth carrying, because the church loses it about once a generation. The ability to speak well and the possession of something worth saying are two separate gifts, and they are not correlated. They can occur together, and when they do it is a great mercy. But an audience cannot easily tell them apart, which is why an articulate man with a thin message will generally be preferred to a plain man with a deep one — and the preference is usually described as a preference for good communication.

Then Paul adds the one claim he does make for his manner: in every way we have made this plain to you in all things. Not impressive. Plain. Whatever he lacked in polish, nobody in Corinth could say they had failed to understand him.

That is a better ambition for anyone who teaches, and a considerably harder one. Being admired is easier than being understood, and the two are frequently confused by everyone involved.

verseByVerse.quote: Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.

Now the strangest accusation in the letter. Paul is having to defend himself for not charging them money.

The question in verse 7 is bitter and it is meant to be: did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted? He is quoting the shape of the complaint back at them. Somehow, working for nothing had been turned into evidence against him.

To see why, you have to understand how a Greek city read this. Teachers of standing were supported — by fees, or by a wealthy patron who housed them and gained prestige from the association. Payment was the mark of worth. A man who worked with his hands to support himself was, by that reckoning, a tradesman rather than a professional, and manual labour carried real social contempt. Paul made tents (Acts 18:3). His rivals took money, lived as guests of important people, and looked exactly like what a serious teacher was supposed to look like.

So his refusal was not read as integrity. It was read two ways, both damaging: either he knew his teaching was not worth paying for, or — worse in that culture — he was refusing to enter the relationship of obligation that a gift creates, which is a way of holding people at arm’s length.

Then verse 8, and the irony is heavy: I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you. The verb is a military one — plundering a defeated city. He is saying, with a straight face: yes, I took money; I took it from Macedonia, and spent it on you. The Macedonians, we already know, were destitute (8:2).

There is a real principle underneath the irony, and Paul is careful about it elsewhere. He believed firmly that ministers should be supported — he argues it at length in the earlier letter, and concludes that the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Cor. 9:14). He is not laying down a rule that ministry must be unpaid. He is describing a right he declined to use, in this city, for a reason.

And the reason was strategic rather than principled: in a place where money bought influence and created obligation, taking it would have compromised the gospel he preached and given his rivals a way to claim equivalence. He removes the stumbling block (6:3) at real personal cost.

Which leaves a question worth asking in any church. Not should ministers be paid? — they should. Ask instead what your giving buys, and whether anyone in your congregation could reasonably think that money has purchased influence over what is preached. Paul was willing to sit up half the night cutting leather to make sure nobody could think it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.

He fills in the detail, and the detail matters: when I was with you and was in need. He was not comfortable. There were times in Corinth when he did not have enough.

And still he did not ask. The word behind burden is a vivid one — to be a dead weight, to numb something by pressing on it. He would not be that to them.

Where did the money come from? The brothers who came from Macedonia. Philippi, most likely; the Philippians sent to him repeatedly, and he thanks them for it warmly (Phil. 4:15–16). So the picture is this: the poorest churches in the empire were funding the apostle’s work in the richest city he served, so that the rich church would not have to pay and could not say it had.

Then the vow, and it is put under oath: As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. He intends to go on refusing their money and he intends to go on saying so.

That sounds stubborn until you see what it protects. The next verse will name the danger, but it is already visible here. If Paul once accepted support in Corinth, the whole distinction between himself and the men who had come for what they could get would collapse — and with it the one visible proof that he was not in this for anything.

There is a lesson here about the cost of an unimpeachable position, and it is not a comfortable one. Paul’s policy did not make his life easier. It made him poorer, it made him tired, and it was used against him anyway. He kept it because the gospel’s credibility was worth more to him than his own comfort or his own reputation.

Most decisions of that kind are invisible and unrewarded. The businessman who loses the contract rather than pay what everyone pays. The person who declines the gift because of what accepting it would quietly imply. The minister who will not let a major donor into the decision. None of these gets noticed, and several of them get misread as pride, as Paul’s was.

And notice the geography: in the regions of Achaia. Not merely in Corinth. He is staking this across the whole province, in every congregation that will hear the letter read. A position taken that publicly cannot quietly be dropped later, which is presumably why he took it that publicly.

verseByVerse.quote: And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.

He anticipates the obvious misreading and answers it before it can be spoken.

Because I do not love you? That is what refusing a gift can look like from the outside, and in that culture it looked like it very strongly. To decline hospitality was to decline a relationship.

And his answer is not an argument. God knows I do. Three words, with God as the witness, and nothing offered by way of proof. There are some things you cannot demonstrate to people who have decided otherwise, and the attempt to demonstrate them usually makes matters worse. He states it, calls God to witness it, and moves on.

Anyone who has been misread by people they love will recognise the position. You can explain once. After that, explaining becomes its own kind of evidence against you, and the only thing left is to go on loving them and let God hold the record.

Then verse 12, and here is the actual strategy: in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.

The rivals wanted parity. They wanted to be able to say: we operate exactly as Paul does, so judge us as you judge him. And the one thing that made the comparison impossible was the money. So long as Paul worked for nothing and they took payment, the difference was visible to everybody, and no amount of talking could close it.

Which explains why he will not give the position up. It is not stubbornness and it is not pride. It is the one piece of evidence he has that cannot be argued with, and it costs him personally to maintain, which is exactly what makes it evidence.

There is a principle in that worth carrying beyond first-century Corinth. When two accounts of a person are in circulation and words will not settle it, what settles it is a pattern of behaviour that would be irrational for a self-interested man to sustain. Paul’s empty purse was an argument no rival could answer, because they could not copy it without becoming what they were pretending to be.

And underneath the strategy is the thing he asked God to witness. He was doing all of it — the night work, the poverty, the humiliation of being thought worthless because he would not charge — for people who at that moment believed he did not love them.

verseByVerse.quote: For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

The gloves come off. Paul has been ironic for twelve verses; here he simply says what these men are.

Three descriptions, and each is worse than the last. False apostles — pseudapostoloi, a word that appears nowhere else in the New Testament and that Paul may have coined for the occasion. Deceitful workmen — skilled workers producing counterfeits; the problem is not incompetence but craft. And disguising themselves as apostles of Christ: the verb means to change one’s outward form, to put on an appearance.

Notice he does not say they are sincere men who have gone wrong. That would be the charitable reading and Paul rejects it. These are people who know what they are doing.

Then the explanation, and it is one of the most sobering sentences in the New Testament: no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

Stop at no wonder. Paul is saying the church should not be surprised by this. It is the expected pattern, working exactly as it always has.

And the pattern is not what most people imagine. The popular picture of evil is darkness, grotesquerie, something obviously repellent — which is precisely why the real thing gets through. Satan’s most effective form is not the monster. It is the angel of light: the impressive, the luminous, the manifestly spiritual, the thing that looks better than what you already have.

Which is why discernment cannot run on instinct. If you are waiting to feel uneasy, you will be caught, because the whole point of the disguise is that it produces the opposite feeling. People do not follow false teachers reluctantly; they follow them enthusiastically, and describe the experience as the most spiritually alive they have ever been.

So the test can never be how did it make me feel? It has to be the one Paul gave in verse 4: which Jesus, which Spirit, which gospel. Those are questions of content, and they can be answered by an ordinary Christian with a Bible, on a Tuesday, without any special sensitivity at all.

And there is a mercy folded into the warning. The disguise exists because the genuine article is the only thing worth counterfeiting. Nobody forges a worthless note. That an enemy has gone to the trouble of imitating apostles of Christ is itself a backhanded testimony to what apostles of Christ actually carry — and the light he borrows to disguise himself is not his own, and never was.

verseByVerse.quote: So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.

The logic completes. If the master appears as light, his servants will appear as righteousness. The disguise runs all the way down.

Note carefully what they are disguised as. Not as scholars, not as leaders, not as men of power. As servants of righteousness — that is, as morally serious people. This is the most effective camouflage there is in a religious community, because it is the last thing anyone thinks to question. A man who is visibly rigorous about right and wrong is granted enormous latitude, and rightly so most of the time, which is exactly what makes the disguise worth wearing.

And it is worth being honest about how the counterfeit usually presents. It is very often more demanding than the genuine article, not less. The Judaizers in Galatia wanted more law, not less. The false teachers of Colossae wanted more asceticism. There is a kind of severity that looks like holiness and is actually a bid for control, and Paul had seen enough of it to name it: it has an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but is of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (Col. 2:23).

Then the last sentence, and Paul does not enlarge on it: their end will correspond to their deeds.

Two things are in it. First, there is an end. The disguise is temporary; it works now and it does not work then. Everything about these men that is currently persuasive has a date attached to it.

Second, the correspondence is to deeds, not appearances. What is judged is what was actually done, not what it looked like — which is the exact reversal of the Corinthian situation, where appearance was carrying everything.

He says it in one line and stops, and the restraint is deliberate. He does not gloat over it, speculate about it, or use it as a threat. He simply notes that the accounts will be settled somewhere he is not required to settle them.

And that is what frees a man to speak plainly and then let the matter go. Paul names these people for what they are, because the church is in danger and somebody has to. He does not have to destroy them, and he does not try. The Judge of all the earth will do right, and he can be left to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — The Fool’s Boast and the Catalogue of Sufferings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul enters the fool’s speech proper (vv. 16–18): “I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.” He is doing what his opponents do — boasting — and says plainly that he speaks “not as the Lord would but as a fool.” He enters a contest he despises because the alternative is to let a church be lost to a different gospel.

Then the irony turns on the congregation (vv. 19–21). They pride themselves on being wise, and they have gladly borne with fools. Paul lists what they have in fact tolerated: someone who makes slaves of them, devours them, takes advantage of them, puts on airs, or strikes them in the face — and adds, with mock contrition, “To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!” A church that would not tolerate an apostle who worked with his hands had tolerated a man who slapped its members. Set beside 1:24 — “not that we lord it over your faith” — the two portraits could not be further apart.

If the super-apostles boast of being Hebrews, Israelites, offspring of Abraham (v. 22), Paul is all of these; the contest of credentials ends in a tie, because credentials are the sort of thing that can be matched. The fourth question breaks the pattern (v. 23): are they servants of Christ? “I am a better one — I am talking like a madman” — and the evidence he produces is not achievements but what has been done to him.

And then the “more” turns out to be a catalogue of suffering that takes the breath away (vv. 24–27). Five times the forty lashes less one (the Jewish synagogue punishment, stopped at 39 so a miscount could never break Deut. 25:3). Three times beaten with rods (the Roman punishment; Acts records one). Once stoned (Acts 14:19 at Lystra). Three times shipwrecked — none of them the shipwreck of Acts 27, which had not yet happened. A night and a day adrift at sea. Frequent journeys, danger from rivers, robbers, his own people, Gentiles, in the city, in the wilderness, at sea — and, held to the end because it is the worst, danger from false brothers. In toil and hardship, sleepless nights, hunger and thirst, cold and exposure.

And then the interior (v. 28): “And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.” The catalogue of external sufferings is capped by the internal burden — the daily, relentless weight of concern for every congregation he has planted. This is the hidden suffering of pastoral ministry that no one sees and that cannot be measured by any external criterion. Verse 29 shows where it comes from: he has no protective distance, going down with the weak and burning over whoever trips them.

Verse 30 is the sentence the whole speech has been climbing toward — “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness” — and the chapter ends by proving it. Under oath (v. 31), Paul closes not with a vision or a conquest but with an escape (vv. 32–33): lowered from the wall of Damascus in a basket. The Roman army gave a wall crown to the first man over the wall of a besieged city; Paul’s wall story is a man going the other way, down, hiding, as freight.
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue of sufferings is Paul’s primary credential. In his opponents’ world, apostolic legitimacy was demonstrated by impressive spiritual experiences (visions, tongues, miraculous signs) and social credibility (letters of recommendation, personal charisma, philosophical sophistication). Paul’s credential is precisely the opposite: a body broken by service, a life spent in the pattern of the cross. This is not masochism; it is the coherence of messenger and message. The one who preaches a crucified Christ must bear in his body the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: A church’s senior pastor has served for 25 years in a difficult context: modest attendance, a neighbourhood in decline, countless crises with little visible breakthrough. When a search committee from a larger church comes to interview him, they ask about his “greatest ministry successes.” He does not know what to say. This passage suggests a different category: the 25-year record of faithfulness in hardship, the daily anxiety for the congregation, the pattern of showing up — this is the apostolic credential. The question “what have you built?” is not the only or even the primary question.

verseByVerse.quote: I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.

Three verses of throat-clearing before the fool’s speech proper, and the hesitation is the point.

He says it as plainly as it can be said: I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. This is Paul telling us that what follows is not how a Christian should ordinarily talk. Our Lord did not go about listing his qualifications.

That candour is worth noticing for what it says about Scripture. Paul is inspired here, and what he is inspired to record is that he is about to do something he regards as beneath the gospel. The Bible is not a collection of model speeches; it is God’s word given through real men in real corners, and here it preserves an apostle telling us he is arguing badly on purpose.

Then why do it? Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.

Because the alternative was worse. If Paul stayed silent while impressive men listed their credentials, the Corinthians would draw the obvious conclusion, and a church would be lost to a different gospel. So he enters a contest he despises, in order to win people out of it.

There is a genuine pastoral principle here and it is easily misapplied in both directions. Sometimes the only way to reach people is to meet them briefly on their own ground — to answer, as Proverbs puts it in one of its two facing maxims, a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes (Prov. 26:5). Paul is doing that. What keeps it from becoming mere worldliness is that he says out loud what he is doing and why, so that nobody can mistake the tactic for the truth.

The misapplication is the church that adopts the world’s methods for the world’s reasons and calls it strategy. The difference is visible in two places: whether the borrowing is acknowledged as a concession or presented as wisdom, and whether the man doing it is enjoying himself. Paul is plainly not enjoying himself.

And watch what he does with the game once he has entered it. He is about to take the conventions of ancient self-praise — ancestry, achievements, hardships nobly borne — and fill them with floggings, shipwrecks, hunger, and an undignified escape in a laundry basket. He does not win the contest. He detonates it from the inside, which is a great deal more effective than refusing to play.

verseByVerse.quote: For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.

The irony turns savage here, and it is aimed squarely at the congregation.

You gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves. He is throwing their own self-image back at them. Corinth prided itself on discernment — the earlier letter is full of their confidence about knowledge and wisdom. And these connoisseurs have been sitting happily under men Paul has just called servants of Satan.

Then verse 20, and it is a list of five things they have put up with. Read them slowly, because Paul is not speaking in generalities; this is what was happening in that room.

Makes slaves of you. Someone had taken control — over consciences, over decisions, over what could be questioned.

Devours you. The word is used of eating something up. It is about money: these teachers were consuming the church’s resources. The Lord used the same word of the scribes who devour widows’ houses (Mk. 12:40).

Takes advantage of you. Catches you, as with bait — exploitation dressed as ministry.

Puts on airs. Literally, lifts himself up. The manner of a man who has let it be known that he is a considerable person.

Strikes you in the face. And here the list stops being metaphorical. Somebody had physically hit a member of that congregation, and the congregation had borne it.

That is the whole indictment: a church that would not tolerate an apostle who worked with his hands, and did tolerate a man who slapped them.

It is worth asking why, because the pattern has never gone away and it is not obvious. Why do people submit to domineering leaders and resent gentle ones?

Part of the answer is that confidence is easily mistaken for authority, and a man who behaves as if he has the right to treat you badly creates the impression that he must have it. Part of it is that being under a strong figure relieves the burden of thinking. And part of it is simply that harshness feels like seriousness, so a leader who is hard on people seems more committed to the truth than one who is gentle.

Set the list beside 1:24 — not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy — and the two portraits could not be further apart. One of these men founded the church and refused its money; the others enslaved it, ate it, and struck it. The Corinthians could not tell which was the apostle.

verseByVerse.quote: To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!
verseByVerse.commentary:
To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!

One line, and it is the sharpest sentence in the letter.

The tone is impossible to miss. Paul has just listed five ways the Corinthians have been mistreated, and now, with mock contrition, he apologises for never having managed any of them. To my shame — I am sorry to say — we were too weak for that. Too weak to enslave you. Too weak to eat your money. Too feeble to hit anyone.

It is sarcasm, and it is worth noting that Scripture contains it. Elijah used it on the prophets of Baal (perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened, 1 Kgs. 18:27); the Lord used it on the Pharisees more than once. It is a legitimate instrument, and like most sharp instruments it is safe only in particular hands and for particular purposes.

Notice what makes Paul’s use of it defensible. It is not aimed at the weak; it is aimed at people in comfortable error who have stopped listening to plain speech. It is used to defend others rather than himself — the ones being enslaved and struck are the ones he is speaking for. And it comes after eleven chapters of tenderness, so nobody could mistake it for his settled attitude. Sarcasm from a man who is habitually gentle is a shock; from a habitually sharp man it is just his manner, and it accomplishes nothing.

Underneath the irony is a real definition of strength, and it is the thing the Corinthians had inverted. They had read Paul’s refusal to dominate as weakness. He is showing them what that judgment commits them to: if refusing to exploit people is weakness, then exploitation is strength, and the men who had been eating them alive were the strong ones. Say it out loud and the position collapses, which is exactly why he says it out loud.

Real strength, in this letter, is the capacity to be wronged and not retaliate, to hold power and decline to use it, to be thought a fool rather than manipulate people into a better opinion. It is the strength of a Lord who could have called twelve legions of angels and did not open his mouth.

And there is a question in it for anyone who has ever confused the two. Think of the leaders you have found most impressive. Was it the force of the personality, or the restraint? The Corinthians got this exactly wrong, in a room where the difference was obvious, with an apostle in front of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.

The fool’s speech begins in earnest, and the rhythm is a drumbeat: three questions, three identical answers.

So the rivals were Jewish, and were making something of it. Each of the three words carries a different weight, and Paul takes them in order.

Hebrews is the language and culture claim — not merely Jewish by birth but Hebrew-speaking, raised in the tradition rather than assimilated into the Greek world. Paul was entitled to it; he tells the Philippians he was a Hebrew of Hebrews, and Luke records him addressing a Jerusalem crowd in Aramaic to their evident surprise (Acts 21:40–22:2).

Israelites is the covenant claim — members of the people God chose, to whom belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law (Rom. 9:4).

Offspring of Abraham is the promise claim — heirs of the man to whom God swore that in him all nations would be blessed.

Paul matches them three times without elaborating, and the flatness of the repetition is doing the work. He is refusing to make a speech about it. Whatever they have, he has, and there is nothing more to say.

What is striking is what he does not do here, and it is worth pausing on. Elsewhere, when the same credentials were being used to bind Gentile Christians to the law, he took them apart completely — listed his own pedigree in full and then said whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ… I count them as rubbish (Phil. 3:7–8). He is capable of dismantling this whole category and has done it.

He does not do it here because it is not the issue. The rivals are not, as far as we can tell, demanding circumcision; they are trading on prestige. So Paul simply refuses them the advantage and moves on to the ground where the real difference lies.

And that is the shape of the whole passage. A contest of credentials always ends in a tie, because credentials are the sort of thing that can be matched. The Corinthians were weighing two sets of qualifications and were going to be persuaded by whoever had the better list. Paul is about to show them that the question was never what a man has been given, but what he has been willing to lose.

verseByVerse.quote: Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one — I am talking like a madman — with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.

The fourth question breaks the pattern. The first three got so am I; this one gets I am a better one, and Paul immediately interrupts himself to say he has gone too far.

I am talking like a madman. The word is stronger than fool — he has moved from foolishness to raving. He can hear himself, and he is appalled.

But he does not take it back, because it is true and the situation requires it. What he does instead is define what he means, and the definition is the turn the whole chapter has been building toward.

A better servant of Christ, Paul says, and then produces his evidence: far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.

Stop and see what has just happened to the argument. Everyone in that room expected the sentence to continue with achievements — churches planted, miracles worked, revelations received, cities won. He had all of those and could have listed them. He lists what has been done to him.

The word servant is diakonos — the ordinary word for someone who waits at table. And Paul’s claim is that the measure of such a man is not what he has accomplished but what he has absorbed. Anyone can serve while it is rewarding. The test is what is left when it costs.

Four items, and each is an intensifier: far greater, far more, countless, often. He has lost count of the beatings. That is not a figure of speech; a man remembers the first three and stops numbering after that.

Which puts a question to every assessment of Christian service that any of us makes, including of ourselves. We measure by output, because output can be counted and photographed. Paul measures by cost. On his accounting, the most useful servant in a congregation may well be someone with nothing whatever to show — who has kept turning up, kept forgiving, kept praying for a family member for thirty years, and has been quietly worn down by it.

And the accounting is not arbitrary. It is the shape of the Master. The Lord’s own ministry, measured by output at the moment it ended, was a failure: three years, a handful of followers, and every one of them gone by Friday morning. What he had was what had been done to him — and it saved the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;

Now the numbers, and they should be read slowly rather than skimmed as a list.

Five times… the forty lashes less one. This is the synagogue punishment. The law permitted forty strokes and no more (Deut. 25:3); Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could never break the command. The victim was bound to a post, stripped to the waist, and struck with a triple-thonged whip — thirteen strokes to the chest, twenty-six to the back. Men died of it. The Mishnah provides for the possibility.

Five times. That is 195 strokes. And it is worth grasping what each one meant beyond the pain: this was the punishment a synagogue administered to its own. To receive it, Paul had to have submitted himself to the synagogue’s jurisdiction — walked in, again, knowing what had happened the last four times, because his own people were there and he would not stop going to them first.

Three times I was beaten with rods. This is the Roman punishment, and it was illegal to inflict it on a Roman citizen. Paul was one, and said so at Philippi — after the beating (Acts 16:37). Acts records that occasion; the other two are nowhere in the New Testament.

Once I was stoned. Lystra. The crowd stoned him and dragged him out of the city supposing he was dead — and he got up and went back into the town (Acts 14:19–20).

Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea. None of these is the famous shipwreck of Acts 27, which had not happened yet. So there were four. And that short clause covers twenty-four hours in open water, alone, waiting.

Notice how much of this the New Testament does not record. Acts gives us one beating out of three and none of the floggings. We have a book about Paul that leaves out most of what happened to him.

Which is worth remembering when you read Christian biography, or measure your own life against what other people report. The account you have of anyone is partial, and the parts that were hardest are usually the parts left out. There are people in your church carrying things that would not appear in any summary of their lives, and the God who kept the real record has not mislaid a single stroke of it.

verseByVerse.quote: on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.

The word danger eight times in a single verse, hammered without a connective. It is the sound of a man reciting a life.

The first two are the ordinary hazards of ancient travel and they were not small. Rivers — unbridged fords, flash floods in the mountain passes of Asia Minor. Robbers — the roads between cities were policed thinly or not at all, and a man carrying a collection for Jerusalem was worth stopping.

Then the list turns human, and it covers everybody. Danger from my own people. Danger from Gentiles. There was no group on earth among whom Paul was safe.

Then geography, and it is total: in the city, in the wilderness, at sea. The three places a person can be. He is saying there was nowhere.

And then the last one, held to the end because it is the worst: danger from false brothers.

Everything before this could be seen coming. A man knows to watch the river, the road, the mob. What cannot be guarded against is the person inside the fellowship who is not what he appears — who is in the meetings, who prays with you, and who is working against you. Paul puts it last in a list that includes being stoned to death and left in the road.

Anyone who has been betrayed by someone inside the church will not need this explained. It is a distinct species of wound, and the reason it goes deeper than persecution is that persecution comes from outside the family and this does not. The psalmist knew it: it is not an enemy who taunts me — then I could bear it… but it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend (Ps. 55:12–13). And the Lord knew it, from a man who had eaten with him for three years.

Then verse 27 turns from danger to the grinding daily conditions, and these are almost harder to admire because there is nothing dramatic in them. Toil. Sleepless nights. Hunger and thirst. Cold and exposure — the last word means without adequate clothing.

No single item here would make a story. This is simply what the life was like on an ordinary week: tired, hungry, and cold. Most Christian faithfulness looks far more like verse 27 than verse 25, and it is the verse-27 sort that wears people out.

verseByVerse.quote: And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.

After the floggings, the stoning, the shipwrecks and the nights in the open, Paul says: and apart from all that, here is what actually weighs on me.

The word for pressure means something set upon a person, a crowd pressing in. And daily — this one does not stop when the ship reaches harbour or the bruises heal. It was there this morning.

Then the word he chooses for what he carries: merimna. It is exactly the word the Lord used when he said do not be anxious about your life (Matt. 6:25), and Paul used when he told the Philippians to be anxious about nothing (Phil. 4:6).

So is this sin? It is worth answering carefully, because a great many faithful people are quietly condemned by the question.

The anxiety Scripture forbids is the fretting of a person who does not believe he is provided for — worry about food and clothing and tomorrow, carried by someone who has forgotten he has a Father. What Paul describes here is not about himself at all. It is the weight of caring what becomes of other people. That is not a failure of faith; it is what love feels like when the people you love are at risk and out of reach.

The two can be told apart, and the test is what the concern is about and where it goes. Is it fear for yourself, or care for someone else? And does it drive you to God or in circles? Paul’s went to God and then to a boat; he crossed a sea because he could not bear not knowing (2:13).

And notice the reach of it: all the churches. Not the one he was in. Every congregation he had ever planted, scattered across four provinces, most of them out of contact, several of them in trouble he could do nothing about from where he was.

This is the hidden half of pastoral work and it is invisible by nature. Nobody sees it. It does not appear in any report. It is the elder awake at two in the morning over a family that is coming apart; the Sunday school teacher who cannot stop thinking about one particular child; the pastor who carries a dozen private disasters that he may not discuss with anyone. There is no metric for it, and it is most of the job.

Paul lists it as a suffering, alongside the whip and the sea. He was right to. And the Lord who said my sheep hear my voice, and I know them carries every one of those churches still, without a night’s sleep lost and without losing one.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.

Two questions, and they explain where the daily pressure of the previous verse comes from.

Who is weak, and I am not weak? He is describing a man with no protective distance at all. When a believer somewhere is struggling — with doubt, with temptation, with a conscience troubled about food offered to idols — Paul does not counsel them from a position of strength. He goes down with them. He had told this church he would give up meat permanently rather than trip one weak brother (1 Cor. 8:13).

Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? The second verb is stronger — literally, I burn. When someone is tripped up, especially by a false teacher, something in Paul catches fire.

Hold the two together, because they are the anatomy of a pastor’s heart and they are not in tension. Tenderness toward the person who is struggling; heat toward whatever is causing the struggle. Get those the wrong way round — hard on the weak, relaxed about what is damaging them — and you have the exact inversion the Corinthians had achieved, tolerating men who devoured them and criticising the apostle who would not take their money.

It is worth testing yourself on. Where does your anger actually go? Most of us find it easier to be irritated by the struggling person — the one who keeps failing, keeps asking, keeps needing — than by whatever is doing the damage. Paul’s reflexes ran the other way, and they were trained by watching how his Lord treated the crowds: he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, and it was the shepherds who got the woe.

Then verse 30, and it is the sentence the whole fool’s speech has been climbing toward: If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.

The contest is over and Paul has changed the currency. His opponents boasted of strength; he will boast of the opposite, and not as a rhetorical trick. He means it, and chapter 12 will explain why — because weakness is where the power of Christ rests.

Which is the reversal at the centre of this letter and of the gospel it serves. The world counts what a man can do. God has arranged matters so that his power is displayed at exactly the point where a man can do nothing — in a clay pot, in a beaten apostle, in a crucified Messiah. There has never been a moment when he needed anyone’s strength, and there has never been a weakness he could not fill.

verseByVerse.quote: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me, but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me, but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.

Paul swears an oath, and then tells a story about a basket.

Take the oath first, because its placement is strange. He has just finished the catalogue — the floggings, the stoning, the shipwrecks — and he calls God as witness that none of it is invented. Why would he need to? Because the whole passage is so far outside what anyone expects a man to boast about that it might be read as rhetoric. He is saying: this is not a device. It happened.

And notice the title: the God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever. Even mid-oath, in the middle of the most bitter passage he ever wrote, the doxology comes out of him almost by reflex.

Then the story, and it is deliberately, almost comically, anticlimactic.

This is his first escape as a Christian, from Acts 9. Newly converted, preaching in the synagogues of Damascus that Jesus is the Son of God, and the authorities are watching the gates. So the disciples put him in a basket — the word suggests a large woven hamper, the kind used for hay or provisions — and lower him through a window in the wall at night, like a delivery.

Consider it as the climax of a boast. The ancient convention had a name for what belongs here: the crowning honour. Roman soldiers had one — the corona muralis, the wall crown, given to the first man over the wall of a besieged city. Paul’s wall story is a man going the other way, down, in a basket, hiding.

That is the joke, and it is a serious one. He has taken the highest military honour available in his world and inverted it. This is what an apostle’s glory looks like: not first over the wall, but lowered out of a window in a laundry basket because otherwise he would be killed.

And of all the incidents he could have chosen to end on, he chose the beginning — the very first thing that happened after Damascus. It set the pattern for everything that followed. The man who would carry the gospel across the empire left his first city as freight.

Which is finally what this whole ridiculous, painful chapter has been for. Christ does not recruit the impressive and he does not need them. He takes a man out of a window in a basket, and thirty years of floggings later the churches he planted are still standing, and the empire that beat him is gone, and the name he preached is known in every country on earth. The glory was never his. It never had to be.
