12.title: The Thorn in the Flesh and Power in Weakness
12.overview:
Chapter 12 contains one of the most personal and theologically significant passages in all of Paul’s letters: the account of his thorn in the flesh (vv. 7–10). It comes framed by an account of extraordinary visions and revelations — a man caught up to the third heaven, to paradise, who heard things that cannot be told — and the divine comment on that extraordinary experience: a thorn was given, a messenger of Satan, to keep Paul from being too elated. The word that comes to him in response to his three-fold prayer for its removal is the word that defines the entire letter: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”

This verse is the theological centre of 2 Corinthians. Every theme of the letter leads to it: the comfort in affliction (ch. 1), the treasure in jars of clay (ch. 4), the outer wasting/inner renewal (ch. 4), the surpassing power that belongs to God and not to us (ch. 4) — all of these are specifications of the principle that divine power is made perfect precisely in the vessel that is clearly insufficient by human standards. Paul’s response to this word is one of the most counter-cultural statements in Scripture: “Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Thorn in the Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul speaks of a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven (vv. 1–3) — and describes him in the third person, a rhetorical distancing device that he drops in v. 7 when he says “to keep me from becoming conceited.” The vision is real; the experience is real; but he was told things that cannot be told and man may not utter (v. 4), and he will not boast in any of it directly — only in his weaknesses (v. 5). Verse 6 gives his reason and it is one of the most quietly impressive sentences in the New Testament: he refrains “so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.” He is deliberately withholding true information about himself in order to keep other people’s estimate of him accurate.

The visions and revelations were so surpassing that a countermeasure was necessary: a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, to harass him (v. 7). The thorn (skolops tē sarki) is one of the most discussed exegetical questions in the Pauline letters. Proposals include: a chronic illness (possibly malaria, epilepsy, an eye condition — Gal. 4:15 suggests an eye problem); the opposition and persecution he constantly faced; a spiritual adversary. The medical interpretation has the longest history: skolops can refer to a sharp stake or a splinter; “in the flesh” (tē sarki) suggests something physical. The uncertainty is probably deliberate: had Paul named it, every sufferer with a different affliction would be shut out of the passage. Whatever it was, it was painful, persistent, and apparently incurable — Paul prayed three times for its removal (v. 8) and was refused.

The divine answer to his prayer is not the removal of the thorn but the provision of a word (v. 9): “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” The tense is a present indicative — not “will be sufficient” or “has been sufficient” but “is sufficient.” In this moment, in this weakness, grace is sufficient. And the power made perfect in weakness is not Paul’s own power strengthened but Christ’s power — the power that rests on Paul as the glory settled on the tabernacle. Paul’s response: “I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.”

Verse 10 draws the conclusion and is the summit of the section: “For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.” The qualifier for the sake of Christ governs the whole sentence and guards it from becoming something unhealthy: Paul does not take pleasure in suffering itself but in what it is for and in who meets him inside it. The then is a hinge — not although I am weak but when I am weak, at that moment, precisely there.
verseByVerse.theology:
The phrase “power is made perfect in weakness” (hē gar dynamis en astheneia teleitai) is the theological summit of the letter. The verb teleitai (is made perfect/completed) is from the root telos — the goal, the completion. Divine power achieves its intended perfection/completion in the context of human weakness. This is not simply a compensation for weakness (“when you can’t do it, God will”) but a statement about the natural habitat of divine power: it is when human resources are exhausted that the divine power is most purely displayed. The implication is not that Christians should cultivate weakness artificially but that they should not be surprised or ashamed when their weakness becomes the occasion for the display of a power that is clearly not theirs.

The three-fold prayer (v. 8) and the divine refusal is one of the clearest statements in the NT that God’s answer to prayer is sometimes “no, but here is something better.” Paul prayed earnestly, repeatedly, and specifically. The thorn was not removed. But what was given instead — a word of grace, an experience of Christ’s power — was worth more than the removal would have been. The “no” was a deeper “yes.”
verseByVerse.examples: A woman with a chronic pain condition has prayed for healing for years. She has been to healing services; she has been told that her lack of healing indicates insufficient faith. This passage speaks directly to her: the greatest apostle prayed three times for the removal of his thorn and was refused. The word he received instead was not a failure of faith but a revelation of grace. “My grace is sufficient for you” is not a consolation prize; it is a gift that the removal of the thorn would not have given him.

verseByVerse.quote: I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.

He is still apologising. Three times now he has stopped to say that what he is doing is foolish, and here he says it is also useless: there is nothing to be gained by it.

I must go on. The word carries compulsion — it is necessary, I am obliged. Nobody would guess from the tone that he is about to describe the most extraordinary spiritual experience recorded of any Christian in the New Testament.

And that reluctance is the first thing to notice, because it is the whole point of the passage. Paul is about to play his highest card, and he does it with visible distaste, having told us in advance that it proves nothing.

Why raise it at all? Because his rivals almost certainly were. Everything about the way he introduces the subject — visions and revelations of the Lord — suggests he is following their agenda rather than setting his own. In a religious culture fascinated by ecstatic experience, a man who could describe an encounter with the heavenly world had credentials nobody could check and everybody envied.

So Paul produces one, and immediately disarms it.

There is something here worth carrying into any age that prizes spiritual experience, and ours does as much as Corinth did. Experiences cannot be verified from outside. Nobody can check whether you heard from God in the night, and nobody can contradict you. Which means that in any contest of spirituality, the person willing to describe the most remarkable inner life wins, and there is no way to test the claim.

Paul knows this, and refuses to compete on the ground where nothing can be tested. His credentials in this letter have been things anybody could verify: a church that exists, a body with scars on it, an empty purse, a life spent in the open. He is about to add a vision, under protest, and then take it away again.

And notice the phrase he uses for the whole exercise: nothing to be gained by it. He does not mean the vision was worthless to him. He means it is worth nothing as an argument. It did not make him a better servant of Christ; the thorn that came with it did rather more, as he is about to explain.

Which is a good deal of humility to find in a man who had been to paradise. Whatever happened to Paul fourteen years earlier, he had carried it for fourteen years without telling this church about it, and the only reason it appears in the Bible at all is that some impressive men in Corinth left him no choice.

verseByVerse.quote: I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows. And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—
verseByVerse.commentary:
I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven — whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows. And I know that this man was caught up into paradise — whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows —

He tells it in the third person, and everybody has always known why.

A man in Christ. He keeps that up for four verses and then gives himself away in verse 7, when he explains that the thorn was given to keep me from becoming conceited. It is Paul. The distance is deliberate — a way of describing the experience without standing next to it and taking the credit.

Fourteen years ago. Count back from the writing of this letter and it lands somewhere in the silent years, after Damascus and before the first missionary journey — the long stretch in Tarsus and Syria that Acts passes over in a sentence. And he has said nothing about it since.

Let that register. Fourteen years of silence about the most remarkable thing that ever happened to him. If it had been the making of his authority he would have led with it in every city. It appears once, under duress, in a passage he calls foolish.

Now, what is the third heaven? Jewish writers of the period commonly spoke of the heavens in layers, and Paul is using the language of his own world rather than teaching cosmology. The first heaven is the sky where the birds are; the second, the sky where the stars are; the third is the dwelling of God himself. He is saying he was taken all the way in. And verse 3 confirms it with a second name: paradise — the word used of the garden in Eden, and the word the Lord used to the dying thief.

Caught up is a strong passive verb — seized, snatched. It happened to him. He did not achieve it by technique, discipline or preparation, which is worth saying in every generation that has produced a method for arranging such things.

And then the phrase he repeats twice, which is the most striking part: whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows.

He was there and he cannot tell you the mechanics. The one man in Scripture who could have written an authoritative account of the geography of heaven says twice that he does not know what happened to him.

Set that beside the confident detail of most modern accounts of visits to the afterlife, and the contrast is instructive. The apostle’s report is short, reluctant, third-hand by choice, and full of admitted ignorance. Certainty about the unseen world tends to be inversely proportional to how much of it a person has actually seen.

verseByVerse.quote: and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter. On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—
verseByVerse.commentary:
and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter. On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses —

Two things happened in paradise, and Paul reports only that they happened.

He heard things that cannot be told. The phrase is doubled for emphasis and the two halves are not the same. Cannot be told — unspeakable, beyond the capacity of language. Which man may not utter — not permitted, forbidden. So there are two reasons for the silence: some of it could not be put into words, and some of it was not allowed to be.

That second reason is the more arresting. Paul was given something and told not to pass it on. Whatever he heard was for him, and the church has never had it.

Which is a useful thing to know when someone claims a private revelation that must be received on their authority alone. God does sometimes give a person something meant for them only — and the mark of the genuine article here is that Paul never traded on it. He did not build a following on the strength of what he could not disclose. Fourteen years of not mentioning it is the most persuasive detail in the account.

And it tells us something about Scripture as well. God has not told us everything he could have told us. There are things about heaven, about providence, about the future, that were available and were withheld. The Bible is not a complete transcript of what God knows; it is what he judged his people needed. The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us (Deut. 29:29). A great deal of unhappiness comes from demanding the first half.

Then verse 5, and here is the reason for the whole third-person device: On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses.

He has split himself in two. The man who was caught up to paradise — that man he will boast about, because everything that happened to him was received. The man writing the letter, the one his readers know, the one with the scars and the tent-making hands — about him Paul will boast only in what shows how weak he is.

It is not false modesty. It is an accurate division. What was given to him is God’s to be proud of; what he actually is, is a clay pot. And the split explains something about how Christians should hold their own best moments: the times when God has plainly been at work in you are worth speaking about, and they are not your credentials, because you did not produce them.

verseByVerse.quote: though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.

A careful sentence, and the care is the point.

First he protects the truthfulness of what he has said: if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth. He is not retracting the vision or hedging it. It happened. He could describe it and every word would be accurate.

Then: but I refrain from it. The verb means to spare, to hold back. And the reason he gives is one of the most quietly impressive things in the New Testament.

So that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.

Read that slowly. Paul is deliberately withholding true information about himself in order to keep people’s opinion of him accurate. He wants to be assessed on what is visible: what he says, what he does, how he lives. Not on a reputation built out of things that cannot be checked.

Consider how far that runs against the grain. All of us manage what people know about us, and the management almost always runs the other way — we curate what is impressive and quietly omit the rest. Paul has the most impressive item any Christian has ever had, and he is suppressing it precisely because it would inflate him beyond what a person could verify by watching.

And notice the standard he is willing to be judged by: what he sees in me or hears from me. That is a hard offer to make. It means no allowance for the private hours, the hidden devotion, the experiences nobody witnessed. Judge the visible man.

Which supplies a test, and it is uncomfortable in an age built on presentation. Is the impression people have of you larger than the reality they could observe? Every one of us has some gap; the question is whether we are working to close it or to widen it. The gap is where disappointment lives, and it is the reason so many admired people are a grief to those who actually live with them.

There is a mercy in Paul’s policy too, and it is worth seeing. A man who has arranged to be over-estimated must then maintain the estimate, and the maintenance is exhausting and never finishes. Paul has spared himself all of it. He is exactly what he appears to be, which is why he can write a letter admitting he despaired of life, was too anxious to preach, and left his first city in a basket — none of which costs him anything, because nobody was ever asked to think otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.

Now the thorn, and the sentence is built with a repetition that cannot be accidental: the purpose clause appears twice, at both ends. To keep me from becoming conceited… to keep me from becoming conceited. Paul bookends the verse with the reason, as though the danger were so real it needed saying on both sides of the affliction.

What was it? The honest answer is that nobody knows, and the guessing has gone on for nineteen centuries. The word skolops means a sharpened stake or a splinter — something driven in. In the flesh suggests the body. The main proposals: a chronic illness of some kind; an eye complaint, since he tells the Galatians they would have torn out their eyes and given them to him, and he writes in large letters (Gal. 4:15; 6:11); recurring malaria; some disfiguring condition that made him hard to listen to; or the relentless human opposition that dogged him everywhere.

The uncertainty is almost certainly deliberate. Had Paul named it, every sufferer with a different affliction would have been shut out of the passage. As it stands, whatever is driven into your flesh fits the gap.

Then the double description, and it is the theological heart of the verse. The thorn is a messenger of Satan to harass me — and it was given.

Hold both. The word for messenger is angelos; the harassment is real and it comes from the enemy. And the verb was given is the divine passive: the giver is God. One event, two agents, two entirely different purposes. Satan sends it to wreck a man. God permits it to save him from something worse.

This is the shape of Job, where the accuser is on a leash and the leash is held; and of Joseph, who told his brothers you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20); and supremely of the cross, where the worst thing anyone ever did was the thing by which God saved the world.

And note what God was protecting Paul from. Not failure. Not danger. Conceit. The apostle had been to the third heaven, and the risk attached to that was that he would become insufferable — and an insufferable Paul would have been no use to anybody. So the affliction is not the price of the revelation; it is the provision that made the revelation survivable.

Which is worth holding if you carry something that will not go away. The thing you would most like removed may be the thing keeping you usable. It is a hard thought and it is not one to say to anyone else. Paul says it about himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.

One line, and it is the verse that keeps a great many Christians in the faith.

Three times. Not a passing mention in his devotions. Three sustained seasons of asking, and the number is probably significant — the Lord himself prayed three times in Gethsemane about a cup he wanted removed.

I pleaded. The verb is parakaleō again — the great word of this letter, which has meant comfort throughout and here means to beg. He is not making a polite request. He is imploring.

With the Lord. Worth noticing: Paul’s prayers here are addressed to Jesus, which he does rarely and which tells you something about who he understood him to be.

That it should leave me. Specific, definite, unambiguous. He knew exactly what he wanted and he asked for exactly that.

And the answer was no.

Every element that is supposed to guarantee an answered prayer is present here. The man praying is an apostle. The request is not selfish — a healthy Paul could serve more churches. There is no unconfessed sin, no lack of faith, no failure to persevere; he came back three times. And the thorn stayed.

That has to be said plainly, because a great deal of teaching implies otherwise, and the people it damages are not the strong. There are believers who have been told that healing is theirs if they can muster the faith for it, and who have concluded, after years, that the fault is in them. Some have stopped praying. Some have stopped believing. This verse was written for them. The greatest Christian who ever lived prayed three times for the removal of an affliction and was told no, and the refusal is recorded in Scripture as a mercy rather than a failure.

Notice also that Paul stopped at three. He did not conclude that persistence was the missing ingredient and press on to three hundred. He asked, he received an answer, and the answer settled it. There is a kind of prayer that will not accept a reply, and it is not greater faith; it is a refusal to let God be God.

What changed was not the circumstance but the man, and what changed him was not the passage of time. It was a word — one sentence, given in reply, which he carried for the rest of his life and which the church has been living on ever since.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

Here is the answer, and it is the summit of the letter.

Begin with the tense, because it is doing more work than any other word in the sentence. My grace is sufficient for you. Not will be, when things get worse. Not has been, looking back. It is sufficient — present, continuous, already true in the moment the thorn is still going in.

The word sufficient means enough, adequate to the need. It is not a promise of abundance or of relief. It is a promise that there will always be exactly as much as is required, and that the supply will not run out before the trouble does.

And notice what was not said. There is no explanation. God does not tell Paul what the thorn is for beyond the one clause of verse 7, does not say how long, does not promise eventual removal. He gives him himself. That is the whole answer.

Then the reason, and it turns the universe over: for my power is made perfect in weakness. The verb is from the root meaning to reach a goal, to be completed. Divine power does not merely cope with human weakness; it comes to its full expression there. Weakness is not the obstacle power has to work around. It is the place power was always heading for.

Guard it from one misreading. This is not a call to cultivate weakness, to refuse medicine, or to make a virtue of incapacity. Paul prayed for removal, three times, and was right to. It means that when the weakness does not lift, you have not been shut out of God’s power. You have been placed exactly where it does its clearest work.

Then Paul’s response, and the word to watch is gladly. Not I will accept my weaknesses. Not I will endure them. I will boast all the more gladly. Something has been so thoroughly reversed in him that the thing he begged to lose has become the thing he is pleased to have.

And the last phrase gives the reason, and it is worth ending on because it is a picture rather than an argument. So that the power of Christ may rest upon me — the verb means to pitch a tent over. It is the word behind the glory that settled on the tabernacle in the wilderness, and behind John’s the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

So the weakness is not merely tolerated. It is the ground the tent is pitched on. Where a man is emptied out, the glory of God comes down and settles, and stays. That is what the thorn was for, and it is what every unhealed affliction in the life of a believer is being turned to. He did not take it away. He came and lived on it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.

The word to start with is content. The Greek is stronger than the English — it means to take pleasure in, to be well pleased. It is the word the Father uses at the baptism: with whom I am well pleased.

Then five things he is pleased with, and they are not a poetic list. Weaknesses — his own incapacity. Insults — the outrages done to him by people, including the men in Corinth calling him contemptible. Hardships — necessity, the grinding pressure of not enough. Persecutions — being hunted. Calamities — the word means being squeezed into a narrow place with no way out.

Nobody enjoys any of these, and Paul is not claiming to. Notice the qualifier that governs the whole sentence: for the sake of Christ. He does not take pleasure in suffering. He takes pleasure in what the suffering is for and in who meets him inside it. Take Christ out of the sentence and it becomes something unhealthy; leave him in and it is the most liberated sentence in the letter.

That distinction has to be kept, because Christianity has repeatedly produced people who sought out affliction as though the pain itself were holy. It is not. Paul prayed to have his removed. What he learned was not to love the thorn but to love what the thorn made room for.

Then the paradox, stated as flatly as it can be: when I am weak, then I am strong.

It is not a play on words. Both halves are literal, and the then is a hinge — not although I am weak but when I am weak, at that moment, precisely there. The strength is not his own returning; it is Christ’s power tabernacling on the empty ground of verse 9.

Which is a genuinely different account of the Christian life from the one most of us carry about. We assume God uses us in proportion to what we bring — that the more competent, the more resourced, the more spiritually together we are, the more useful. This verse says the arithmetic runs the other way at exactly the point where our resources fail.

And it is worth testing against your own history rather than resisting it in the abstract. Think of the times you have been most obviously useful to another person. It is very rarely the season when you were flourishing. It is nearly always the time when you had been through the thing they are going through now, and had nothing to offer but that.

The whole letter has been circling this. The treasure is in clay so the power is plainly God’s (4:7). The captive is the one in the triumph (2:14). The Lord of glory became poor (8:9), and was crucified in weakness — and it is the one event in history that has changed everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — Signs of Apostleship and Pastoral Fears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul closes the fool’s speech with the acknowledgment that he has been a fool to boast (v. 11) — but the Corinthians forced him to it, since they should have commended him and did not. He is not inferior to the super-apostles, even though he is nothing; both halves of that sentence are true at once. The signs of a true apostle were performed among them (v. 12): signs, wonders, and mighty works — but note the phrase attached, “with utmost patience,” which is the qualifier his rivals could not match. The only thing in which they were less favoured than other churches was that he refused to take financial support from them (v. 13), and he asks the ironic question: forgive me this wrong.

He is coming a third time and the policy will not change (v. 14), because “I seek not what is yours but you” — six words that draw the line between a shepherd and a hireling — and because parents save up for children, not children for parents. He speaks now as a father, not as an apostle with terms. Verse 15 is the great statement of pastoral love and of pastoral loneliness in one breath: “I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?” To spend is to lay out what you have; to be spent is to be laid out yourself, used up — and the adverb is most gladly.

A new accusation surfaces in vv. 16–18: unable to deny Paul’s personal financial integrity, his opponents claim it was a cover for embezzlement by proxy through Titus and the brother sent with him. The very transparency Paul built (8:20–21) has been turned into evidence of a more sophisticated fraud. His answer is not another protestation but a series of questions with names attached — did Titus take advantage of you? did we not take the same steps? — because a public record of consistent behaviour, with witnesses, is the only thing that answers an unfalsifiable charge.

Verse 19 then reframes the whole four chapters: they have not been a defence conducted before the Corinthians at all. “It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.” The audience is God; the purpose is their construction; and the last word of the sentence — beloved, used here for the first time in the letter — is the tone the whole passage was meant to be heard in.

The pastoral fears that close the chapter are deeply personal (vv. 20–21). Paul is coming for a third visit, and he fears what he might find — quarrelling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, disorder: eight relational sins that are the photographic negative of the fruit of the Spirit (Gal. 5:22–23), and every one of them survivable indefinitely by a congregation that would be horrified by anything more obvious. Note the twice-repeated perhaps: he is dreading a possibility, not pronouncing a verdict. And he fears what they might find: a Paul humbled before them, mourning over those who sinned earlier and have not repented. The man who catalogued third-heaven visions in vv. 1–6 is the same man who would weep over unrepentant sin in his congregation — not the administrator worried about institutional health, but the father who grieves over his children.
verseByVerse.theology: The “signs of a true apostle” (v. 12) — signs, wonders, mighty works — are offered not as the primary credential of Paul’s apostleship but as evidence that the Corinthians have already received from him what a true apostle gives. His primary credential, as the entire letter has argued, is the cruciform pattern of his ministry. The miraculous signs are additional evidence, not the foundation. This ordering matters: making miraculous signs the primary criterion for apostolic authenticity is precisely the error of the super-apostles.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation’s governing board is reviewing the annual ministry assessment and focusing entirely on measurable outcomes — attendance, baptisms, giving — as indicators of pastoral effectiveness. This passage suggests a broader criterion: has the ministry demonstrated the signs of true apostolic work (transformed lives, gospel truth, pastoral care), and has the minister borne the cruciform character that authentic ministry requires? The absence of spectacular growth does not disqualify; the absence of gospel integrity does.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.

The fool’s speech ends, and Paul steps out of the character with obvious relief. I have been a fool!

Then he says whose fault it was: You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. And that is the real grievance of the whole four chapters. They should have defended him. He founded that church, he was publicly humiliated in it, he was traduced by newcomers — and the people who owed him everything sat quietly. He should never have had to speak.

Anyone who has been left undefended by people who knew better will recognise the note. It is not the attack that wounds most; it is the silence of the ones who could have spoken and did not.

Then the two halves of verse 11, held together without embarrassment: I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing.

Both are true and neither cancels the other. Measured against the men impressing Corinth, he is not behind by a step. Measured in himself, he is nothing. That is not self-hatred; it is the settled realism of a man who wrote that our sufficiency is from God (3:5) and that the treasure is in a clay pot. A Christian can hold a very high view of what God has done through him and a very low view of his own contribution, at the same time, without either being false modesty.

Then verse 12, and it is the closest Paul comes to the credentials his rivals traded in: the signs of a true apostle were performed among you… with signs and wonders and mighty works.

So the miracles happened. He does not deny them, and this is one of the plainest statements in the New Testament that the apostles worked them. But look at where he has placed the fact: at the end of four chapters of weakness, mentioned once, in a single line, after the beatings and the basket and the thorn.

And look at the phrase attached to it: with utmost patience. The signs came wrapped in endurance. That is the qualifier his opponents could not match, and it is the one he puts first in the sentence. Power without patience is what they offered. Paul had both, and he lists the patience as the more significant of the two — because anyone can be impressive for an evening, and only a certain kind of man is still there eighteen months later, making tents.

verseByVerse.quote: For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong! Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong! Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

The irony has one more turn in it. In what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong!

It is bitter and it is funny, and the sarcasm is aimed at an accusation so absurd that stating it plainly is the best refutation available. The single respect in which Corinth received less than any other church Paul served is that he refused to take their money. He asks their pardon for it.

Then the announcement: here for the third time I am ready to come to you. The first visit founded the church; the second was the painful one; this will be the third. And the policy has not changed and will not: I will not be a burden.

And then the sentence that is the heart of pastoral ministry, and it should be written over every church door: I seek not what is yours but you.

Six words, and they draw the line between a shepherd and a hireling. The false teachers wanted what the Corinthians had — their money, their allegiance, their admiration, the standing that came from leading a well-known church. Paul wanted the Corinthians. Not what could be got from them. Them.

It is worth running as a test in both directions, because it exposes a great deal. Of anyone who ministers to you: does this person want you, or something you can supply? And of yourself, in whatever relationships you are the stronger party: is it the person you are after, or what they give you — the gratitude, the loyalty, the usefulness, the sense of being needed?

Then the reason, and it changes the whole register: children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

He has stopped arguing as an apostle and started speaking as a father. And the argument is simply how families work. A father does not present his children with an invoice. The flow of money in a household runs downhill, from the ones who have it to the ones who do not, and nobody regards it as a transaction.

That is how Paul saw his relationship with this difficult, ungrateful, easily-impressed congregation. Not a professional engagement with terms. A family, in which he was the one who paid — which is exactly the position taken by the Father who spared not his own Son, and who has never once sent anyone a bill.

verseByVerse.quote: I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?

Two sentences. The first is one of the great statements of Christian love; the second is one of the loneliest questions in the New Testament.

I will most gladly spend and be spent. The two verbs are the same root, active and passive, and the difference between them is everything. To spend is to lay out what you have — time, money, energy, effort. To be spent is to be laid out yourself: used up, exhausted, consumed in the process.

Anyone can spend for a while. Being spent is a different order of thing, and it is what actually happens to people who serve others for a long time. They do not merely give things away; they are gradually used up. The mother of a disabled child knows this. So does the man who has cared for his wife through a long decline, and the pastor at year twenty-five.

And the adverb is the astonishing part: most gladly. The superlative. Not willingly, not without complaint. He is delighted to be used up for them.

For your souls. Not for their approval, their project, or their good opinion. He is spending himself on what will still exist in a thousand years.

Then the question, and Paul lets it stand without answering it: If I love you more, am I to be loved less?

Something has gone wrong that everyone recognises. He has loved them more than any of the newcomers ever will, and it has cost him their affection. The men who exploited them are admired; the man who worked nights so as not to burden them is suspected.

It is a real pain and Paul does not pretend otherwise. But notice that the question does not become a threat or a withdrawal. He asks it, and then goes on loving them and announces he is coming again. Love that stops when it is not returned was something else all along.

And there is only one place this pattern comes from. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (Jn. 1:11). The one who loved most was loved least, and was spent entirely, and did it most gladly — for the joy that was set before him — for people who at the time were shouting for his death. Every servant of his who has loved and not been loved back is standing in a very old and very honourable place.

verseByVerse.quote: But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?

A new accusation, and it is the meanest one yet.

The logic runs like this. Paul’s personal integrity about money could not be denied — he had never taken a penny and the whole province knew it. So the charge mutated. Very well, he did not take it himself; that was the clever part. He was crafty and got the better of you by deceit — meaning that the Jerusalem collection was the real operation, and the money would be siphoned off through the men he sent.

Notice what has happened. The very transparency Paul built — the delegates chosen by the churches, the multiple overseers, the refusal to handle funds alone (8:20–21) — has been turned into evidence of a more sophisticated fraud. That is the nature of a certain kind of suspicion: it is unfalsifiable. Honesty becomes proof of cunning, and precaution becomes proof of something to hide.

Paul’s answer is not another protestation. It is a series of questions with names attached, and that is the only thing that works against an unfalsifiable charge. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent? Name one. Did Titus take advantage of you? They knew Titus. He had been among them twice; his conduct was a matter of public record and it was spotless.

Then the two closing questions, and they are quietly conclusive: Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps? The word for steps means footprints — walking in the same tracks. Paul and Titus behaved identically about money, and everyone had watched both of them do it.

That is the answer to a whispering campaign, and it is worth knowing because whispering campaigns have not gone out of fashion. You cannot disprove an insinuation by denying it; denial only spreads it. What answers it is a public record of consistent behaviour, and other people who have been seen behaving the same way in the same room.

Which is one more reason for the arrangements of chapter 8. Paul did not build that structure because he expected to be believed. He built it because he expected not to be — and when the accusation finally came, the answer was already years old and had witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.

Paul stops, and reframes the entire four chapters.

Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is the obvious reading, and he knows it; he has spent four chapters answering charges, matching credentials, listing sufferings and refuting accusations. Anyone would call that a defence.

He says it is not — or at least, that they are not the court.

It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ. There is the correction. He has not been standing in the dock before the Corinthians. He has been speaking with God as the audience, and the Corinthians have merely been in the room.

That single shift changes what all of it was. A man defending himself before people is managing an impression; everything he says is shaped by what will persuade them. A man speaking before God says what is true and lets the impression fall where it will — which is why these chapters contain so much that no advocate would ever have included. No one building a case mentions that he despaired of life, was too anxious to preach, is unimpressive in person, and left his first city in a basket.

And it explains the freedom running under the bitterness. Paul is not frightened of losing the verdict, because the verdict is not theirs to give. He said it at 4:5 and again at 10:18: the one who is approved is the one the Lord commends.

Then the purpose, and it is the second half of the correction: and all for your upbuilding, beloved.

Every word of it — the irony, the sarcasm, the catalogue of floggings, the fool’s speech he found so distasteful — was construction work on them. Not self-protection. He is back to 10:8: authority given for building up and not for destroying. Even the sharpest chapter in the letter was aimed at making them stronger.

And then the last word of the sentence, dropped in after everything: beloved.

It is the first time he has used it in the letter, and he saves it for here — after four chapters of conflict, addressed to the people who have doubted him, listened to his enemies, and left him to defend himself alone. That is the tone the whole passage was meant to be heard in, and he makes sure they cannot finish it without knowing so.

verseByVerse.quote: For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish — that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.

The chapter ends in fear, and it is worth noticing what Paul is and is not afraid of.

Twice he says I fear, and both times the word perhaps guards it. He is not predicting; he is dreading a possibility. That small word matters — he has not given up on them, and he will not describe their sin as settled before he has seen it.

Then the list of eight, and read as a group they are not the sins of a pagan city. They are the sins of a church. Quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, disorder. Every one of them is a relational sin, and every one is survivable indefinitely by a congregation that would be horrified by anything more obvious. Nobody is disciplined for gossip. Nobody leaves a church over conceit. And these eight are the exact photographic negative of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Gal. 5:22–23). Where the Spirit is not being followed, this list is what grows in the space.

Then verse 21, and it goes deeper. He is afraid that my God may humble me before you — that he will arrive and find the situation such that he is brought low in front of them. And then the specific dread: I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented.

The verb is the strong one — to grieve as at a death. Not to discipline them, though he will; not to be angry, though he might be. To mourn.

And the three sins named are the old Corinthian ones, the things the first letter dealt with: impurity, sexual immorality, sensuality. Some had never actually turned. The letter had been received, the crisis had been resolved, the church had come back to Paul — and underneath it, quietly, a number of people were still living exactly as they had been.

That is a sober note for any church that has come through a good season. Corporate reconciliation is not the same as individual repentance. A congregation can be genuinely restored at the level of its relationships and still contain people for whom nothing has changed at all.

But end where Paul does, on the word mourn. He is not looking forward to the confrontation and he is not sharpening his authority for it. The thought that keeps him awake is that he will have to weep. The apostle of the third heaven, who had been caught up into paradise and heard what may not be repeated, is afraid of arriving in a Greek port and finding people he loves unrepentant — and grieving over them the way a father grieves.

Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.<sup>2</sup>I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows.<sup>3</sup>And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—<sup>4</sup>and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter.<sup>5</sup>On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—<sup>6</sup>though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.<sup>7</sup>So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.<sup>8</sup>Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.<sup>9</sup>But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.<sup>10</sup>For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. 13.title: Self-Examination, Final Warnings, and the Grace Benediction
13.overview:
The final chapter of 2 Corinthians brings the letter to its conclusion with a series of warnings, an extraordinary call to self-examination, and the most famous benediction in the New Testament. Paul announces his coming third visit: “This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses.” He will not spare those who have sinned and not repented. He is not weak toward them: Christ is not weak in dealing with them but is powerful among them. The one crucified in weakness was raised in the power of God; Paul, who shares the weakness, also shares the power.

The call to self-examination (vv. 5–6) turns the tables on the Corinthians: they have been examining Paul, demanding proof that Christ speaks in him. Paul says: examine yourselves — test whether you are in the faith. This is not an invitation to doubt but a call to genuine self-knowledge. The Corinthians who know Christ is in them will recognise that Paul too is not disqualified. And Paul's ultimate desire is not that they recognise his authority but that they do what is right — even if it appears to disqualify him: “We cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.”

The letter ends with the Trinitarian benediction of v. 14 — “the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” — the most explicitly Trinitarian formula in the Pauline letters, placing all three persons in coordinate relation and ascribing to each a distinctive gift: grace (Christ), love (God the Father), fellowship (the Holy Spirit).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's announcement of his coming third visit carries the legal weight of Deuteronomy 19:15: every charge must be established by two or three witnesses. He has given a warning when present the second time; he is giving it again in writing now; when he comes, he will act. He is not weak toward them. The contrast with Christ is important: Christ was crucified in weakness but raised in power; Paul likewise, who shares Christ's weakness in his suffering, will also display the power of God when necessary. The weakness and the authority are both real and both derive from union with Christ.

The call to self-examination (vv. 5–6) is the most important pastoral move in the chapter. Rather than spending more time demanding that the Corinthians recognise his credentials, Paul redirects: examine yourselves. Test whether you are in the faith — ei este en tē pistei. The test he suggests: do you recognise that Christ is in you? If Christ is in you, then you can recognise the evidence of Christ in Paul. The sceptical Corinthians who demand proof of Paul's apostleship are being asked to first certify their own standing before God.
verseByVerse.theology: The call to self-examination (v. 5) has been used in Reformed tradition as the basis for the practice of self-examination before the Lord's Supper (1 Cor. 11:28–31). Genuine self-examination is not the cultivation of paralyzing doubt but the honest assessment of the soul before God: am I in the faith? Is Christ in me? Is my trust in Christ or in my own religious performance? The examination that produces assurance is the examination that finds Christ as the ground of hope, not the examination that finds sufficient personal righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation prepares for a communion service and the pastor leads a five-minute self-examination period before the elements are distributed. Some members treat it as a routine; others spiral into anxiety. This passage clarifies the goal: not to find sufficient personal holiness to “qualify” for the table, but to find whether Christ is there — whether the faith that receives him is genuine. The person who comes to the table trusting Christ is examining themselves correctly; the person who comes evaluating their performance has missed the point of both the examination and the table.

verseByVerse.quote: Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? — unless indeed you fail to meet the test!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peirazete heautous (examine/test yourselves) — the verb peirazō means to test with a view to proving, often used for testing metals for purity. The self-examination is not navel-gazing but quality assurance: is what I believe genuine faith, or is it religious habit, cultural Christianity, or self-deception? The criterion is not the absence of doubt or the presence of strong religious feeling but the recognition that “Jesus Christ is in you” — the indwelling Christ as the ground of assurance.

“We cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth” (v. 8) — one of Paul's most striking statements about the ultimate invincibility of the gospel. Paul's authority, his ministry, his entire apostolic enterprise is in the service of the truth; it cannot be wielded against it. This is the principle of ministerial accountability: the minister's authority is derived from and limited by the truth of the gospel. Any exercise of authority that contradicts the gospel is not legitimate authority but its perversion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Final Greetings and the Trinitarian Benediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul closes with a rapid series of imperatives: rejoice, aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace — and the promise: the God of love and peace will be with you. The holy kiss and greetings from the saints of Macedonia complete the personal frame.

The final benediction (v. 14) is the most explicitly Trinitarian formula in the Pauline letters: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.” Each person of the Trinity is named; each is given a distinctive gift. Grace (charis) is attributed to the Lord Jesus Christ — the undeserved favour that flows from his person and work. Love (agapē) is attributed to God the Father — the initiating, originating love that sent the Son (John 3:16; Rom. 5:8). Fellowship (koinōnia) is attributed to the Holy Spirit — the participation in the divine life, the communion with God and one another, that the Spirit creates and sustains.
verseByVerse.theology:
The benediction is not a formula but a theology: it presents the three persons in distinct but coordinated action, each contributing uniquely to the believer's life. The order (Christ, Father, Spirit) is unusual — the more common Pauline order puts the Father first — possibly because the letter's concerns have centred on the grace of Christ (the atonement of ch. 5, the self-giving of ch. 8). The coordinated action of all three persons in the single benediction is an implicit trinitarian claim: to receive grace, love, and fellowship from these three distinct persons is to receive from one God in three persons.

Koinōnia of the Holy Spirit — three possible meanings, all theologically valid: (1) the fellowship that the Spirit creates among believers; (2) participation in the Spirit — sharing in the Spirit's life; (3) the Spirit as the one who communicates fellowship with the Father and Son. These are not mutually exclusive; the Spirit's work achieves all three simultaneously. Those who are indwelt by the Spirit share in the divine koinōnia — the mutual love and life of the Trinity — and that sharing is expressed in genuine community with one another.
verseByVerse.examples: A church that closes every service with this benediction has been pronouncing it for decades as a familiar liturgical ending. A new pastor stops before pronouncing it and asks the congregation: do you know what you are about to receive? Each phrase is unpacked slowly — the grace that flows from Christ's cross, the love that originated in the Father's heart before creation, the fellowship that the Spirit creates both with God and among the gathered community. The familiar words suddenly land with the weight they have always carried. The benediction is not a farewell; it is a sending into the world with the fullness of the Triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The benediction formula is unique in Paul — no other letter has exactly this form, though the components appear throughout his writings (grace of Christ: Rom. 16:20; Gal. 6:18; Phil. 4:23; love of God: Rom. 8:39; fellowship of the Spirit: Phil. 2:1). The explicit coordination of all three persons in a single benedictive statement is the NT's clearest pre-Nicene articulation of what will become trinitarian doctrine.

“Be with you all” (meta pantōn hymōn) — the benediction is inclusive, even of those who have been resistant and challenging throughout the letter. Paul does not conclude with a blessing for the faithful and a warning for the recalcitrant; he extends the grace, love, and fellowship of the Triune God to the whole community. The Trinity does not play favourites; the grace that is sufficient for Paul's weakness is offered to the whole Corinthian church in all its messiness and division.
